YOUNG LADY (to gentleman who put his arm round her chair: "Does your arm pain you, sir?" Young Gent: "Not at all, miss; but why do you ask?" Young Lady: "I noticed that it was out of place, sir; that's all." "You say he called you a -donkey ?" "Yes." "What did you do about it ? " "Nothing." "Well, if a man should call me a donkey I'd kick him with both feet." Certainly, any donkey would naturally do that." -A LADY was called on by a poor woman, .who earnestly solicited a dispensary ticket. On the lady inquiring the nature of her ailment, the woman re- plied that she felt very bad all over; for Mr. Bun, the scripture reader, told her yesterday as how she had et a stony heart. "t WISH I were you for about two,hours," she said to her husband with great tenderness. "And why, my dear," he asked. - "Because," she said, toying affectionately with his watch chain, "because then I would buy my wife a new bonnet." . •

"You say your husband has a good memory,- do you, Mrs. Crimson ?" "Oh, excellent,' responded the lady addressed. "And how do you know it is so very good ?" "Well, I asked him to bring me home a mackerel a week ago, and he brought it home to-day." AT a spiritual seance a woman desired to com- municate with her dead husband. "Is it really such a dreadful place, John." "Not at all; heaven is a delightful place." "Mr. Medium," said the widow, turning to that personage, "you have called up the wrong party." THE late. Mr. Van homrigh, who represented. Drogheda in Parliament, was seized with a com- plaint which gave more concern to his friends than to himself. "How do you treat your inflam- mation, Mr. Van Homrigh ? " said a sedate member for one of the midiaaid counties. "Sir," answered Peter, I trate it with sovereign con- timpt.-' " THERE is good deal of religion in nature," solemnly remarked a young clergyman while call- ing upon a lady of his congregation the other evening. "There is," was the quiet reply. "We should never forget that there is a sermon in every blade of grass.' "Quite true. We should also remember that grass is cut very short at this season of the year." .PEEL is said to have once inquired of a warns admirer what he thought was the chief qualifi- cation of a Prime Minister. "I think," was the ready answer, "that he should have £2U,OOOa year." "No ! no ! " exposrulated the. wealthy Premier, "I don't mean that." "I think,' was the equally ready rejoiher;" he should be five feet ten high." PnoiEs;son : "NOw, I've put you ten questions, none of which put have answered tight. I nope it won't,' said the wee girl; "it would be too mean if it did—before I got a chance to be married.' WHEN the Rev. Mr. C— was minister •of the U.P. AN old Baptist preacher, so straight a Calvinist . that he leaned over backward, was defending his doctrines against a man as ignorant .as he was obstinate. At length the preacher said, to his opponent, "Now, look here, my friend, don't you believe what is to be will be ?" "No, I don tat all. I believe what is to be won't be." "On," gasped fat Mrs. Weighty, as she ascended the second flight ot stairs in her new residence, "I really cannot run up any more stairs." "Of coarse not," testily answered her husband; "bat if the stairs were made of dressmakers bills, you could run them up very easily." "1 do detest puns," exclainiecl Mrs. Weighty, the next day, reeonuting the conversation to a friend. div.head: CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: CAPITAL" CHAT.

I hear a rumour that the health of Lord Esher, the Master of the Rolls, is likely at no distant date to necessitate his resignation.- It is stated to be probable that he will be succeeded by Sir John Rigby, the Solicitor-General.

The building of the great tower for London at Wembley Park is so far advanced that the legs of the structure are now finished, and the steel work rises to a height of 150 ft.. This lower part of the tower has involved expenditure to the extent of half the estimated cost. It is hoped that the tower will be completed in the coming spling.

There is now little doubt that the co-operative authorities will soon be the owners of a colliery. It will run on the "living wage '!principle. This has been insisted on by every district wleich has con- sidered the question. Co-operation, it is declared, must in this matter set an exansple.

I learn from" New Australia," the iournal of the New Australian Co-operative Settlement Associa- tion, that the first contingent ofpioneers have ar- rived safely at Paraguay. They, cabled from the set- tlement as follows :—" Have taken possession of cur land,and we are all delighted with our country. We are perfectly satisfied." It was the original in- tention to despatch another vessel with married women and young girls early in December,but this plan had to be abandoned on account of a telegram instructing the agents at Sydney to detain all women for six months. In their place about 200 bushmen were to be embarked before the end of the I year. A wide interest, it is said, is being :aken in the movement, and applications for membership have been received not;only from Australia, New &eland, and Tasmania, but also from England, and even•from English residents in India.

Sir W. Harcourt is being pressed to announce in his Budget that the Government will introduce a sharply graded income tax, bringing realised pro- perty and capital more under contribution and re- ducing the burdens on industry. A recasting of the death duties so as to tap the resources as yet un- touched—the vast ground values of great towns and the accumulated values of real estate every- where—is another point. On the other band, the problem, so often talked about, of relieving the in- comes of professional men when below a moderate maximum, for example, must be disposed of. Fur- ther, the deficit canhot and. must not be met by a heavier strain upon those sources; of national in- come—the Customs and Excise—to .which the working and poorer classes already contribute in an altogether disproportionate degree. So far as can be judged from whatAis heard in the lobbies, this very explicit and important document has received the signature of nearly every Liberal present in the House on Thursday. When the signing has been completed the letter will be presented and banded to the Press.

There is much soreness., among the members who support Church interests in regard to the arrane,- meat come to between the two front benches oi. the parish rooms question. The provision that th.- rooms shall not include any building erected or. provided "within forty years" entirely by or at t he cost of members of any particular church or con- 44regation was regarded as particularly badly drawn, and many strictures were passed by the want of loyalty to the Church shown by Mr. Balfour and his colleagues in agreeing to such an arrangement. It was particularly pointed out that the burden of vroofin all cases of forty years' tenure would b(- thrown on the Church,and that any small contribu- tion by Dissenters might vitiate the claim of tl,e Church. It has turned out, however, that Mr. Bal four and Sir M. Hicks-Beach did not "give away" the Church party with the recklessness which som- a the followers supposed. It is stated on very good authority that the author of .the maligned provision was no other than the Archbishop of Canterbury himself, who if he did not .actually draft it at least ;suggested. the atlbStaneP of it.

The attention of the ilowe Secretary is being given at the present moment to the excessive infant mortality in certain artisan towns where women are largely engagea in factory labour. The subject has been brought prominently forward by Di. ,Reid. the medical officer of health for the Staffordshire County Council, and an elaborate report' has been prepared for the use of the Home Office- by the Parliamentary Committee of the -British Medical Association. Dr. Reid's just published annual report gives the average infant mortality for this county for the four years 1889-92. The. deaths of children under a year old in groups Of towns where .many women are engaged in work were 196 per 1.000 registered births; in groups where fewer w4,men were engaged in work they were 173 per , 1,000; and practically where no women were so en- gaged they were 160 per I,ooo—rates which corre- spond very closely to those for the ten v previously analysed and submitted to the Home 1 Office. There can be no question that the excessive mortality in many towns is partly attributable to the practice of nursing mothers engaging in factory work. Propositions are being prepared for legis- lative enactments to diminish this excessive mor- tality.

Very sad indeed, is the news from Sierra Leone, although the bacrifice of human life was not so great as was at first reported. Six native soldiers, :Ind four British officers perished, besides some Ft ench natives. The deepest sympathy will be felt for the sufferer& families on all sides, and I trust they will be remembered by the State. The French papers have dealt with the matter very fairly and generously up to the present. With his last breath, the French officer responsible admitted his mistake.

He died in the camp of the men who had been shot down by his troops. Lieuteuant Maritz,thonght that the British force was a detachment of the com- mon savage enemy. It was a natural mistake— Amilar ones have been too often made—but the result of this discharge of firearms into an English camp ought to enable us to appreciate better what similar treatment means to the miserable savages whose fate we concern ourselves so little about when it becomes necessary for our own purposes to cruise them outof South Africa and elsewhere. A better feeling between France and England may probably spring from this tragedy

It is not too much to suppose that Mr. Cecil Rhodes is still a British subject. The fact that ,oine troops of Civilised white men with repeating rifles and deadly Maxim guns, drove .a wretched collection of naked and almost unarmed savages trom their kraals • while lie_ lounged behind and wrote vain-glorious telegrams scarcely emancipated Lim from his allegiance to the ruling:aut\ orities of the Empire. But that is very far from being the opinion of Mr. yecil Rhodes.

His Cape Town admirers fêted him on Saturday, said he favoured them with a speech. Mr. Rhodes was in his best form. He was in a condescending mood, too. He told the wondering Colonists that "he had no objegtion to the Crownit, the Crown woald'recognileits 'duties to the Colonies.:- If not, he. Colonies might deal elsewhere!' Nothing could be plainer. If the Crown does' not recognise its duties" towards South Africa—that is, give Cecil Rhodes permission to make a private estate 04- Mivabeleland—he will pitch the Crown to the winds —or kick it into the Orange River, just as some Irish Unionist once threatened to perform a similar teat in the neighbourhood of the Boyne. Mr. Rhodes is mainly supported by" Loyalists" and Unionists it this country.

The poor old " Times!" It backed this potential ebel fin South Africa- from the beginning; but Saturday night's performance was too much for it. True, it carefully avoids referring to Mr. Rhodes .i,tinct, threat to bring about a separation of the Colony from the Mother Country. It simply denies , ha 3 right to appropriate the conquered land—and it ! does it in such a fashion that one feels it is afraid , to speak harshly to the Great Man whom it has , been painfully exploiting for months. We all know the value of Mr. Rhodes' loyalty now. He will be loyal to the Empire just while the Empire remains loyal to him. What do the people who rave about the "integrity of the Empire "every other day say to the situation?
Lord Randolph Churchill has. written to.a corres- pondent at Halifax on the currency question. He says he is an inexorable opponent of anything in the nature of bimetallism for this country.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEAREST NELLIE, It is almost unnecessary to say that a dressing- gown should be found in every woman's wardrobe, and if only one can be indulged in, it shbuld be really warm and servioeable, not a flimsy article of cotton or flannelette—pretty as these are for sum- mer wear—lout a substantial garment in which one will feel fairly well clothed if called up suddenly on a cold winter's night.. The nicest material for such a garment is. Moncton flannel, although ordinary twilled flannel lined with veiling or flannelette Will answer fairly well. The .price of Molleton ranges front is. ,4d. to 3s. 6d. a yard, but one at 2s. 3d., 50in. wide, will serve admirably, and peacock:blue, crimson, and terra-cotta red are the most useful tints for a gown that is meant for wear—not only for show. Amongst some pretty dresses for children was a frock and suit. The frock is in the popular Empire style, of a fine white net, mounted on an ivory satinlining, and stripped with bands of Valen- ciennes insertion, edged op either aide with a bead- ing, through which is run belie ribbon of white satin. Another had a blouse of poplin, suited for a little boy of three or four years old, and revers and'hem are trimmed with a fine Irish lace, .while the shirt is made of soft white silk. A very pretty snit this is, not too elaborate, and yet smart. Here is a frock for a smaller child, and is very pretty, thouglisimple.

A model of the latest cut had the skirt.exces- sively sloped, and the waist fitting closely, whilst the, top is widened by large lapels, and by cape epaulettes *over the sleeves. Very heavy cloth should not be selected for these long, full coats, but a thin cloth, lined to the waist or hips with woollen plaid, or with Italian cloth, is admirable both as regards weight and warmth, and a facing silk on each side can be made from a width of silk divided in the centre, which looks neat when the skirts open and the coat is unfastened. The open- ing in the neck can be filled up with a plastron and high collar 'of the same material, the top of the collar edged fur, or one of the fashionable little boas made of the entire skin can be worn.

The Bathurst dress is made in cardinal cloth, outlined with silk and fur. The sleeves, basque, and underskirt-is in black moire. This charming design can be executed in all shades of the present season. Pelisses are quite the fashionable outdoor gar- ments. Soine are very tight-fitting at the waist, but the skirt is gored, and hangs quite fall, and the sleeves are wide, and generally finish in the bell or Russian style. A smooth-faced steel-grey cloth, trimmed with jet, and with wide bretelle arrangements of black velvet, is very handsome, especially with the grey •cloth liberally trimmed with jet. Another pelisse is of petunia cloth, with sleeves to the elbow of velvet, and wide pelerines of velvet, also long stole ends fringed with jet, these falling just below the waist at the back, and quite to the edge of the pelisse in front.

A very prol,ty bodice which would grace alike a theatre or a social gathering is made of pale green soft silk, drawn in to the figure with rows of fine jet. For a tea gown the velvet weal(' be nice and warm. Have it made in the 13CW Princess style, very full in the skirt ; the fulness, however, hidden away at the waist in invisible pleats, which expand greatly towards the feet. Use the soft flowered satin for the front; leo it fall from the neck in an unbroken lint to the feet, falling very full, and having four gatherings at the neck. Use the _lace fichu on the bodice, allow the point to fall in the centre of the back, and the bring the ends over the shoulders, and let them taper to the waist. Make the sleeves with one deep, and one narrow puff, and fall of lace. Masked balls are likely to be a popular form of entertainment this winter. Great improvements have been made in the dominos, and some very handsome ones are to be seen. A pretty one in a very delicate shaae of pale green satin mery is fastened at the throat like a long cloak, and falls in folds to the feet. Ulmer the hood is a thickly. pleated cape, which forms a sort of sheath over the outline of the arm, and is caught in a bunch and tied with ribbons at the waist-line. A very hand- some domino of White satin has the upper cape heavily embroidered with steel embroidery. Yours as ever,
JENNIE.

Miss Dorothea Klumpke, a young lady who has for sometime been attached to the Paris Observatory, has now passed her examination before the Faculty of 'Science in that city for the degree of Doctor of Mathe- matics. . She rears only the black or field crickets, keep- ing them in large glass jars ranged about the room. She sells the little insects to the superstitious, who believe in the luck that crickets bring.

Willard, an enterprising Chicago woman, is the proprietor of a barber's shop which balks six chairs, each one in charge of a woman barber. Each of the assistants makes two .pounds„ten shillings a week, and half of all their takings beyond four pounds ten shillings.• Revs. Mr. and Mrs. A. E. Wright were recently in- stalled as pastors of the Universalist Church of the Reconciliation, Greenpoint, N.Y. It is not unusual in the Universalist Church for women to become minis- tprs. In fact, there are about forty such in the United States. Bessie Bonehill, one °Ube English music half singers, has a two-year-old son, and the two-year-old son has a bank account of one thousand two hundred pounds. In pne of her most popular" turns," Miss Bonehill makes up as a ragged newsboy, and enthusiasts in the audi- ence often toss coins on the stage for her. These she has carefully banked for her boy, and hencn the one thou- sand two hundred pounds.

Scotth Haggis. Buy a sheep's heart, liverand lights; thoroughly wash the heart, cut it in slices, dry, and dip each piece in flour; lay them on a dish while you cut the liver and lights in slices. Peel six large onions, cutt hem up small iind put them into a frying-pan, in which you Have melted a piece of dripping as large as the bowl of a tablespoon; fry the onions a light brown, and put them as you fry them into a basin, then fry the pieces of heart, liver, and lights. When fried, chop them all up rather small, and put in the basin with the fried onions half a pound of chopped suet, a heaped tablespoonful of parsley, lemon-thyme, and basil, half a nutmeg grated, pepper, salt, and one pound of oatmea4. Mix these all Well together, tie them in a puddmg-cloth—not too tight, as it must have room to swell; but there must not be any holes in the cloth—put into a saucepan of boiling water, boil three hours and a half, remove the cloth, turn on a hot dish, and serve at once'.

Buying a:Sewing Machine. When purchasing a sewing machine don't let the shop- keeper persuade you to buy one of the new-fangled machines at a Mg price,•as it is to his advantage to push' thehi, but consider what kind of work ycu require it to do. If for household purposes only, the old style easy- running " family" hand or treadle machine. with the boat-shaped shuttle and patent "winder," a. great improvement on the old system, is the cheapest andbest machine, and it is capable of stitching the finest linen and very coarse cloth. These machines cannot be expected to turn out the work at the same rate of speed as those, used for manufacturing, but i have known nunierous cases where dressmakers and mantlemakers have used them for years. Wline a •..nachine is required to serve both household and manfacturing purposes,the latter being the most important (which necessitates speed and light running, Combined with a good stitch),' then it will be good policy to obtain one of the many new machines, among them The " Rotary," "Oscillat- in," or "No. 9," which are capable of doing heavy f; great speed, and will serve the double purpose.. —G. C.

div.head: Heart and Recreation.
div.p: The Heart and Recreation.

It may not be generally known that so apparently trivial an act as that ot yawning betrays a tired heart. ' and is an effort of Nature to stimUlate that organ to the getting rid of venous blood by pumping it into the lungs. What is commonly known by the term "stretching one's self" (and this, by the way, is usually accompanied by yawning) is another sign of fatigue, and has for it 3 object, like a yawn, the stimulating of a tired heart. Those who lead sedentary lives,sitting long with head and back bent over the desk, and probably thinking hard all the while, are subject to fits of stretching and yawning. Out they ought to go,into the fresh air,as soon as Nature vouchsafes these warnings; a brisk walk, especially if accompanied by a pleasant companion, will then do , wonders in restoring the circulation and oxygenising the blood. These are really not trivial matters, for, what- ever we do, we should not age the heart. It is not that heart decease in a valvular or organic shape is to be greatly feared, but something as bad in the long run, though the symptoms may never at any time be very urgent. What we mean is this : if Vit e neglect recrea- tion, if we work to hard and sit too long at desk-work, the heart becomes feeble, and virtually old. If, on the other hand, we carry exercise to excess; if we row too hard, if_vve Constantly" spurt ". when cycling, if we are in the habit of lifting weights unsuited to our strength, then we are apt to stretch—the • right side of the heart. And the life of one who has either a feeble heart Or an enlarged right-heart is not to be envied. It is mostly a weariness, and one afflicted thus is generally nervous, and hardly ever knows ,what it is to be otherwise than tired. It is well to know that wisely chosen and regu- lar exercise and recreation are the remedies for such states of being, for the heart being, like the arm, com- posed principally of muscle, is rendered stroager by judicious use. Medical men have lately recognised the truth of this, and it is a common thing nowadays for a patient with a feeble heart to be ordered regular exercise in hill-climbing, while but a few years ago the same indiviaal would have been condemned to rest in the recumbent position or in a rocking chair.—" Cassell's Book of the Household."

div.head: SNUB-NOSED REGIMENT.
div.p: A SNUB-NOSED REGIMENT.

Lady Dufferin was once present at areview of Russian soldiers which struck her as remarkable, for that one regiment was named after the Emperor Paul. Now, it so happened that this Czar had a turned-up, or, as some say, snub nose, and the odd thing about this body of troops was that all the men had been selected because their noses turned tip. This was carrying imitation to an absurd length. There is, of course, no harm in an upturned nose—in fact, Tennyson seemed to regard it as d mark of beauty—but there Is also no need to make too much of it.—" Littlz Folks."

That was very kind of you; but it must not be—we must not accept presents. What is the price of the-hare?" The contractor replied, " Well, if you insist on paying, twopence." "Very well, here is a shilling. For the tenpence send us five more." SYLLOGISM. —A sailor is not a sailor when he's aboard. A sailor is not a sailor when he's ashore; but he must be either aboard or ashore—therefore a sailor is not 'a sailor. -

div.head: PARTED BY FATE;
div.p: PARTED BY FATE;
THE MYSTERY OF BLACK-TOR LIGHTHOUSE.
BY LAURA JEAN LIBBEY,
Author of "lone, the Pride of the Mill," &e., tze.
CHAPTER XXIX.
"BE MY BRIDE, \TERME," WHISPERED RUTLEDGE.

It was quite two miles to Renwick Villa. Uldene knew the road well. She would have no convey- ance, and undertook the journey on foot. "She would fellow Rutledge there," she told herself, "creep into the grounds of the villa unob- served, and watch him through the window." She could not withstand the temptation. How brightly the moon shone down upon the earth, bathing the trees, the flowers, and the white, winding road in its silvery light. flow the golden stars glowed in the blue sky. The birds had folded their wings and sought their nests among the leafy branches ; tho flowers had folded the dew-drope close to their hearts with their tender petals, and were' rocked to sleep by the gentle night winds. Uldene passed slowly along the well remembered road, tears falling like rain from her dark eyes. ! how often she had cintered over that same road, riding by Rutledge Chester's side. How gay and roseate the world bad looked to her then! Could she be tee same creature, changed so com- pletely ? The beautiful bride, Uldene, Whom every one petted, worshipped and spoiled, and who was fairly idolized for her beauty and pretty, wilful ways? Now, dead to the world—a living lie—flying like one accursed from him whee.m she loved better. than life itself, lest the family doom should fall upon him whom she loved so well. At last an abrupt curve in the road brought her in sight of the villa, and then she saw by the brilliantly illuminated grounds, the merry throngs, and the music, that a lawn fete was in progress, which would, no doubt, end in a grand ball. Rutledge bad come to the lawn alto. it hurt her heart a little—the thought that he could mingle in gay festivities while he believed her lying cold in death in the lonely graveyard. No doubt he came there to drown his sad thoughts for a brief hour. Ah, yes that must be it. No one saw the white, wistful face peering in through the scroll-work of the tall iron fence. Uldene was not near enough to distinguish many of the faces. A great longing came to her to enter the grounds. She remembered there was a small wicket in the rear of the house ; toward this she made her way, entered the grounds, and stole up the lilac walk to the rose-arbour beyond; sinking down exhausted on the rustic bench, quite hidden by the drooping branches and the dense shadows. Here she could have a full view of the ground* and the merry revellers. She knew it was hazard- .ous' daring, to venture here, lest some one should see her and recognise her; but her intense longing to see Rutledge, remaining the while unseen her- self, had overcome prudence. A moment later and the fall of a light footstep, that seemed strangely familiar to her, sounded on her ears.
"Am I mad, or do I dream?" she murmured, aghast. "It is—Verlie ! What can she be doing here? I did not know that she knew Mts. Ren- wick ! "

_ How calm and placid Verlie's sweet face looked in the white bright moonlight. "Life would have been so different with both of us if I had not cheated her out of her lover," thought Uldene, with a sob. Still she knew Verlie loved her so dearly she would have given her lover up to her, even at the cot of breaking her own heart. Ah, yea I Uldene knew that well. She knew, too, how Verlie must have grieved over her supposed death, refusing to be comforted. A great longing swept ovet her ltmely, yearning heart to creep after Verne, to fall on her knees before her, cling to the little white hands, and sob out to Verlie all her pitiful story—surely the sad- dest that was ever mektd in a young girl's breast. Oh, how Verlie would gather her in her arms and weep over her as she told her piteous story ! She would readily agree with her that Rutledge must believe her dead, although it was cruel, oh, so cruel, to break two hearts by keeping them asunder.

Poor,- hapless Uldene—always a creature of impulse—stole after Verlie as she passed the flower-beds' the lilac atid magnolia walks. Both had crossed the star lighted park, and were near- ing the shadows of the trees but a few feet apart. "Verlie !" called Uldene, softly. But Verde did not hear the low voice, so engrossed was she in her own tumultuous thoughts. Uldene was silent for a moment. A bird flew from its nest in the nearest tree; a rabbit rusta; in the brushwood ; the wind stirred some fallen leaves; the sound of the dance music in the dis- tance died away in a low wad. "Verlie 1" she called again, more .softly than before. The girl paused in startled, solemn wonder. "It must be only fancy !" she marmured, half aloud. "On this night, of all nights, the memory , of Uidene haunts me. Even the winds sighing among the trees seem to whisper to me with Utdene's voice. Heaven grant that it is no sin to love him, even though he belonged to Uldene first." Before Uldene could speak again, another step came swiftly down the gravelled walk. With a quick motion Uldene drew back among the dense ehadows of the tree, until he should pess. Ali, heavens ! it was Rutledge Chester. He was almost abreast of her now. She never knew hew she restrained the mad impulse to cry out to hist: " Rutledge ! Rutledge ! weep for me no more. Mourn for me no longer, my love! I iam here !" Oh. how her soul went out to him! I He had brughed the drooping branches of the trees carelessly aside with his hand as he passed them. He would never know of the lonely figure that stood under them, pas- sionately kissieg the green leaves his hand had touched. She saw him join Verlie; but instead of passing on with a nod and a smile, or some gay word, he quietly drew the little white hand within his arm, exclaiming, in a glad voice : "Here you are, Verne, darling. I have been searching everywhere for you. lam sure you ran away to avoid me." The girl crouching behind the flowering shrubs, which separated her from these two, listened it: wonder. His voice bad never sounded like that when he addressed her. There was an under- current in it that ptizzled her. She saw Verlie's fair, sweet face flush hotly in the bright moonlight. She looked up at Rutledge with a smile, drawire; in girlish, bashful confusion away from his outstretched arms, answerieg, con- fusedly: "I did not know that you were searching for ma —that you wanted me, Rutledge." His reply was like the /Shuck of doom to the beautiful hapless creoaute listening to them both so intently. "You did eot know that I wanted you! Oh, 1 Verlie, what eousense I Is tilt%f e a moment in my life that; I do not want you, my darltug ? " These were the words that broke a hunian heart ! Clearly, through the solemn stillness of the summer night, the words tell train Rutledge Chester's lips upon the heart of the beautiful, solitary figure crouched among the flowering all rubs. _ _
Rutledge believed biumelf quite alone with Verlie • be cen!,3 thonutitm freely now. 1611211 11.yOU pArQqouly. V trtio, Way war
not tell you what ia in my heart. You must have read what I wanted to say in my eyes, you cruel dear."

"&,, Rutledge !" breathed Verlie, shuddering, "1 I--cannot bear to hear suy more to-nigh. It almost seems as though the spirit of Uldene comes between us. I almost think I ought not to listen to you. You belonged to her living--it almost seems that you belong to. her even though she is dead."

"Verlie," he answered, gravely, "I agree with you. I belonged to Uldeue while she lived, but the love of mortals blends into tender, devoted memory when one or the other, whom God joined together in holy wedlock, dies. Heaven knows I did my duty, my, whole duty, by my beautiful Uidene. I gave her every thought of my heart— my whole love. I have worn 1,,y life out in grieving over her untimely fate. Now, because Heaven has sent a balm to my sorely wounded heart, do not seek to hurl it back into bitter despair again. It is our duty to forget a dark, sorrowful past, and try to live in the brightness of --a future. I shall always love and reverence the memory of Uldene • but, because of that, do not, I implore you, withhold your love from-me, Verlie; it would be unjust." "Am I mad, or do I dream?" sobbed the wretched girl who watched these two, who were so utterly oblivious of her presence. What Verlie's answer was she never knew. She saw Rutledge clasp the little white hands he held fondly—bend his handsome head over them, and raise them to his lips tenderly. "Remember, Verlie," Rutledge went on, piti- lessly, "I have told you the exact truth as to how I happened to wed Uldene—not but what I loved her well after she became my bride,—but you, • Verlie, were my first as well as my last love ; but for that strange death-bed prayer, it is you whom I should have asked to become my bride." The words fell like drops of molten lead upon the breaking heart so near them. The swaying figure ' had sunk down among the sharp thorns and brambles, but she did not even feel the pain of them. The earth and sky seemed to meet above , her; the leaves of the trees seemed, to moan in the ni,l4lit-wind ' • the moon hid her sorrowful face in the white clouds.
If the hand of God had stricken beautiful, hap- less Uldene dead, the white face, upturned to the night skies, could not have been whiter.
CHAPTER XXX. "I COULD FIND REST IN THE DARK WATERS," SHE
MURMURED, PITEOUSLY.

Uldene crouched motionless among the swaying roses, like one turned to stone, looking and listen- ing. In that moment the great, yearning love in her heart was slain ; no words could picture such griefs as her. It would have been a thousand times more merciful if Heaven, in its infinite mercy, had let her die that night in the awful collision, than let her live to face this. The moon in all its rounds, looking down in its pure white light upon sin, suffering, pain, and all, human woes, never looked upon a sadder sight. "In my thoughts I go over the past time and time again," continued Rutledge Chester, slowly. "In the moment you and Uldene stood before mei my heart went out to you. Beautiful as Uldene was, she was not the mate my heart craved. Imagine my intense surprise, Verlie, upon making the discovery, in an unexpected manner, that Uldene loved me. I was amazed, bewildered at the worshipful love a human heart had lavished upon one who had not sought it. "I was intensely sorry for Uldene," he went on, huskily, "and through pity that marriage was consummated. In the after days I saw the folly of giving the hand where the heart could never go. "Since Heaven has severed the bonds that united me to Uldene, and I have again met you, I have begun to realise that the sweet possibilities of life are not yet over for me. The happiest hour of my life will be the moment in which I call you mine, Verlie, darling." They passed on, arm in arm, through the lilac grove, over the moonlit lawn, making a tour of the circular path. They must not find Uldene there when they reached that spot again. Like a hunted hare, Uldene sprang to her feet, hurrying through the pleasure grounds, through the arbour, and into the heart of the grove that lay beyond. No human being was near; but the birds were soon startled by the passionate cries of a broken heart; cries that fell freely and clearly on the soft, sweet air, and seemed to pierce the heavens; bitter, passionate cries that took with them the burden of a most unhappy soul. After a time they died away—the moans and sobs ended. - -
The girl lay among the crushed goldenrods, with wide:open, hurror-stricken eyes, looking the future full in the face.

"Oh, broken dream of love !—oh, dark future, without one gleam of light !—how was it to end 2" "How strange it was that the thought had never occurred to me of the possibility of Rutledge re-marrying, believing himself free," she moaned out, piteously. Ah, no, she had never dreamed that his heart, having once been hers, would return again to Verlie, his first love. How cruelly Heaven had punished her for taking him from Verlie in that dark past. Oh, the pity of it the pity of it ! A step among the brushwood startled her. What if some one passing that way should happen to find her ! What a terrible exposé there would be.
Her future mattered little enough to her now. She would go quietly away. Rutledge and Verlie should never know she lived. He had not grieved for her untimely fate.

It was no bitier sorrow to him that matters had turned out as they had, for it left him free•to woo and win his first love. The words of an old poem, even in that moment of acute sorrow, recurred to her :
"Compulsion may a while detain Thu magnet from its accustomed course; But when not withheld by force It travels to the north again."

As "the magnet, when not withheld by force," Rutledge Chester's heart had returned to Verlie again. There was nothing to do now but go out of his life quietly. It mattered little enough where she went.

Silently she turned her beautiful face from all she had loved best on earth, and crept slowly out of the grounds and away from the villa, without casting one glance behind. How the sound of the light, gay dance music and the rippling laughter of merry, girlish voices tortured her I Would they laugh so gayly if they knew a heart so near them had broken to-night? she wondered vaguely. "Good-bye, lost love, whom I have loved so well !" she sobbed. "Good-bye, fair face, that has won him from even my memory! I shall never look on either of you again." Like a shadow Uldene flitted down the white moonlit road, never pausing until she found her- self on the wharf that overlooked.the river.

how peaceful it looked, reflecting the myriads of silver stars in its clear depths " Dawn there I could find rest I" she murmured, piteously, clasping her trembling hands close together, and gazing down into the limpid water like one fascinated by a subtle thought.• • Suddenly a hand was laid on her arm, and a gentle voice murmured softly in her startled ear: "Whatever your sorrows may be, my poor child, do not contemplate that l" Uldene sterted back with a cry of dismay, and saw stanclieg before her a young girl, neatly but - poorly dres..ed, with an eareest, pale face, and large, dark, :,ad eyes. " I was not thinking of drowning myself," said Uldene, with a shudder. "I would not, have such a sin on my soul as that—bitterly as I may have been tempted to do so." "I ate glad to hear it," returned her companion, "for M,yl.y a young girl with whom the world has gone wrfmg comes here for that purpose and no other," " I was evendering,, an I stood here, where I had better go,' l Ulauee, wearily. "Have vol 00 home--no mother?" asked the gentle Ulden,. i into tears. " Nlv c ur died when I was a babe," she Bobbed," :. ey one cry to Heaven by night and by day kite:. • why did not God take me, too, when me • elee mother died? Life has been a cruel Curse LO "You eee you were thinking of where you could go, ee night," said the gentle stranger. 44 Will ).c., • • eene home with me? lam one of the 1»:ee, • eiee My lodging is of the plainest, yet I it, such as it is, with you to- nigh t." Emily fi x did not quite like the wild, de- ; - • the dark eyes of the beautiful, - BObb if. 4 she had found gazing breathlessly rlown I. . . . eeilLete weters ef the deep flowing river.

More than one young girl this good angel (as those who knew her called her) had snatched from an untimely fate. She had expected she would have to persuade Uldene to accompany her from this alluring 3pot ; DIA to her surprise the ycung girl consented readily mough. "You are very kind," said Uldene, gratefully. "I will go with you gladly. I was wondering a few moments before where I should find a lodging. place, my—my means are so limited," she added, flushing painfully. "Then come with me," said Emily, drawing the little white hand within her own. She was sur- prised to see how delicate and dainty it was— like those of fortune's favorites, who " neither toil nor spin." "I have a great horror of seeing a young girl stand where you did, with such a look on her face," continued Emily, "for not very long ago I stood in the self•same place, eagerly watching my opportunity to plunge beneath those waves, and leave the world which had narrowed down to a grave for me." For a brief moment Uldene forgot her own intense sorrow in listening to her companion. "Would you like to hear what tempted me to such rash folly?" asked Emily, seeing she had attracted her companion's attention. "I can tell you as we walk home." "I should like to hear, if the memory of it is not too painful," assented Uldene, "Love drove me to it," replied Emily, calmly— "love, that brings with it either a blessing or a curse to the hearts of women who indulge in its golden dreams. But to the story : There was one whom I loved better than life itself, a fair-haired, handsome lover, who had placed the betrothal ring on my finger, and named the day I should be his bride. _ _

"One day a girl friend came to pay me a visit. She was as gay and handsome as I was quiet and plain. I was not inclined to be jealous by nature, but when I introduced my lover to my lovely friend a pang like the bitterness of death smote through my heart as I saw with keen eyes the gaze of rapt admiration he bent on her. I saw all that happened after as in a glass, darkly. You can guess the result. My friend won my lover from me, and on the eve they were wedded I crept out hose to die, and end my woe. I flung myself into the water with a bitter cry. Oh; I loved him better than life! I was saved, and I knew then my time had not yet come. God intended me to live and endure. I was needed in this world. Slowly the thought came to me what Heaven had assigned to me. I afterwards realized it was to save young girls from the fate that had so nearly been mine. I pass this way from my work at night, and many a young girl I rescue from a suicide's fate."
- "Oh I how I pity you !" sobbed Üblene. "There is no pain in this world so great as the pain the heart endures when one finds the one whom we

love has given his heart to another. Oh, poor girl! I can understand what you have suffered but too well. Death would have been welcome rather than face life after that with such a sword rankling in the heart." As Emily listened she realised that the beautiful girl before her had a tragic love-story, as pitiful, perhaps as her own which she had related • and Emily determined to bring this young girl and her lover together again, if it lay within human power, little dreaming fate itself had set its seal of defiance against this.
(To be continued.)

'HOW TO TURN BACK THE CLOCK. " What time is it, Maggie ? said John, with an un- easy sense that he ought to be on his homeward way. L " I'll go and: look," she answered. Stepping quietly into the kitchen the girt pushed the clock hands back an hour, and returning said," It's only half-past nine by our clock ; you can stay an hour longer." So John stayed, for lovers are never eager to part, and he needed no coaxing. The next morning, how- ever, he overslept himself, and Maggie's father, at his breakfast, having missed the train, he intended to jour- ney by that day, wondered how the good old clock ' could have lost an hour inithe night. But Maggie didn't explain. She meant to set:it right again before going L:o bed, but forgot4which;shows once more what every- body should remember—that,wo can set back the clock, but we cannot set back the time. All the same it is possible occasionally to regain lost things. In a ',";'wornan's ;letter recently received, I find this sentence : "They tell mel look ten years younger than .1 (lid." And if she felt as se looked she was to all practical purposes ten years younger. Fcr, although a clock face looks the same no matter what time it is, a human face doesn't. That changes with the condition of the " works," or the life behind it. The letter goes on thus : "In the spring of 1880 I felt weak and low. I had a bad taste in the mouth and al thick slimy phlegm covered my mouth and tongue. I was sick into, rmorning, retching and vomit lag a wateryfluid. I had great pain in the head and was very mazy, being at times so bad I could hardly stand upon my feet. After eating the simplest food I had a dreadful pain in my chest, and a tightness across the chest and sides. Fornhours together I have sat be- fore the frec4rubbing:My chest to try and get relief. I had great pain in the left =side and palpitation of the heart, and could get but little sleep at night on account of it. Graddally Ugrew weaker and weaker, until I could scarcely walk about the house, and but for the necessity of attending to my family, I should have been laid up. My life was a burden and a misery to me, I often wished myself dead. Sometimes better and other times worse ; this was my general condition for ten years, during which long period of suffering I was treated by the doctor, and took every kind of medicine I could hear tell of, but got better.

In November, 1890, I read in a book of a medicine called Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and got a bottle from Mr. E. Banks, the chemist. After I had taken a few doses I found my food agreed with me better. I kept on with the Syrup and gradually gained: strength. I had become so thin and emaciated throughgall those years of suffering that it took time to fully restore me. But lan now in, better health than I ever valin my life, and my recovery has astonibhed my friends.firThey tell me I look ten years younger'ithan I did for taking the Syrup. flow I wish I had known of it;_vears soonero My husband and friends tuui.givellup all Fie of my/getting better,lbut none of us knew of Mother,Seigel's!Syrup. On:inenticning to the*„Rev. E. Harries, the Vicar of Christ Church,i:,what had wrought the cure, he said I should write :and!.let the proprietors know what the Syrup had done:: for me, so as to benefit others. You may publish this statement as you think proper and I will gladly answer inquiries. Yours truly, (signed> (Mrs.) Elizabetlit'i Greenhalgh, 21, Rutland-straet, Newtown, l'endlebury, (near,. Manchester), May 4th, 1892."

Thus was this good waman enabled—not to turn back her nominal age,nbut what was better—to recover the priceless treasure of health,without which neither youth nor age has any comfort. Her malady was the same wretched indigestion and dyspepsia, the curse of all ages and nations.
ANOTHER SHIP CANAL SUGGESTED.

On Tuesday afternoon at a meeting of the Wakefield Chamber of Commerce, J.‘ll..Cliarles Clay, J.P., who pre- sided. again brouOt before the Chamber the question of a ship canal between Wakefield and Goole. Mr. Clay said that in 1887 he introduced this question at one of the meetings of that Chamber, but the matter fell through owing to the financial embarrassment of the Manchester Ship Canal Company at that period. Now • that the undertaking was likely to prove a success he thought the matter of a canal between Goole and Wake- field should not be lost sight of, and he suggested that a day should be fixed upon for a special meeting and a thorough discussion of the matter.—Theidea was favour- ably received.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the above board was held on Wednesday in the board room of the Work- house. Mr. G. Ratcl.ff, presided, and there were also present Messrs. R. Heaton, W. Houghton, 11. J. Longton, A. J. Jolley, W. Shrtw, S. Davies, J. Muir, W. Turton, E. Auklancl, T. Smith, T. Mather, A. Jolley, P. Warburton, J. Swinton, J. Clarke, J. Dob- son, J. Hill, R. Owen, jun., Dignum, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (deputy clerk), C. H. Ward (mas- ter), H. Al. Mines (superintendent of Padgate ichools).

div.head: INDEBTED TOWNSHIPS.
div.p: INDEBTED TOWNSHIPS.

The CLERK said that following townships had not yet paid their second call : Cuerdley, Rixton, Great Sankey, Winwick, and Latchford. Every other parish had paid both their first and second calls.—Mr. HEATON moved, and Mr. DAVIES seconded, that the Clerk be instructed to press the townships for payment.—The proposition was carried.
A PRESENT OF TOBACCO.
The House Committee acknowledged a present of tobacco from Mr. Harry Tat, Sankey-street.
THE HOUSE COMMITTEE.

The House Committee reported that they declined to allow any extra payment for the lengthening of the shoots by Messrs. Rose and Co., Salford.—Mr. DAVIES in moving the adoption of the minutes said that before the Shoots were supplied the firm sent an experienced man to take the proper measure, so that the committee did not consider that they should be held responsibie.—Mr. A. J. JOLLEY seconded the motion which was carried.

TUE screooLs COMMITTEE.—THE CHILDREN OUT TOO LATE. The School Committee's minutes which were of a routine character were passed unanimously after which W. HOUGHTON said that he wished to mention a Matter which had come to his knowledge. On the Sat- urday before Christmas, the superintendent of the schools at Padgate, took the band into the town, at a Late hour. The committee had heard the Superintend- ent's explanation and had taken steps by which nothing of the sort would occh- faure.—Mr. DOBSON : Why do they go out ?—Mr Hon ;HTON replied that they went out to pay compliniGas t tie ratepayers. He did not, however, approve of te children being out so late at night ; in fact he strongly disapproved of it. If the band went out, they should (To i the afternoon before the streets became rough. On the occasion in question, they did not return until 11.30 p.m. There had been an anonymous letter in the papers which cast a slur upon the publicans, but he believed that there were respect- able publicans in Warrington as there were in other Places. The publicans visited were subscribers to the band.—Mr. DOBSON asked if the band did not go, doing What was termed, " busking."—Mr. HEATON repudiated ;,his.—The CLERK said that it was contrary to the regula- ‘lons of the school to be out so late.--:-Mr. SHAW protested against the discussion. He asked whether they did not g° to Newton in summer at a late hour. Some of the Members were always finding fault with Mr. Mines.— Donsos said that they were trying to bring up the children in a respectable manner, They did not wish to encourage them to go " busking " about the town. It 'svas a great shame that they were out at such a time.— LONGTON protested that the children were under the Control of Mr. Mines, so that he was sure that they Would be well looked atter. It was very hard if they Could not have a little festivity at Christmas time.---The CHAIRMAN said that several of the ratepayers disapproved of the children going round soliciting. Personally he thought that the children should not be out at such a late hour.—The di,cussirn then dropped.

THE REGISTRAR OF WINWICK. •The CLERK read a letter from the Registrar General with reference to the vacant post of registrar of Win- wick, recommending that the district be merged in the Newton district. The letter pointed out that the popu- lation had been 1601 in 1891, which was 160 less at the Previous census. The whole sub-district appeared to form part of No. 2 district, and the relieving officer Ought to be able to fix registration stations for the parish, which would be ample—Mr. W. HOUGHTON 103ved that it was necessary to have a separate registra- tion district as heretofore ; Mr. Bowes had plenty to do at. Newton, and ,:s !11,2, asylum was to he built at Win- "tch, there was a probability of an increase of popula- tioa--Mr. SHAW seconded the motion, and Mr. MATHER SUPPOrted.—Mr. A. J. JOLLEY moved and Mr. Muni seconded, that the recommendation be adopted.—Upon being plat to the Vote only four, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, A. Jolley, Muir and Turtoi;, Anted for the amendment which was lost. The CLERK announced that there were three applicants for the p3st which would be filled at th next meeting.

It was also pro- were .that tirappenhall,Thelwall, and Latchford, which unionla. the district would shortly be cut off from the. Parincy?hir.:, A. J. div.head: NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMDi- SIONERS.
div.p: NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMDi- SIONERS.
SPEECH BY MR. J. W. EMMETT.

The Newton Board of Commissioners for the first time, met in the New Town Hall, Earlestown. on Monday afternoon, when they held their monthly meeting. There were present Mr. J. W. Emmett. (chairman), and Messrs. T. Ormand, T. Foster, P. McMahon, G. Ratcliffe, and J. Collingwood, also J. E. Worsley (law clerk), and R. Brierley (surveyor).

div.head: INTERESTING SPEECH BY MR. EMMETT.
div.p: INTERESTING SPEECH BY MR. EMMETT.

The Chairman, before proceeding to the usual busi- ness, said that as they were met in that new Hall for the first time, he should like to take the opportunity of saying a few words about the building and also about the progress that Earlestown had made during the past quarter of a century. It was now 20 years since he came to the town. Before he arrived in Earlestown lie received the impression that the town was a model one. Well, he could only say that upon reaching EArlestown, he discovered that his expectations had been raised rather too high, for he discovered that the sanitary arrange- ments were by int, means of a perfect character, and certainly nothing like what he had been led to anticip- ate. Many of the streets were unpaved and unsewered, and, in fact, some of tkem when there had been two *r three days' rain were some inches thick with mud, and it was not an unfrequent occurrence for a woman,when crossing a street, to lose one of her shoes in the mire. (Laughter.) So much for the sanitary arrangements of the town at the time. Then the place was also badly lighted with gas of a very impure character. He wished them to understand that he did not find any fault with the gas manager of those days because he had not such perfect arrangements for the purifying of gas as existed to-day. In regard to the water supply he could assure them that there was practically no source for obtaining water at all. What they did obtain was received from the heavens, and was caught in water tubs as it drained from the slates of the houses. There was, indeed,a small pump, which if he was not mistaken, stood in close proximity to the site of that new Hall. Well now, he would compare those days with the present. He could say that now the sanitary arrangements of the town were almost perfect,and there was no doubt that had the Local Government Board given their sanction to certain borrowing powers which the Commissioners applied for, there would have remained very little in the sanitary ar- rangements of Earlestown for the most fastidious sanit- arian to cavil at. (Hear, hear.) Of course there was no reason why the Local Government Board should not grant those powers,but still they all knew that at present there was no immediate prospect of their doing so. Then turning to the making of the streets and their condition, they were all aware that the streets were well paved, well kept, and indeed almost as complete as could be reasonably expected. (Hear, hear.) There was the question of the gas supply. They had now the advan- tages of proper purification in addition to an ample sup- ply at charges of a reasonable character. (Hear, hear.) And now he would come to a very important question, namely,othat of the water supply. They were all aware that much had been said on this question,and he thought it was due to his position that he should offer a few words of explanation. (Hear, hear.) In order to do this it would be necessary for him to refer back to ancient history. Some of them—particularly Mr. Foster—would recollect that in 1873 the Commis- sioners entered into an agreement with the London aed North-Western Railway Company. The terms of this agreement were that the Commissioners should supply the company with gas at 3s. 3d. per thousand, whilst they were charging the public 4s. 3d. In return the company agreed to supply the Commissioners with water at threepence per thousand gallons ; and it was agreed that should the price of gas increase,the company should be charged in ratio to the reduction which was made to them at the outset. Well now in 1874, in the month of January, the prite of gas was increased to the company to 4s. 4d., the public getting it at the same price, and thus in the second year the Commissioners broke faith with the company. In June of the same year the price of gas was reduced to the public and the company alike to 45., and in July, 1877. it was reduced again to 3s. 3d.to the company and 3s. 61to the public. Again, in April, 1879, it was reduced to 3s. to the com- pany and to 3s. 3d. to the public, so that there was now threepence difference between the prices charged to the public and to the company. This continued for some length of time, in fact, until 1883, when a redection to 2s. 3d. was made alike to the public and. to the com- pany. So they would see that although there had been a general reduction in the price of gas of a shilling, no reduction in ratio as was agreed upon, had been made to the company. In January, 1888, however, he (the speaker) raised the question, and brought home to the Commissioners the fact that they had broken faith with the railway company. The Commissioners ultimately agreed to reduce their charges to the company by 2d. per thousand; but in 1890 it was raised again to 2s. 2d. They would be aware of the cause of that further in- crease; for they knew that Mr. Gillespie and several others would never allow the question to rest until they had got reduced the prices to their own and other firms. Well, the company stood the advance as long as they could, and then he was afraid that had it not been for his interposing and advising the directors of the com- pany, they would have raised the price of water. He begged of them not to do so, and they took his advice for some time, although they had been compelled to sink a new well, and lay fresh J?lant. They could not fail, then, to se that the... company had be- haved more fairly to the Commissioners, than the Commissioners had behaved to them. They were aware, of course that the price of water had been increased, but ho wished them to understand that he was in no way responsible for this. Somebody else must take upon their shoulders the burden. He had nothing to do with the supplying of the water or the prices—he was simply responsible for its conveyance. (Applause.) In conclusion he would refer to the new Town Hall. He thought no one could accuse the Commissioners of an unwise step in erecting such a fine, substantial building. (Hear, hear.) It was an ornament to the town and would be for generations to come. (Hear, hear.) With those few remarks he would conclude sincerely hoping that Earlestown would continue to prosper as it had pros- pered during the past quarter of a century. (Ap- plause.)

div.head: HIGHWAYS COMMITTEE.
div.p: HIGHWAYS COMMITTEE.

The ordinary business was then proceeded with. The minutes of the Highway Committee were read, showinge that a meeting of thki Commissioners was held on th 19th December. An application was then read from the Postal Authorities asking permission to place a pillar letter box opposite the post office Earle-street. It was resolved that the sanction of the authority be given sub- ject to the approval of the Surveyor. Correspondence was read from Messrs. Neill and Sons as to the payment of £2OO retained on the architects last certificate. It was ordered that a cheque be drawn in their favour for the amount. Plans for the erection of two houses in Park-road for Miss M. Appleton, and alterations and additions to " Picton Villa " High-street for Miss M. Winstanley were submitted and approved.—The Chair- man in proposing the adoption of the minutes said he wished to propose that the minute referring to the pillar box he left in abeyence, as he had come to the conclu- sion that the matter had not been properly considered by the Committee.—Mr. G. Ratcliffe seconded the motion and the minutes with the exception of the one referring to the pillar box were adopted.

div.head: GAS COMMITTEE.
div.p: GAS COMMITTEE.

A meeting of this Committee was held on the 19th December. The gas manager's report was then read. It slowed that the cost for coal and cannel had been ,12s. 6d. per ton against us. 6d. during the same month last year. Correspondence was read by Mr. Brierley, with the Whitecross Company respecting their short supply of cannel and nuts, and it was agreed that unless the supply was delivered in pccordance with the con- tract, supplies should be obtained elsewhere, against the Company. The carbonizing account for the month showed that the fuel used was 461 tons, 14 cwts., and gas made was 4,633,800 feet or an average of 10,657 feet per ton for fuel used.—The minutes were adopted.— The minutes of the other Committees which contained nothing of public interest, were also adopted.
AN IMPORTANT RESOLUTION.

The Chairman preposed the adoption of the following resolution: "Resolved that the Improvement Commis- sioners for the district of Newton-in-Makerffeld, in the County of Lancaster, being the Urban Sanitary Autho- rity for the said district, do hereby adopt the following Acts of Parliament, to wit: The Public Healths Act Amendment Act 1890(53 v., 54 Vict., Chap. 59) and the Private Street Works Act 1892 (55v., 56 Vict., Ch. 57), the said Acts to come into operation and to extend and- apply to the said district of Newton-in-Makerfield on and from' 20th of February, 1894."—Mr. Ormand, in seconding the motion made a comprehensive statement in favour of the resolution.—Mr. G. Ratcliffe and Mr. McMahon strongly opposed the resolution, the latter because it would cause too much litigation, and the former because it was against the interests of property owners.—A somewhat heated discussion followed, after which a vote was taken.—Messrs. Emmett, Ormand, and Collingwood voted for the resolution and Messrs. Rat- cliffe, McMahon and Fester voted against it.—The Chair- man recorded his casting vote in favour of the resolu- tion, which was accordingly adopted.
APPLICATION FROM THE LIBERAL CLUB.

A letter was read from tke Secretary to the Liberal Club asking if the Commissioners were prepared to let the buildings on the market ground, formerly used as municipal offices, for political club purposes, and if so, to favour him with the amount of lease and general con- ditions of tenancy.—The Chairman: I am afraid that we cannot let these premises, seeing that they are on the market groand.—The Clerk: We cannot let them for any but market purposes. This concluded the business.

div.head: TITLE EXAMINER, SATTTRDAY, JANUARY 13, 1894.
div.p: TITLE EXAMINER, SATTTRDAY, JANUARY 13, 1894.

connection which has extended over seventeen years. I feel I should like to express to you my sincere thanks for the courtesy and kindness which I have received at your hands, and to assure you that any assistance that it may be in my power to give you in the future I shall be most happy to render.—l am, gentlemen, yours respectfully, D. M. F. GASKIN."—The Town-clerk (Mr. W. J. Jeeves) said the proper course would be to accept the resignation, leaving the question of the date upon which the notice should take effect to be arranged by the cliairman.--Alderman Cook, in moving that the resignation be accepted, commented upon the admirable manner in which Mr. Gaskin had constructed permanent works, which were a very great credit to him, and upon the efficient way he bad for seventeen years conducted the business of the water department.—Councillor Forster considered it very generous on the part of Mr. Gaskin to say the Corporation might call upon him for any special knowledge he possessed, and which would materially assist his successor.—The Chairman (Alder- man MlBryde) also paid a tribute to the efficiency cf Mr. Gaskin as an engineer.—The resignation was accepted, and Mr. Gaskin said he had arranged with the chairman of the Water Committee at Nottingham to be allowed to render assistance to St. Helens if called upon. (Hear, hear.)—The St. Helens Corporation are about to proceed with the construction of new waterworks at Melling, and Mr. Gaskin, who has prepared plans and estimates, will probably be consulted during the progress of the works.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
THE WATER ENGINEER.
The appointment of Mr. Gaskin, the water engineer of St. Helens, to be water engineer of Nottingham, at a salary of £6OO, was confirmed at a meeting of the Not- tingham Town Council on Monday.

div.head: BREACH OF THE COAL MINES REGULATION ACT.
div.p: BREACH OF THE COAL MINES REGULATION ACT.

At St. Helens on Tuesday, John Sumner collier, of Rainford, was fined lts. 6d , includinz costs, for corn- itiitting a breach of the Coal Mines Regulation Act by carrying a pipe in the Rainford Coal Company's colliery.

div.head: DEATH RATE.
div.p: THE DEATH RATE.

At the fortnightly meeting of the St. Helens Health Committee on Wednesday, the medical officers (Drs. McNicoll and Robertson) reported that the death rate had been only 17.5 against 18.74 in the previous fort- night and 29.10 in the corresponding period of last year. The rate of mortality was very low considering the very severe weather. There had been two deaths from typhoid fever,and five notifications of the same disease.
GREAT CONSUMPTION OF WATER.

The water engineer of St. Helens reported on Wednes- day that during the four wevits ending the 30th ult, the total quantity of water pumped amounted to 91,837,518 gallons. They had had all their engines fully at work, but still the water was dropping. The amount going into the town was enormous. He complained of the great waste occasioned by persons leaving their taps running. This did not refer to the frosty weather, but to the general waste. It was decided to warn house- holders against wasting water.

div.head: SATURDAY'S POLICE COURT.
div.p: SATURDAY'S POLICE COURT.

On Saturday a youth named Joseph Handley,of Cyril- at., was fined 53. or seven days for stealing six herrings, value 2;1-d.,be1onging to Thomas Crane —John Hasleden, an elderly man, of Bickerstaffe-st., was charged with stealing 53. from a drawer in a bedroom which he and a fellow lodger named James Rose occupied. Prisoner had been previously convicted of stealing money. The magis- trates said this appeared to be a habit which was grow- ing on him. It seemed a very bad case, and he would be sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment without the option of a fine.
A LUNATIC AT LARGE.

At St. Helens Police Court, on Wednesday afternoon, an order was made to commit John Edmondson, of Rimmer-st., a painter in the employ of the St. Helens Corporation, to the asylum, he being a lunatic at large. Edmondson imagined that a number of persons were trying to poison him, and was on Tuesday night found wandering in an excited condition in Church-st. THE LOCAL BRANCH OF THE PRESTON BANE.

The Preston Banking Company have arranged to pur- chase the valuable central block of property at the corner of Church-street and Naylor-street, St. Helens, and expect possession at the end of this month. Altera- tions will then be at once proceeded with. Mr. W. Varley, the branch manager, on Tuesday received the gratifying information from the general manager that the directors had decided to refund him the £250 which he had to pay at the instance of Parr's Banking Com- pany, when he severed his connection with them and undertook the branch managership for the Preston Company. The fine was divided between the local hospitals.

div.head: ANGLING ASSOCIATION.
div.p: THE ANGLING ASSOCIATION.

At the annual general meeting of the St. Helens Anglin°, Association, on Wednesday night, a hearty vote of thanks was passed to the owners and agents of the Eccleston Mill Dam, Garswood and Stanley Dams, Farn- , ! worth Water, Sherdley Dam, Eccleston Pits', the St. Helens Corporation Parks Committee, and the Newton Dam for the privileges enjoyed and tor the support received, without which they could not continue to find waters to fish under their present low subscription, as nearly all the public waters are untishable. Mr.J.Wood, the hon. secretary, resigned, and a vote of thanks was unanimously accorded to him for his past services, and for which he was voted three guineas. The officers elected were :—Mr. R. G. Brook, president ; Mr. F.A.R. Neill, chairman ; Messrs. H. Waizbom, J. Woods, J. H. Richardson, C. Anders, C. Datige, W. Moore, J. Wells, P. Houghtom, J. Gerard, and W. Morris, committee ; Mr. G. Burdikin. treasurer; and Mr. R. W. Whitaker, lion. secretary. This is the second time Mr. Whitaker has undertaken the duties of hon. secretary. He was the first secretary, and one of the original promoters of the association. DEATH OF ALDERMAN WILCOCK.

The death took place on Tuesday morning of Alderman Thomas Charles Wilcock, provision merchant, Baldwin- st., St. Helens. Mr. Wilcock was taken id on Decem- ber 26, and Dr.Masson was called in. Typhoid fever set in, and despite all e&rts, he succumbed as stated. The deceased gentleman was a Conservative in politics, anti entered the St. Helens Town Council in succession to his father in March 1877. He had since sat continuously for Windle Ward until 1889, when on the enlargement of the Council he was elevated to the alderma.nic bench. He was chairman of the School Attendance Committee, and was a member of the Health, Parks and Markets Public Buildings and Cemetery, Horses, Parliamentary, and Finance Committees. He was also chairman of the St. Helens Rugby Football Club Committee, and was formerly a lieutenant-colonel in the 2nd Lancashire Volunteer Royal Engineers. Deceased was fifty years of age, and leaves a widow and family. The flag was flying half-mast from the Town Hall. It is, perhaps, prema- ture to mention what may be done by the St. Helens Town Council with regard to the aldermanic vacancy but there is already a probability that the Mayor (Mr, Arthur Sinclair) will be elected.

div.head: WAT/R-SOFTENING PROCESS.
div.p: THE WAT/R-SOFTENING PROCESS.

At the monthly meeting of the Water Committee of the ‘E.t. Helens Corporation yesterday, Alderman J. C. Gamble re:erred to remarks made at the last Council meeting that although the new water-softening plant had been in work for some considerable time, the water was still very hard. There appeared to be 14 degrees of hard- ness in the water, and it should, in Alderman Gamble's opinion, be much softer than that.—Mr. John Forster said very soft water was not palatable,—Mt. James Burchall said there were complaints that the pans be- came white after using the water, and he would like to know if there was any explanation.—Alderman Gamble, C. 8., replied that the St. Helens water had always made the pipes scaly.—Dr. Robertson said the cause of the white scale was their having taken the iron out of the water.—Mr.F. R. D. Nuttall (Deputy Mayor) said there used to be an incrustation, but since the softening plant had been in work it was a fine white powder. The pipes from the reservoir to the town had become incrusted, and it would take a considerable time to clear that in- crustation away.—The Chairman said there was not the least doubt the water was improving, and that one-third of the hardness had been taken out at it.—Alderman J. C. Gamble said they ought to be taken one-half out of it. The Water Engineer said there was still a considerable quantity of iron in the pipes. and that had to be cleared it was decided to take daily tests near the softening works and at the Town Hall.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF THE WATER ENGINEER.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF THE WATER ENGINEER.

At the monthly meeting of the Water Committee of the St. Helens Corporation on Wednesday, the following was read from the water engineer (Mr. D. M. F. Gaskin, M.1.C.E.) :—" To the Chairman and Members.—Gentle- men,—l beg to inform you that I have been appointed water engineer of Nottingham at a salary of £6OO per annum, and therefore have to tender my resignation of the post I hold as your engineer. div.head: PITSHAFT E-XPLOSION AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: THE PITSHAFT E-XPLOSION AT ST. HELENS.

PROSECUTION OF COLLIERY PROPRIETORS. At St. Helens, on Monday, before Messrs. W. J. Thomson, W. Gamble, and B.A. Dromgoole. the Sut- ton Heath and Lea Green Colliery Company, Limited, and Mr. Thomas Pennington, their certi- ficated manager, were summoned at the instance of Mr. Henry Hall, Government inspector of mines,for not having an adequate amount of ventilation in ,their coalmine so as to render harmless the noxious gases; and for allowing naked lights to be used in such coalmine. Mr. Mulholland (instructed by Messrs. Collins, Robinson, and Co., Liverpool), ap- peared for the prosecution ; Mr. T. Swift appeared for the defendant company ; Mr. J. 0. Swift for the manager; and Mr. P. Mearns held watching briefs for the relatives of the deceased man Jones for four of the injured men, and for Richard Crean, a wit- ness subpcened by the prosecution. Mr. Mulholland stated that section 75 of the Coal Mines Act made it obligatory upon colliery proprietors to provide sufficient ventilation to render harmless noxious vapours, and the term "mine "included all new shafts in course of sink- ing. Defendants were sinking a new shaft, and on the 14th October men were engaged bricking sixteen yards from the bottom, and had bricked round a seam of coal from which gas came in large quantities, when a piece of lighted candle, by which the men were working, fell down into the gas, and an explosion occurred,eight men being seriously injured,death ensuing in one case. It ap- peared that at the inquest Mr.Pennington,the manager, admitted he was not aware, and did not contemplate, that he had any supervision over a shaft which was being sunk by a contractor, and he (Mr. Mulholland) ventured to say that a large amount of what had occurred arose from that understanding. The shaft was 400 yards deep, and the men were working sixteen yards from the bot- tom, and the air brattice was carried down to ten yards above the scaffold. This distance, it was contended, was too far up, and did not allow a draught of fresh air to reach the men or go to the place where the gas had es- caped, and of which there had been warning. Mr. Hall, Government inspector, said the air boards ought to have been carried four yards lower down, and then there should have been crinoline battice (canvass fixed on hooks). When gas was found steps should have been taken to get the air below the scaffold. The length of the bricking was too great, and he had told them pre- viously that bricking should only be done in lengths of ten or twelve yards. When he (Mr. Hall) visited the pit in the atterneon after the accident, he found gas coming up from behind the brickwork. Mr. Swift asked if the Government inspector could suggest anything more that the company ought to have done after the appointment of all the required officials and publishing the rules? Mr. Mulholland objected, and Mr. Swift said he would not press it, as a refusal answered the purpose just as well as a reply.—The next witness was Patrick M'Nulty, labourer, who sa.ici there was gas which fired eight days before this occurrence.— Richard Crean said the gas took fire twice on the day before the accident, and was put out by the men's waist- coats. They, however, continued work. Witness averred that if the chargeman did his duty he would be " sacked."—Mr. Thomas Swift submitted that the defendant company could not be convicted, because they had taken all reasonable means by publishing and to the best of their power enforcing rules and appointing all officials required by the Act. This accident was unfore- seen. and one which human foresight or ingenuity could not prevent, and the company were not liable for such things.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, for the manager, said Mr. Pen- eington did not at the inquest repudiate his responsibil- ity for the management of the sinking pit, and he had exercised a constant supervision over it. On the after- noon prior to the accident he had been down twice. He had not heard of any gas being seen, and it would not be right to convict him.—Mr. Isaiah Pigott, of Burs- cough Junction, the contractor, said No. 1 pit had been sunk to a depth of 500 yards without anything occurring and this pit was at a depth of 400 yards when the acci- dent occurred. The appliances were the same in one as the other. The ventilation was on a perfect system, and naked lights were used in No. 1 as well as in No. 2. Witness had been connected with collieries for forty-four years, and had taken sinking contracts for twenty-seven years.—Mr. J. Martland, foreman sinker; Mr. T. Pen- nington, certificated manager; and Mr. Clark, mining engineer, Newton-le-Willows, were then called and gave evidence.—Jeseph Eddy, one of the injured men, who had his hands bandaged, said from first to last there was nothing to lead him to think there was danger. The magistrates retired, and in about fifteen minutes returned and said they had decided to dismiss the charge of not providing adequate ventilation. Mr. Mulholland then said he would proceed with the second information, of not using safety lamps. Mr. T. Swift thought it an ungracious thing to go on with this case. The prosecution had tried to prove that there was not adequate ventilation, but the defence had ,hown that there was. The questi-m was whether there was likely to be an accumulation of gas, and on this point the Government inspector admitted that until the explosion took place he did not think there was likely to be an accumulation. After some argument, this charge was also dismissed.

div.head: HAWARDEN RENT AUDIT.
div.p: THE HAWARDEN RENT AUDIT.
MR. GLADSTONE AS.A. TREE-FELLER.

Mr. Henry Gladstone presided at the Hawarden rent audit dinne.r on Wednesday night. Mr. John Roberts proposed the health of Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone. and spoke of Mr. Gladstone's wonderful tree-felling perform- ances. Mr. Gladstone was a true tree-feller, and with his sons William and Herbert once felled 58 trees on his farm. Mr. Henry Gladstone, responding, said cir- cumstances had recently led to the banishment of his father at this season, but next year he hoped to be present.
