div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

' FRIDAY. In the House of Commons on Friday evening Mr. CAMPEELL-BANNERMAN I:1 answer to Mr. -13nitics, said the Government had come ii the conclusion that the condi- tions and circumstances of the ordnance factories and the nature cif the work done in them were such as to admit of a reduction of the hours of labour to forty-eight per week with advantage both to the public service and to the men employed, and he would direct that the change should be brought into operation as soon as the neces- sary arrangements could be made. He had no expecta- tion that there would be any necessity for an alteration in wages. Sir U. KAY-SHIITTLEWORTH, replying to a question ,said ; the officering and manning of the fleet would be the sub- ject of announcement when the Estimates were laid be- fore the House, and he did not think the House would be disappointed at the result. The House again went into Committee on the Local Government (Parish Councils) Bill. Mr. FOWLER an- nounced that the Government proposed to continue in office all local authorities till the first election under the bill. The "appointed day "day was to be the Bth of November, and a bill would be introduced to accelerate the registers. The right hon. gentleman moved his new clause removing the new qualification of women. Mr. STOREY moved an amendment to limit the powers of the clause to " the purposes of the Act.' The CHAIRMAN ruled that the clause would not be in order unless the words" for the purposes of this Act " were inserted at the beginning, and in this form the clause was added to the bill. An amendment moved on behalf of Mr. CAINE providing that no meetings should be held on premises where intoxicating liquor- was sold or supplied was op- posed by Mr. FOWLER and was defeated by 70 to 52. On the motion for adjournment of the House Mr. MAJORI- BANKS said there would be one day's interval between the Committee and Report stages of the bill, and that time would be utilised in part for a discussion on the Feather- stone Inquiry report.

div.head: MONDAY.
div.p: MONDAY.

In the House of Commons on Monday evening Mr. A. MORLEY explained, in reply Loa question put by Captain M'Calmont, that the irregularity in the mail service from Great Britain to Ireland via Stranraer was due mainly to the late arrival of the mail train at Carlisle, and said that the p,sAibility of relieving the train to some extent was under inquiry. Mr. J. Morley, in answer to Mr. Sexton, said an order would shortly be issued reducing the rating qualification for poor-law guardians in Ireland to £l2. Sir M. Hicks-Beach having asked for information as to the affray on the West Coast of Africa, Mr. BUXTON said the Government had received a telegram from the Gy- enor of Sierra Leone, and it did not amplify but only confirmed the telegram already published. The Govern- ment were under the belief that the collision occurred in the English sphere of influence, but on that and other points they awaited further information before making any definite statement. The House again went into Committee on the Local Government Bill, and discussion was resumed on Mr. Fowler's new clause giving the Local Government Board power in certain cases to authorise a parish council to hire laud compulsorily for allotment purposes. Mr. CHANNIIM while admitting the importance of the raform proposed, expressed regret that this clause had been selected for compromise. Mr. Chaplin spoke against the principle of compulsory hiring. Sir W. Harcourt, said the Government was prepared to stand or fall by this proposal. In the subsequent discussion Mr. ARCH said the bill would lay the foundation of the future prosperity of rural life. The clause was read a second time without a division. Mr. Chaplin moved an amendment giving the owner of land proposed to be hired the right to require the Parish Council to purchase on terms of pay- ment by instalments. Mr. Fowler opposed the amend- ment, which on a division L-iy defeated by 129 to 78. An amendment, moved by Mr. Charming-, to omit from the clause the limit of four acres in respect of hired allot- ments, was rejected by 138 to 47. TUESDAY.

In the House of CommNns on Tuesday evening, Mr. MUNDELLA, answering a question, said that if it could be proved that any person applied a false or misleading description to foreign or colonial meat he was liable to penalties under' the Merchandise Marks Act. Sir U. KAT-SHUTTLEWORTH, in reply to a question put by Mr. Banbury, stated that a charge brought against a Government contractor at Willenhall of" sweating "and infringing the terms of the resolution of the House of February, 1891, had, in the opinion of the Admiralty, been established, and he had been informed that he would be removed from the list of contractors unless he complied with their requirements. Mr. BUXTON said, in reply to a question, that he was afraid there was no hope of safety of Captain Wilson. Mr. ASQUITH was questioned by Sir F. Mappin about the prosecution of a number of men and boys for taking part in the Rockingham and Elsecar colliery riots, and he said he was informed by the Judge that in his opinion the magistrates would have failed in their duty if they had not committed the defendants for trial. The House again went into Committee on the Local Government (Parish Councils) Bill. After several amend- ments had been rejected Mr. Fowler's new clause relating to the hiring of land for allotments was added to the bill In the course of the discussion on a new clause proposed by Mr. Atherley Jones, which was withdrawn, relating to women's suffrage, Mr. FOWLER said he was prepared to move to recommit the bill on report in order to carry out his promise on this question in its entirety. On consideration of the definition clause Mr. Fowler moved an amendment defining " ecclesiastical charities." To this several amendments were moved, but they were defeated on a division, and the clause was added to the bill. The Committee stige was completed before mid- night, and the Report stage was fixed for Thursday. WEDNESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Wednesday Sir. U. KAY- SHUTTLEWORTH, in reply to Major Jones, said the Admir- alty thoroughly recognised the importance of dividing the shipbuilding work between the dockyards and private firms. The House considered the Lord's amendments to the Sea Fisheries (Scotland) Bill, disagreed with thesq amendments, and ad )pted Sir George Trevelyan's motions for the division of the seaboard counties into fishery districts, and for the more popular constitution of the fishery district committees. The debate en the bill was adjourned. Mr. MARJORIBANKS, in answer to Mr. Balfour, said the House would have to meet on February 12 to receive the amendments to the Local Government Bill from the Lords ; but the amendments could not be considered on that day. Mr. J. AUSTIN called attention to the Featherstone Commission report, and moved that it was desirahle that reasonable compensation should be awarded to the families of the two men who were shot dead by the military during the riots on September 7. Mr. NUSSEY seconded the motion, and a long debate followed. The report of the Commission was considered an impartial one, but the action of the magistrates and the military was by some speakers strongly condemned. The chief plea in support of compensation as that the two men were peaceful citizens, mere onlookers, and took no part in the riot. Mr. ASQUITH, in reply, said it had been the imperative duty of the Government to sift the facts. Those responsible for the preservation of order in the clunty had shown a certain want of foresight. In fact there had been a deplorable absence of co-operation
between the civil and the military authorities. Soldiers

in putting down civil disturbances should act in the ' presence of magistrates ; but in the emergency which aros':- the firing of the troops on the crowd was justified. That being the case there could be no legal claim for compensation, but the Government would take the request into consideration, and, without making any promise, he thought compassionate compensation might be gtanted. TIP: motion was withdrawn, and the H.,use adjourned at five o'clock. THURSDAY

In the Floue of Commons on Thursday evening, the HOME SECRETARY, answering several questions, said that in admonishing recently appointed magistrates not to allow politics to influence their conduct on the bench the Clerk of the Peace for the West Riding of Yorkshire had strangely misconceived the duties and privileges of his office, and that the fee of four guineas which he de- manded from the new justices had never been author- ised by statute.

Mr..J. LOWTHER asked whether it was the intention of the Government to enforce their labour stipulations on home contractors only, leaving foreign competitors free from such restraints. :Sir J. T. HIBBERT said he saw no reason why foreign contractors should be placed at an advantage over the traders of this country. Mr. ASQUITH, interrogated as to the appointment of a female factory inspector for the Belfast district, said he did not see a prospect of having more than four such inspectors for the whole of great Britain and Ireland, and he could not undertake that any one of them should be permanently resident in any one centre. Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNER3LAN in reply to Mr. Hanbury, I said it was not expected that any additional workmen would be required as a result of the reduction of hours at the War Office factories, save in exceptional cases. Mr. J. MORLEY informed Mr. Dodd that up to the end of August last there had been provided in Ireland under the Labourers Acts 10,142 cot'ages at a cost of £1,206,000, an average of about £ll9 for each cottage. Answering Mr. Bytes, Mr. GLADSTONE said he was very doubtful whether the present moment was one at which any representations in favour of mutual disarma- ment could be made advantageously to the European Powers.

The House proceeded to consider the Local Govern- ment Bill as amended in Committee. Mr. TRITTON moved that no meeting of a parish or district council should be held on premises licensed for the sale at intoxicating liquor, except where no other suitable room was available. Mr. FOWLER said the Govern- ment prupo3ed to accept the clause with the addi- tion of words to the effect that no meeting should be so held except where no other suitable roam was available either free of charge or at reason- able cost, and thus amended the amendment was adopted. Mr. Courtney moved an amendment to pro- vide for minority or proportional representation. Mr. Fowler opposed and Mr. Balfour supported the amend- ment, which on a division was rejected by 153 to 80. Mr. H. HonritusE moved an amendment to give the parish meeting a voice in the expenditure of the Parish Council when it exceeded a rate of a penny in the pound. With the substitution, at the suggestion of Mr. Fowler, of threepence for a penny, the amendment was agreed to. Mr. LONG moved to insert a clause the object of which was that occupiers should pay the rates them- selves. The motion was defeated by 123 to 68.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHITRCHES-WARRINGTON.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHITRCHES-WARRINGTON.
WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.

Special New Year services were held in Wycliffe Church on Sunday. A young people's service was held in the morning, when suitable hymns were sung. The Pastor (the Rev. J.Yonge) delivered an address to young people from the text "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom ; a good understanding have all they that do His commandments." At the close of the service Mr. Yonge presented Bibles to the members of his catechu- men class. The class is composed of young persons who have attained the age of 15 years. Since its inaugura- tion in 1881 the class has had upon its roll almost 350 names. Preceding the presentations Mr.Yonge addressed a few appropriate remarks to the class. At the evening service the subject of the sermon was the Wycliffe motto for 1894 "Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, to-day,and for ever '.' Hebrews 13c., Bv. There were large congre- gations at both services.

div.head: SA'NKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CHAPEL.
div.p: SA'NKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

The Rev. J. Kirain occupied the pulpit of the above chapel on Sunday night, and took as the subject of his discourse "Say unto the children of Israel that they go forward," from which he drew lessons suitable to the first Sunday in the year. After the sermon, a covenant service was held, at which about fifty persons attended. Mr. Kirtlan at the commencement of the service said that this meeting was peculiar to the Methodists,and was very appropriate as the beginning of another year. The service, which was a very impressive one, was then pro- ceeded with, and was brought to a close by prayer by Mr.J. Summersgill, and the pronouncing of the Benedic- tion by the Rev. J. Kirtlan.

div.head: ADDRESS TO WORKINGMEN.
div.p: ADDRESS TO WORKINGMEN.

At the Unit Irian Chapel, Cairo-street, on Sunday night, the pastor, the Rev. W. H. Drummond, gave his monthly address for workingmen, entitled " Onward, Upward, Heavenward." It was, as usual, of an able and interesting character, and considerable interest was taken in the discourse, by the large congregation which was present.

div.head: 'VVYCLIFFE P.S.A.
div.p: THE 'VVYCLIFFE P.S.A.

The usual meeting of this P.S.A., was held on Sunday afternoon, and was largely attended. Mr. J. Podmore was the chairman, and addressed the meeting on the brotherhood of man, urging on all the necessity of doing; some service in helping forward "the good time com- ing." Mr. Power of Manchester, who paid his second visit congratulated the church on having such a large attendance. He thought that they in Warrington had great powers, and many opportunities for doing good. The speaker afterwards delivered a powerful address, basing his remarks on the Jews' choice of Barrabas, giving instances from his own experience showing that the same choice was being made at the present time. He looked forward to a better state of things, when there would be fewer public ;houses, when the betting men would be looked upon as the parasities of Society, and when masters,would take men into their confidence, and not look 'hem out, When they chose Christ as their best friend there would be a brighter time. Mr. U. Jeffery contributed a solo. The Rev. J. Yonge and Mr. A. Long also took part in the service.

div.head: WHO WOULD BE CZAR?
div.p: WHO WOULD BE CZAR?
WHOLESALE POISONING.

The St. Petersburg press is instructed to deny that an attempt was made to poison the Czar at the recent ban- quet to the members of the Order of St. George. The facts, however, remain that the Czar was present at the banquet, that forty of the guests died from eating poisoned food, and that his Majesty was ill for some time afterwards. Whatever the Russian authorities may say, the shocking results of the banquet, whereby forty brave men lost their lives, will be classed with the terrible " accident "at Borti, ' when the Imperial train was thrown off the line and the Czar and his family had an almost miraculous escape from a dreadful death.

div.head: BOLD STABBING OUTRAGE. SHOCKING INJURIES TO A WOMAN.
div.p: THE BOLD STABBING OUTRAGE. SHOCKING INJURIES TO A WOMAN.

MEDICAL WITNESSES AT VARIANCE. On Monday afternoon, at the Widnes Police Court, before Councillor Gossage and Alderman Timmis, a married woman named Ellen Ellison, Union-lane, Bold, near Widnes, was again brought up on remand, charged with unlawfully wounding a young woman named Margaret Rimmer, at Bold, on the 11th ult. The case has been remanded several times, but the prosecutrix's condition was so serious that Monday was the first time she was able to appear in court. Mr. J. W. Knowles defended.

Margaret Rimmer, the prosecutrix, wh) was in a very weak condition, said she was a single woman,. and re- sided with her mother at Union Bridge Farm. Formerly her sister Jane was living at home, and did dressmaking. She made a dress for one of Mrs. Ellison's children, and on Monday, the 11th of December, the child came to her house and asked for some of the stuff which was left be- longing to her frock. Witness told-the child there was none left, but later on the same day her mother sent witness to the prisoner's house. It was about eight o'clock in the evening. Witness went to tell the prisoner that they had not got any stuff. The prisoner opened the door, and witness asked her what she meant by send- ing the little girl to ask for some stuff. Prisoner said to- witness, "You need not be offended by people asking for their own." Witness replied that she was not, and added, "We have lived thirty-two years in Bold, and you can inquire into our characters, as we always reckoned to do all that is right, and if you are not satis- fied you can bring an officer to search the house." Pri- soner said she, too, was decent, and, turning towards the kitchen, said to someone, " Thou'rt not of a drunken breed, art thou, Harry ?" Witness said, No, he is not; he is a gentleman for anything I know," The prisoner then slammed the door in her face, and witness turned to go away, w hen suddenly she heard the door open again. She turned her face aside to the sight, and then she saw the prisoner. Mrs. Ellison struck her with some- thing sharp about the face and ear, saying, "Take that." Prisoner then shut the door. Witness put her hand to the side of her face, and found that her ear was hanging, and that there was a big gash behind the ear. Blood was streaming across her face. She then went to the window and called to Mr. Ellison " Will you please let nne in, or come and do something for me ; your wife has hurt me, and lam sure I shall bleed to death." No one came out to her, and witness called again, and then Mr. Ellison came and opened the door. Just as witness was going in the house the prisoner made a rush towards the door, but her husband pushed her back against the wall. Mr. Ellison put a cold water bandage round the wound, and while doing so said to his wile," What bast thou done it with 9" The prisoner made no reply, but afterwards said to witness, " I'll teach you better." Witness did not say anything then, but afterwards she said to the prisoner, " I did not think people were al- lowed to murder people on their own premises." Wit- ness was quite sure she did not fall, and she afterwards walked home by herself. Dr. Casey was sent for, and he put stitches in the wound, but after he hai gone the wound commenced to bleed again, and Dr. Bates then came, and had attended her since. That day was the first time she had been out of the house since the occur- rence. At one time she thought she was going to die, and a magistrate was brought to take her depositions,but she was not able to make any statement. Cross-examined: She did not have high words with Mrs. Ellison, nor the prisoner with her. The prisoner first lost her temper when she slammed the door. Wit- ness did not use abusive language, and she did not, be- fore Dr. Bates came, take off the bandages which Dr. Casey had put on. She did not fall anywhere. Witness did not say to the prisoner, after she had struck her " Pll go to Police-constable Forster and make it warm for you." Prisoner struck her at least twice.
Mrs. Rimrner, mother of the prosecutrix, gave corro- borative evidence.

Dr. Hutchinson, ol Widnes, stated that on the 15th ult. the small carving knife (produced) was handed to him by Inspector Pattinson. He found blood upon it at a little distance froim the point, close to the edge. Dr. H. B. Bates. of St. Helens Junction, deposed to being called to Union Bridge Farm, Bold, about one o'clock in the morning of the 12:h ult, to see the injured woman. He found her suffering from a wound an inch and a half in length, extending from half an inch behind and cutting the right ear in two pieces. he 2.150 had two wounds on the right cheek. There had been hemor- rhage, and the patient was in a collapsed condition. The woman was in a very serious condition, and he did not think she would live through the night. The three wounds were clean cuts, and were probably done by blows from some sharp instrument. The knife pr4duced might cause them. He hardl.v thought a fall would produce the wounds he saw. It was possible, but not probable.

Dr. Casey, of Sutton,said that on the night of the 11th December he was called to see Miss Rif-rimer. He feund one wound on the scalp, one on the ri:..ht ear, and two on the right cheek, which were all superficial. About two-thirds ot the lobe of the right ear was divided. The wounds on the cheek were very slight, and he put two stitches into the upper one for appearance sake.. Ha did not consider the wound at the back of the ear of any importance, and he simply bandaged it. A little after midnight, and again between two and three o'clock in the morning, he was sent for, but he did not go, because he had been up three nights previously. and he did not consider another visit necessary. He w is teld the bleed- ing had started again,and he sent word that the wounds were to the bandaged. He could not say that ha told the women the wounds were serious. He might Maya told them that the wound on the ear was serious. The present weak condition of the injured woman had prob- ably nothing to clo with the wounds. Str.showed a deal of emotion, and the fact that she had been in bed some time might account for the weakness,

Mr. Knowles : Plenty of women with injuries stiqh as the prosecutrix suffered from would have been able to go about the following day. He did not consider the wounds dangerous per se. He now admitted that there was some seriousness about the wounds in consequence of the hemorrhage. Inspector Pattinson and Polioc-consble Forster also give evidence.

- Prisoner, in reply to the charge, said the prosecutrix made some nasty remarks,and she (prisoner) pushed her, and she fell on some broken crockery near the door. Prisoner was sent to the assizes for trial, bail being allowed.

div.head: LATE PROFESSOR TYNDALL.
div.p: THE LATE PROFESSOR TYNDALL.

As a lecturer, Professor Tyndall occupied a position almost by himself. It is no exaggeration to say that his lectures were models of what such efforts should be. Be led his hearers lightly and delicately through perplexing analyses and passages of thought without wearying, them, lighting up his address with little asides and local allusions. All through the delivery we were conscious that we were not listening simply to an investigator of Nature's secrets ; like the prophets of the old, the lec- turer was always looking beyond the mere question of the moment ;he saw visions of what the consequences. of any new discoveries might be. Science cannot bridge the gulf which separates the known from the unknown, so, by insensible gradations the restraints of the scien- tific investigator were laid aside, a rich vein of poetical fancy was brought into play, and generalisations were often made which were ph-haps more startling than legitimate. Those who heard Profes-or Tyndall' ad- dress in 1874 at Belfast, as President of the British As- sociation, will remember the storm of indignation which arose in the country as a result of one of these flights of the Professor's fancy. None the less, Professor Tyndall's , taste for speculation of this kind was the secret of much of his charm. . . Professor Tyndall married, In 1876, daughter of Lord Claud Hamilton ; and he resided for la greater portion of the year at Hindhead, Though for some time past his health had been in a fail- ing condition, his death at Haslemere on the 4th Decem- ber, 1893, came rather unexpectedly. He had been for his usual trip to Switzerland in the summer, but came back rather weaker than stronger for the change. His tailing health probably explains the force and bitterness kof his later public utterances on questions of the day. In reply to one of his sharpest letters on the Irish question 'a year or two ago, Mr. Gladstone playfully reminded him of the offer the Professor once made to him to take him up the Matterhorn. He said he preferred to remem- ber the Professor Tyndall of that day, and not as the angry controversialist and reviler of himself. That is how we all wish to remember Tyndall, and we should be worse than ungrateful if we flung any stones at him be- cause in his old age he sometimes' looked at life in an old man's way.—" The Cabinet Portrait Gallery."

THERE is no more important ques- Warrington and • Mon for Warrington at the presext the Canal. time than that to be found in its relations with the Ship Canal. It has been the fashion to talk as though the making of the canal would, as a matter of course, ensure a great future for the town as a centre of manufacture and commerce. Talk of that kind is rather mis- leading. What the Canal does is, so to speak, to bring to our very doors the possibilities of such a great future. This week we give interviews upon the subject of the canal with Mr. F. MONKS, J.P.,C.C., and Councillor R. T. FAIECLOUGH, both of whom are well qualified to give an opinion in the matter by reason of their life-long connection with the trade of the town and the interest they have displayed in municipal affairs. It will be noticed that both of these gentlemen agree that it almost entirely depends upon local enterprise whether Warrington is to derive any great advantage from the Canal or not. The opening of the Canal, in fact, affords one of those opportunities for the development and pros- perity of the town not likely to occur again for a very long time. Warrington has the advantage of being at the end of the tidal portion of the Canal, and of having a complete system of railway connections to all parts of the country and this gives it a splendid opportunity of making here a great centre of distribution, and also one of the nearest loading depots of the South-West Lanca- shire coal field. We have running in direct com- munication. with the town the five great trunk railway lines of the country—the London and North-Western, the Great Western, the Midland, the Great Northern, and the Manchester, Sheffield and Lincolnshire with all their connections. It may, of course, not be to the interest of the Man- ; chester Corporation to foster the growth of War- rington as a port,but it is quite possible that circum- stances may be such as to make it almost neces- sary for the large oce an-going steamers to stop here. The tides and the river Weaver give to the , portion of the Canal between Latchford Locks and Eastham an unexhaustible supply of fresh water, and the depth. of the Canal between these two points can be increased from twenty-six to thirty feet at any time and without any cost. After passing the entrance to the Canal at East- ham there are no practical difficulties in naviga- tion .either by day or by night, and the traffic over the Swing bridges at Runcorn, Moore, and Wal- ton is not likely to interfere seriously with the use of the waterway. A very proper and natural question to ask is : Upon whom falls t!,le duty and responsibility of taking the Iniative ? And,again, it may be asked, What can be done? In answer to these questions we mlay *refer to the suggested openings for private enterprise in developing shipping traffic made by Mr. MoNfis and Mr. FAIRCLOUGH ; and then, again, it may be pointed out that the Town Council, through its Rieis Committee, can do very much in two ways—first, by securing for the benefit of the town access to the docks where it is not already secured by the Canal Company itself, and affording to those likely to develop° the interests of the town easy and cheap co7:nectlons toL:n(1 from the

ways; secondly, by pressing the various railway companies to make connections with the docks and canal, and by at once officially calling the at- tention of the shipping companies to the position of Warrington as a cheap and convenient centre. Already there are complaints of the cost of deal- ing with traffic at the Manchester end, and it is possible that, after all,m he a tolls and other charges are met, there may be very little saving over the cost of landing at Liverpool. At Warrington, however, and at comparatively small cost, every railway company may have direct access to the Canal, so that goods could be dealt with in bulk without the cost and charges of transhipment or cartage. We have no doubt that our local manufacturers will be able to deal with their own traffic, but it will be an immense gain to them if Warrisgton could be made into a safe centre for loading the largest vessels with a full cargo, and also a coaling station with cheap fuel. Consider- ing the advantages possessed by Warrington,which are not equalled by those of any other place on. the Canal, our local authorities ought not to be slow in making the most of them. To adapt a. well-known quotation to the present situation ir, , may be truly said that there is at present a tide in the affairs of the town which, taken at the flood, may lead on to fortune.

The THE labour policy of the Govern- Government's ment has received a development, Labour Policy, within the last week or two which must give satisfaction to workmen in every trade and in all parts of the country. We do not now allude to the Parish Councils Bill, although it is. in some most important respects a labour measure. That Bill, when it becomes law, will inaugurate a change in rural life which will be far-reaching in its effect upon town as well as country workmen. • When Parish Councils get into a way of using the powers with which they will be endowed the attractions of village life for the best and most self-respecting labourers will be vastly increased. Such men will have opened before them a prospect, of something better than a long life of hard and poorly remunerated toil and an old age dependent upon private or public charity. It is reasonable, therefore, to anticipate that the mischievous migration of workmen from country to town will be checked, and it is perhaps not too sanguine to expect that a tide may begin to flow in the other direction. In either case the pressure in the labour market of the towns would be relieved to an extent that would fully entitle the Parish Councils Bill to be ranked as an important measure for the relief of labour. But, in other ways, the Government are more directly still meeting the wishes of workmen as declared through trades unions and labour congresses. We have already referred to the expressed inten- tions of the HOME SECRETARY to ask Parliament to sanction interference with the eXcessive hours of labour that are worked in the alkali and other dangerous trades.. This has been followed by an important announcement from the Secre- tary of War. Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN de- clares that he has carefully considered the question of reducing the hours of labour in the great ord- nance factories, and, as a result, has decided to introduce the" eight hours" day. This is, to say the least, a great victory for the advocates of shorter hours of labour. It is said that something like twenty thousand men who are directly under the control of the War Office will be affected by the change, and if, as is generally expected, the Admiralty follows sui t,those numbers will be very largely augmented. But these are only the direct results ; the indirect results are likely to be of even more consequence still. It is hardly likely that other Government departments which em- ploy any large number of workmen can for long ;ag behind, and, over and above this, the Govern- ment is "setting the pace" for the private em- ployers. Already, in fact, a few of the more en- lightened or venturesome of large private firms have adopted the eight hours systems—and no- tably those with which Mr. MATHER, M.P., and Mr. ALLAN, M.P., are connected. Their example will, however, be more convincing and contagious now that it is backed by the approval of a State department which employs a large body of work- men, both skilled and unskilled,

AN interesting debate took place The Featherstone • in the House of Commons on Tragedy. Wednesday evening with regard to the tragedy which was enacted at Featherstone during the late coal strike. The Government very wisely appointed a Commission to inquire into the circumstances which led up to the shooting of the two miners, GIBBS and DUGGAN, and the wounding of several others. No one has disputed the impartiality of the Commissioners' report, and the report very clearly showed that neither the
two miners named nor the others who wero

FOWL STEALING- AT THE WORICHOUSPI• . 9n Saturday night, or early on Sunday mallin'd some thieves got into the Workhouse grounds, an_ stole about IS fowls belonging to the master, Mr. Ward. Some of them were prize bird,: and had taken prizes at different shows througholtil the country. Not the slightest trace was left of t thieves. Thefts of a similar character have be% rather numerous in other parts of the town and I the siirm nding district. Worldru_s,t;

wounded, deserved the punishment that was in- flicted upon them. There had been rioting and some destruction, but, as it happened, not one of these men could be described as a rioter. They were at most merely spectators, and some of them were a considerable distance away from the scene of disturbance. The report went further than that; it very clearly implied that a good deal of remissiness and mismanage- ment had been displayed by the Yorkshire magis- trates and other authorities who were renponsible for the peace of the country. Had the police not been drafted away Wholesale from the disturbed districts to the race meeting at Doncaster there would, probably, have been no riot and no long- range weapons would have been discharged upon an unarmed crowd. When everything is taken into account it is not suprising that the House of Commons should give a sympathetic reception to a motion calling for compensation to the relatives of the two slaughtered miners as well as to the si%' who were maimed. When we say " sympathetic reception " we refer exlusively to the Liberal majority of the House,for the Tories with singular unanimity refrained from taking any part in the discussion, either on one side or the othe r. HOME SECRETARY was, no doubt, perfectly righ from a lawyers' point of view in saying that th° injured miners had no legal clai m for compensc- tion. No doubt everything was done by the act" ing magistrate and the military in strict accord" ance with law, but, in spite of that, we believe tlia't almost every one • will feel that a case has bee" made out for equitable compensatiomand that Dlr. Asurrx rightly interpreted the feeling of the country in practically pledging the Government te give compensation.

div.p: MARRIAGE OF MR. WASS,_ OF RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Parish Church on Wednesday morning a marriage was celebrated between Mrs. Nellie Hanson, daughter of Mr. R. C. Tinley, of Burton-on-Trent, and Mr. William R. Wass, proprietor of "The Wellington." The ceremony was carried out very quietly. Miss Nicholls acted as bridesmaid and Mr. T. H. Annett offi- ciated as groomsman, and the minister was the Rev. Joseph Holden. Subsequently the happy couple received the hearty congratulations of their numerous friends and acquaintances and a number of handsome presents. SUOCKING DEATH OF •AN OLD WOMAN AT WESTON POINT. On Thursday mornincr, Mrs. Tabitha Dutton, aged 66 years, of Weston Point, succumbed to fearful injuries ' sustained by burning. The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery Office on IVednesday. Mr. E.. 'Alison presided, and there were present Messrs. IL Coleburn and R. Mnrris, with Mr. W. F. Salkeid (secretary). The Secretary reported that the interments for the nine months ending December 25th numbered 409 ; corresponding period last year 327; in- crease 82. Leigh on December 26th. The defendant, who is blind and very deaf, it was stated ,had acted of late in a very strange manner. He had .been examined by a medical gentleman, who certifinl that he was of unsound mind—Mr. Cooke, the relieving officer, asked for an order for his removal to the County Asylum. In doing so he said they had had complaints respecting Reynolds, and for the safety of the family he was removed to and detained in the Workhouse at Dutton 14 days.—S uperintendent AthQrton informed the Court that the man was not safe to be at liberty. He had flourished his stick in the street to the great danger of pedestrians.—The order for his detention in the asylum was granted. ALLEGED SERIOUS ASSAULT ON A WOMAN AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, befo7e Coun- cillor W. W. Gossage and Alderman H. S. Timmis, a labourer named James Noon, Grenfell-st., was charged with having assaulted a married woman, named Sarah Potter, 7, Hutchinson-street.—Prosecutrix stated that the prisoner came home with her husband on Saturday night. A short time afterwards her husband went out, leaving prisoner and the lodger with her in the house: Prisoner beckoned her to the front door, and asked her if she would go for a drink of beer, but she refused. He then went to sit down again, and in a few minutes fol- lowed her into the yard, when the alleged assault was committed.—Prisoner, who denied the charge, was committed to take his trial at the County Quarter Sessions.

The first annual meeting in connection with this class was held on Wednesday evening, in Brunswick-street schoolroom. There was a good attendance. The school was made to present the appearance of a drawing-room, it having been neatly decorated by Mr. T. Leach, jun., assisted by a number of ladies. BRUTAL ASSAULT ON AN OLD WOMAN AT DUTTON VV ORKTIOUSE.

On Thursday morning, at Runcorn Police Court, be- fore Mr. John Brundrit and Major Hazlehurst, an inmate or Dutton yVorkhouss, named ecifla Givansn,'aged ;30 years, was charged on remand with assaulting Jane Barnsley, aged,76 years, at the Runcorn Union Work- house, on December 27th.—Complainant stated that about Wive o'clock on the ilate nail.* she had charge of the nursery, which contained a child belonging to the prisoner. A dispute took place about an orange. After a few words Givanan picked up a can, and struck Barns- ley on the head with it, inflicting a wound measuring 11 inches, and extending to the bone on the left side. She was dazed and rendered very weak, and had been under medical treatment since. Corroborative evidence was gived by Mary Hancock, another inmate, and George Frederick Batchelor.—Accused stated that the assault was commenced by the prosecutrix, who took hold of her hair and struck her twice.—The Bench con- sidered the assault a cruel and unprovoked one. The person attacked was a very old woman. The prisoner was evidently of a violent disposition, and althctigh she had been in custody a fortnight, the sentence upon her was one of six weeks' imprisomiknt, with hard labour.

ST. JOHN AMBULANCE ASSOCIATON, RUNCORN BRANCH. A meeting Of the above association was held In St. .Tohn'ssehool, Runcorn, on Wednesday evening, for the purpose of forming an 'Ambulance Brigade. The chair was occupied by Dr. McDougall, and a good number of members were present. In his opening remarks the Chairman stated that the formation of a brigade was desirable in order to enable those who held certificates from the St. John Ainbulance Association to have op- portunities of meeting together for ambulance practice, and for the further development of the means of ren- dering first aid to the injured, so as to be better able to concentrate their efforts foi the public advantage. It was unanimouslydecided to form a brigade which should be known as the Runcorn Corps of-the St. John Ambul- ance Brigade., it was further decided that for purposes of drill the corps should be divided into two divisions. an 3 the following members„were elected by ballot as officers :—First Division : Ist. Officer, Mr. S. Henderson; 2nd Officer; Mr. J. Rhodes • 3rd Officer, Mr. J. H. Clare. Second Division: Ist Officer. Sergeant Woolley ; end. Officer, Mr. W. Banks 3rd Officer, Mr. R. Foulkes. The meeting endorsed the decision of the committee to pur- chase a fully equipped band ambulance litter, to-be placed at the disposal of the Runcram public. .so that it is hoped there will soon .be an efEcient ambulance bri - gade in the town. As the cost at the litter is very con- siderable. Mr. Epps, hon. secretary, or any member of the committee, will be glad to receive subscriptions. The monthly meeting of the Warrington Amateur Photographic Society was held on Tuesday evening, in the Committee Room of the Museum,Bold-street. There was a good attendance ot members. Mr. H. Bond brought for inspection his newly invented lantern " The Unilux Bi-unial " (Messrs. Archer and Son's Patent), and showed • the same in operation with four-wick paraffin lamp, and blow-through limelight jet. The demonstration was thoroughly successful and aroused considerable interest on the part of the members. The lantern is a novelty,and set MS to combine the advantages of an ordinary Bi- unial with the compactness and easy control of the ordindary single lantern, the special feature being the employment .of a centre light for illuminating two optical systems. A number of members' slides illustrating some interesting scenery, were passed through the lantern, and at the close a hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Bond. POACHING AT WINWICK.

At the Town Hall, Newton, on Monday, before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, John Williams, collier, of 61, Derby-street, Earlestown, was charged with poach- ing on Sunday afternoon, on the farm of Mr. Peter Longton, Winwic::, he was also further charged with assaulting Mr. Longton by striking him with a stone. Shortly after 3 o'clock on Sunday after- noon, the prisoner and four other men, were ferret- ing for rabbits on Mr. Longton's land. Mr. Longton went towards them, but they ran away. Between then and a little before six o'clock he went, to them

four times, and on going to them the third dna--; prisoner and the other men threw stones at him. Shortly before 6 o'clock he went- again and found the men there, and the prisoner threw a large stone at him which hit him on the hang. Mr. Longto ii then seized prisoner, who said if ,he did not let him go, he would set his stacks on fire, and some of the other men also used threats. Prisoner i'as giyen. into the . custody of P.C. Groarke, and on being searched at the Police Station 21 nets were found in his possession. Mr. Longton afterwards found a ferret, which the prisoner .akd the other men had been using, in the field. He was remanded until Saturday next, and was afterwads admitted to bail.

A W ARRINGTON HOTEL IiERPRR AND ,HIS WINDOW BLINDS. At the Warrington County court'on Thursday, be- fore his Honour Judge J.D.Craw lord, James Thomas Locker, wire weaver and brush maker, Warring,- ton, sued Laurence Flood, Queen's Hotel, Sankey- at., for money due for blinds supplied. Mr. A. Browne, who represented plaintiff, said that the plaintiff claimed _lls. 9th from defendant for wire window blinds, which- he had supplied to the defendant., .The dispute was realty as to the price of the blinds, 'arid the defendant had Paid .C 7 17s. 9d. into court, saying that that wae'a sufficent price for them.. The sum now in .dispute Was a -- 148.7-ThOmas Locker, btother of .PlEiintiff, said that in consequence of a message he received, he Went to see Mr. Flood in October. Mr. Flood told him that he wanted some window blinds of a first class quality, and of the best workmanship. He did not want ordinary looking letters on the blinds.. Wit- ness took all measurements,and theiblinds were put in the window, there being no objection raised at the time. The blinds were charged at the rate of ,2s.Bid. per square foot, which was a very low price, in fact, they had lost on. the transaction. .k letter was subsequently received from the defendant, and an interview took place in which the defendant complained that the prize was ekcessive.L-Janies Thomnii LoCker, the ,plaintiff, said that the blinds Were Of the best workmanship. The reason that he charged such a low price was because .he hoped to have them as an advertisetnent.—Joseph .Rudd, • wire wotker, Turner-street, Said that he considered the price charged vas very low. He would have charged 3s. a 'square foot for them.—Joseph Hard- ing. and George llfolyneuX, wire manufacturers, gave similar evidence.—George %Venter, of 'We firm of Messrs. G. and J. 'Weaver, Cabinet makers; also Considered the price to be very low. His firm had done the wood work, which was Mahogany, the bill of -which amounted to £5 15s. —The defendant be- gan to give a history of the establishment of the Queen's Hotel, when the judge interrupted him and told him that the only question before the court was as to the price of the blinds. The defendant then &led two witnesses, George Dixon and Charles Zarinetti who however had only had ex- perience, in plain blinds, and .not in the kind in question.—His.Honour said . that the ease,was very clearly against the .:'«cfettilant, for it was shown. that the price had been a very reasonable one. He ac- cordingly gave judgment for the plaintiff for the amount, clamed.

div.head: THEN-GS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THEN-GS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
EY AN OCCASIONAL CORIMSPONDENT.

That the Ship Canal dues have been the chief topic of conversation this week, awl the general opinion expressed is that the Sip Canal Company in consequence of the valuable property they have at stake cannot afford to drive trade from Runcorn docks by unfair charges.

That Runcorn Docks and the Bridgewater canal cost the Company a million and three-quarters sterling, that the profit has averaged between £60,000 and £70,000 a year, and the Company are as much in need of this money now as ever they were.

That the concession -to the pottery trade, made known on Thursday, will ensure the retention of tnat trade at Runcorn, and it, is believed that this is only the forerunner of other concessions to the " good old .port."

That all the same, the ship owners, and traders, and the Board of Improvement Commissioners ought to join in a complete representation of the position of affairs to the Ship Canal Company, and make a strong request for such a reduction of dues and toll,' as will not only retain the present trade, but double it, and if possible quadruple it.

That traders and ship owners should arouse them- selves from their lethargy, form themselves into an ii.sociation, call it Trades Association or Chamber of Commerce, or what they will, and thus be in a position for acting on this question, or any other queition as it may arise,and by this means they will add to the security of their own businese,and to the prosperity of the town.

That the directors of the Williams, Deacon and Manchester and Salford Bank, Limited, have de- clared adi widend for the half year ended 31st Dec. last of 10i. per share teing at the rate of 12i per cent. per annum. They have also added £20,000 to the reserve fond, and £a,ooo to ouildings deprecia- tion fund ; carrying forward £10,403.
That Runcorn Savings Bank as shown by the re- port, in another column, has had a most successful year, and the number of transactions is striking tes- timony to the usefulness of the institution.
That Mr. Leach has been appointed vice- chairman of the Health Committee of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners in the place of Mr. Wynne Humphreys.
That Mr. Samuel Taylor, and Mr. Frederick J. Norman of Runcorn, have been placed on the com- mission of the peace for Cheshire.

That Mr. Taylor has had a long and honourable connection wilh public affairs in the town, and has been twice elected Chairman of the Improvement Commissioners ; his elevation to the magisterial bench will give the utmost satisfaction.
That the honour has come to Mr. Norman early in life, and although he has filled no public office he is widely known and respected.
That, .Ir. James Handley, who has been a J.P. for Cheshire for nearly ten y ears, has been also placed on the commission of the peace for Lancashire.

div.head: CONGREGATIONALisIi AT RUNCORN.
div.p: CONGREGATIONALisIi AT RUNCORN.

The annual meeting of the members of the Bethesda Congregational Church, Runcorn, was held in the schoolrodm, on Wednesday evening, under the presidency of the pastor, the Rev. J. Simpson. There was a good attendance.—Mr. Holt, the secretary, submitted the report, in which he stated that the work of the church daring the past year had been very successful. Their Sunday services • had on the whole been better attended than previously, and the prayer meetings, which were alwees oon3iderpd to demonstrate the strength of the church, had also been much better attended. The membership roll had been largely increased. The number of members for the year ending December, 1892, stood at 138, and their losses , through death and other causes had been seven. They had admitted during the twelve months one by transfer and 26 by profession' making a uresent total of 158, or a net increase during the year of 20. The averaee atten- dance at the Sacrament had been 62, against 43 in 1892. Those facts showed that the church was doing a good work in the town, and he was sure they could congratu- late themselves upon the ability and diligence of their pastor, upon whom their success depended to a large extent. He had gone through the roll book, and dis- covered that since Mr Simpson's settlement in Runcorn 90 had been admitted into fellowship. This proved that the duties devolving upon him had been successfully performed. The bazaar held in November was an un- qualified success, the amount realized being about £3OO, so that after paying back the loan of £2OO, and the ex- penses incurred, he believed there was still a balance in hand of something like £5O. He was sure the result far exceeded the expectations of the most sanguine, especi- ally considering the state of trade at the time. He thought a word of praise was due to the ladies of the church and congregation for the important work they performed. He urged the importance of attending the monthly church meeting, and expressed a hope that dur- ing the year upon which they had entered each member would give the pastor and deacons hearty co-operation and support. If they did he felt sure the present year would be out of the most successful in the history of the church. Mr. W. i. Chadwick, the treasurer, submit qa I the financial statement, which was highly satisfactory. It showed an increased income on any previous year. The report and balance sheet were aetopted.—\r. T. Hand • ley the bazaar treasurer, gave the results of that under- taking, from which it anpeAred that after paying all ex- penses and the loan for the renovation of the church they had in hand a balance of £42 .—Vetos of thanks were accorded to the secretary, treasurer, organist, and choir for their services during the past year. A similar compliment was paid to the bazaar officials, to the ladies who presided at the stalls, and to all who exerted them- selves to make the event such a decided success. Re- ports were also given from the different organi•atione associated with the church. It. was decided that Messrs. William Handley and Thomas Handley should be the delegates to the Congregational Union of England and Vales ; and that Messrs. Chadwiek and 'Rutter should represent the church at the Count; Union meeting. This concluded the proceedings. -

div.head: AT THE WARRINGTON THEA,TRES.
div.p: AT THE WARRINGTON THEA,TRES.

At the Itoyal Court Theatre., during the 'week, there he been a change in the nature of the enter- tainments. The drama has been substituted by an entertainment provided by Professor E. IL Crocker and his,•equirationals, and the result has been that the public have seen One of the most high-class and wonderful performapces on record. The Prafessor has trained 30 horses, ponies, mules, and donkeys to such an astnunding state of perfection that, to quote a cdnimon saying, "the animals can do almost anything biat talk." Upon the rising of the curtain the horses are seen on their way to "se. ool." ' On'the arrival of the Professor, whip in hand, k• Lewis "—and each animal answers quickly folds name—takes acieiV his master's hat, and brings him a chair, while " Frank" takes his cost from ' him. "Turk "—the favourite-:-.rings the bell • for the class in Mathematies,and one of the anisnalS,findieg the example wrong,erases it from the blackbord by means of 'a Wet Sponge he holds in his month. Letters are brought to the Professor, desks .pened,bolours of hand- kerchiefs distinguished, a hoop is skipped, barrels rolled about the stage, bells rung, and then 30 horses- are seen on the stage at the same time. After thiS an irnitation battle IA gone through, and the animals with surprising sagacity perform drills Of vari- ous discriptions. It almost appears incredible that work- ing on initinct alone,the Professor should have obtained Such wonderful results: The performance throughout is of a most interesting and marvellous character. Oppor- tunities of witnessing the feats' of Professor Crocker's Equirationals in this districtseldorn occur,and we would recommend all who ,:vonld• like to see the extent to which horses can be trained to visit the Royal Court Theatre either this afternoon or to-eight. At the Theatre Rcyal, Scotland .road, there will con- Chide to-night the engagement Fitli Mr. T. VV. Robinson's " Western Life Co'inpany," which has been performing during the week in " My Partner" and" The Danitei." The latter will be again performed this evening. It is a drama containing many exeiVng situation' arid incidents and the company capably discharges its ta:k.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL.
INTERVIEW WITH COUNCILLOR It. T. FAIRCLOUGH AND MR. F. MONKS.
SOME INTERESTING STATEMENTS.

Of late much interest has been shown in the question of the construction of Ship Canal docks at Warrington. Many persons indeed are sceptical as to the possibility of the work being completed before the stipulated term of three years, whilst many others—in fact one might almost say the majority of the townspeople—are practically in the dark as to what is going to be done with regard to the docks. With a view of gathering information, a representative of the Examiner" the other day I called upon two local gentlemen, both of whom are very intimately concerned in the trade of Warring- ton, and who are as likely as anyone to have well thought-out and judicious views on the subject,viz.: Councillor It. T. Fairclough au oi Mr. F. A,loults, J.P., C.C. Councillor R.T.Fairclough's opinions were first canvassed. COUNCILLOR It. T. FAIRCLOUGH'S VIEWS.

"There is a rumour abroad" said our representa- tive" that a company is likely to be formed in Warrington to carry on the construction of the docks. Can you inform sia on the matter?" "1 do not think there can be any truth in the rumour" replied Councillor Fairclough. "Of course the Ship Canal Company have undertaken to con-. struct the dscks, And their permission svculd have to be obtained before a company could attempt to carry out the work. Besides they hold the land, and so far as that aspect of the question goes, they hold naatters in their own hands. When the subject first came under discussion a year or two ago. 1 did advocate the formation of a Trust which should receive the financial support of the Corporation. Had this been acted upon the work could have been proceeded with long ago, and besides the many other advantages which would naturally have accrued through the dccks being under local control, the town would have received the benefit of dock rates and dues. However, the proposition was not taken up." "Do you think that the docks will be constructed before ' the stipulated term of three years has expired." "I cannot say, lam sure. The Ship Canal Com- pany have got the whole thing in their own hands, and so far have apparently decided upon not taking any immediate. steps." "They appear to be waiting to see the develop- ment of things at Manchester.' "Yes, that is very true to a great extent. The Company has been chiefly supported by Maochester money and one cannot expect them to neglect their own interests; it is only natural that Manchester, people should look after themselves before looking after others. The Manchester Corporation no doubt has great influence with the Company, and they will insist upon seeing .their own shipping de- veloped before they encourage it here. Indeed, the , Company have intimated indirectly that before they commence operations on the Warrington docks they must see some prospects of a return upon the money that would have to be expended. So, prac- tically, the matter depends now upon local enter- prise. It is necessary to build up a shipping trade, and then, even though the Company were indis- posed to plunge into the expense of making docks, they wou!d be forced to do so." "There is some talk of achieving this end by con- structing jetties along the Ship Canal banks." "I don't think there-is much talk of such a thing —at least not among local people. However, a scheme of that character ought not to be considered here; it should be very emphatically discouraged. Indeed, I should think it would meet with. great opposition here. A scheme which I very strongly advocate, and which I think cannot be re- ceived otherwise than favourably, is this:— You will be aware .of the .short diversion which is made from the Canal at the spot where 'an entrance will be made to the docks. My scheme is that as the Walton Arches side of this basin a " berth" should be constructed for the unloading of one or two vessels. This scheme possesses several advantages. In the first ' place, a vessel being unloaded or loaded there would be altogether out of the way of the traffic on the canal ; it would be no impediment. Secondly, it possesses every convenience, so far as either vehicu- lar or railway connections are concerned. At the present time there is a short length of railway which runs from the basin to the London and North Weston Railway at Walton Arches. This of cdurse would enable goods to be unshipped and, transported to any place in the country, by rail, or in many cases, to be shunted down to the sidings of several manufacturers in the town. Of course the new road is quite hard by, and goods could either be shipped from or delivered on to vehicles which could travel the new. road. London, or other coasting vessels could use this basin, and thus a trade could soon be built up That of course is the main thing we have to look to, and it is highly necessary that steps should be taken as quickly as possible. The work cannot be commenced too soon. I cannot see how, under present circumstances, the scheme I have mentioned can be very well improved upon. Another feature, in connection with it,by the way, it is that the " berth" could be utilized as a stage for passenger traffic." " Do you think there are any possibilities in the opening up of a passenger boat service, Mr. Fair- dough." "Decidedly. Why should stations not be con- structed at certain spots along the canal? In many cases, I can assure you, one could reach certain places much more expeditiously by canal than by rail. Take far instance, Runcorn, and other similar places. They could be reached mucla more easily by boat than by rail. There are innumerable possibilities in the canal which should be grasped and worked up .by local enterprise.—Here Mr. Fair- (dough mentioned several cases of local towne,whick do shipping trade with Liverpool,but which could do their business cheaper by exporting from Warring- ton. There were cases where small canals had now to be used fear the conveyance of goods in barges to tlse sea-going vessels at Liverpool. Merairclough showed that this trade could be done from Warring- ton eta great saving to the exporters. "Respecting the effect of the canal upon the river "asked our reporter "can you enlighten us upon that?" "It is impossibl e,at present, to arrive st any defi- nite conclusion " said Jr. Fairclough, who by the , way, is very well acquainted with the character and tidal peculiarities of the river, and is consid- ered one of the most reliable authorities thereon. "There is no doubt about this" he resumed "that, we shall not have any more floods or freshets." This he went on to explain, might be instrumental in changing the whole character of the river,taken in conjunction with the fact that the channel of river was going to be dredged to a uniform depth of Bft. " How this effect would be produced, Mr. il'airclough I kindly illustrated. It seemed that the freshets, I which are very common in winter always flowed in a certain course along the river bed. Then the tides, in towing up invariably ran along an oppo- site course of the river bed. That is to say where at a certain point the freshet would flow strongly against the south hank of the river;the tides would flow aesthe north side. The result Of this has been that the river bed has been gradually widened. :Nits Faiiclough thinks that, now the freshets are stopped, and the channel of the river is. to be deepened, the tides by continually running in one set course will have the effect of gradually narrowing and deep- ening the river. " Is is not a fact," concluded our reporter, " that in low tides the water level is lowered by the. canal ?" "Yee; and to the 'extent of 18 inches, ercept in cases whir there is a breeze behind the tide, which brings the water up much sooner and stronger. Still the effect in tow tides is certainly not bene- ficial. I am, however, testing the effect on all tides, and no doubt I shall soon be in a position to give a more definite idea of the sffects on the tides." .

div.head: 'MR. F. mortrs VIEWS.
div.p: 'MR. F. mortrs VIEWS.
Our reprftentative later on called upon Mr. P. Monks, and drew his attention to the rumoured formation of a company for the construction of the docks: ' . . _ __

"I have not; heard of any such movement," replied Air. Monks. 'When the question of the docks wash rst mooted, however. I strongly advo- cated the formation of a public Trust in the town for carrying out the" work, and I still hold the same views on the matter." "What is your opinion about the prospects of the construction of the docks, Mr. Monks?" "1 certainly think that %Try much depends upon local enterprise. It is highly necessary. that War- , Tinton should give unmistakable evidence to the Company that the construction of the docks would be fully,. justified by the use. that would be made of I them. To do thiq it is essential that a local shipping I trade should be built up,and then the company will no doubt hurry cu the work.'

"What, is your opinion, would be the most feas- able scheme for carrying this out?" "The most feasable scheme which presents itself to me is to utilize the river basin, or cul de sac,about which the docks are to be constructed. This could be done by erecting jetties along the side of the ' basin nearest the Wilderspool-road, and there an easy access to or from the town would be obtained. Shipping could proceed here while the docks were being made, without being any impediment to the works. It would not require a very large sum of money to carry out this scheme, and there is tio I doubt it would be greatly beneficial to the town." *Do you suggest that the scheme should bt.. car- ried out by municipal funds or by private enter- prise ?" "Oh, I think it could be carried out by private enterprise. Of course it would only be a temporary arrangement. It would succeed, however, I think, in building up a shipping tra le, which is the all- important point, and which rehuires very urgent attention."

div.head: PADGATE CHURCH TEA PARTY.
div.p: PADGATE CHURCH TEA PARTY.

The annual tea party in connection' with Christ Church, tadgate, was held in the schoolroom, Pad- gate,on Thursday evening. There was a large com- pany present at the tea,and at the entertainment the room was crowded, many persons having to stand. The tea tables were presided over by the following. ladies :—Mrs. J. J. Lengha.m, Mrs. Beevers, Miss Apple- ton, Mrs. Royston, Mrs. Potter, Mrs. Hndgkinson, Ws. Litton, Miss Houghton, Miss Warburton, Mrs. Grainger, Mrs. Woods,Mrs.Fairhurst, Mrs. Hartwright, Mrs. Mines, Miss Bennett, and Mrs. Mather. The chair at the enter- tainment was occupied by the curate, the Rev. R. W. Hartwright. The programme submitted was of a mis- cellaneous character, and comprised songs by Miss Grounds, Miss Florrie Royston, Mr. John Grounds, and Mr. Mines ; pianoforte duets by Mrs.H.and Miss Thomp- son, and Mrs. and Miss Beevers. Miss Cooper gave two violin solos. A dialogue was also given. During an interval the Rev. R. W. Hartwright deli- vered a short address, referring to several matters relat- ing to the parish. He said they would all be sorry to l'kuow that the Vicar had been obliged to leave home by the doctor's orders, and much against his will,Mr. Lang- ham had felt compelled to comply with the mandates of his medical adviser,and left Padgate on Monday last. He was sure they would be with him in wishing him speedy restoration to health and strength. Mr. Laugham had been vicar of that parish three years,and he (the speaker) didn't think he was saying too much by saying that he was one of the most popurar clergymen in the district of Warrington. (Applause.) He had been much struck, by the unanimous opinion of people he had met.with regard to Mr. Langharn, not only of Church people, but also of Dissenters who had expressed their desire to help Mr. Langham as much as they could, because he was a hard working and faithful minister of Christ. During the past year the great event in the parish had been the bazaar which was held in October to raise funds for the church Institute. It was desirable that there should be a place of recreation for the youths and men of every parish where they might meet at nights and , enjoy innocent pleasure and amusement, and for this end it was necessary that they should have a building. For some time past the Institute had met in that school- room, but it had only been held on certain nights during the week. He hoped, however, that by this time next year they would have their Institute, at which they would be able to meet every night in the week, and en- joy the intellectual recreation which every working man required. The bnzear in its aid was a great success, although it was held at a time when there was very great distress,and when there were many calls upon the public. But in spite of this they were enabled to raise £350, which he thought was a remarkably good sum to raise in a place like that room. (Applause.) They had a great deal to be thankful for, and although there was yet a small balance to be raieed to enable them to build the Inetftute, yet he was sure that that sum would be raised, and they would be able to open it quite free from debt. (Hear, hear.) • They had lately started a Church Lade Brigade, a brigade to which lads beeween the ages of 14 and 18 years were admitted. It had suc- ceeded exceedingly well. They dnly started it two months ago, and during that time they had enrolled no fewer than fifty names. and been enabled to obtain the neees- sary eqipment. They had also started last Saturday a Juvenile Temperance Society, and he urged parents to send their children, AS every parent must feel that it was for the child's benefit to be taught that the undue use of alcholic beverages was certainly most ruinous to a man's career. He (the speaker) was to a certain ex- tent strange amongst them as he had oniy been in the parish three or four months, and he wished to take that opportunity to thank them all for the very kind way they had received him. Referring to the change in the Orford district,Mr. Flartwrizht said that, as they knew, the trustees had decided with the sanction of the vicar of Padgate, and the Bishep of the dioceee,to place Orforel perish under the spiritual supervision of the vicar of Padgate. 'Orford had never been a separate district, though it had been to some extent worked on separate liner. The Bishop would net sanction the separation of Orford entirely from Padgate, and therefore the trustees thous..ht it would he far better under the spiritual super- vision of the vicar of Padgate. He thought the Orferd people were perfectly satisfied to remain under the wise government of Mr. Langbam. It might be that in the future, circumstances would permit of Orford being made a separate districtemd he knew that Mr. &Ingham would throw no obstacle in the way. (Applause.) A vote of thanks was moved by Mr. Mather, to those who had taken part in the proceedings. Mr. Appleton seconded, and the vote was carried unanimously. Danc- ing was afterwards indulged in.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT 'WARRINGTON.

It does sometimes happen that the defendant ' summoned at the police court does net appear, and the excuse is generally that he is at work.and could : not appear. Quite a novel excuse was made on Monday, when a young lady solemnly told the as- tonished court, that her brother, who was sum- ' moned for that morning, could not appear becayse he was " in the river." To be in the river, of course, can only have one meaning to the average English- man, and that is, that the person was at the bottom. . The consternation which was aroused by this state- ment was however allayed by the explanation that . . . .
he was on board a vessf74 on the river, which is a different thing altogether. Tne incident se' ved as a welcome change, in a rather monotonous morning at the court.

The Warrington magistrates do not err on the side of severity in cases brought before them for neglect of children. In the case yesterday of a man and his wife who were charged with gross neglect. of five children,the sentence was a xery lenient one indeed. The two defendants pleaded guilty to the charge, the evidence in support of which, showed a discreditable state of affairs. The magistrates, how- ever, only ordered the costs to be paid, and ad- journed the case for a month. The defendants must consider themselves very fortunate in getting off 3o easily.

Mr. Mines, the superintendent of the PadgaLe In- dustrial schools was the object of a rather lengthy ciiscussion at the meeting of the Board of Guar- dians on Wednseday. He had taken the Workhouse band out on the night of the Saturday before. Christmas day, and kept them out longer than the regulations of the school permitted. Some of the , Guardians were inclined to be severe upon Mr. Mines, and spoke in quite a fatherly tone about the children. Mr. Dobson even went so far. as to say... that such conduct would teach the' children to go- *" busking ". Mr. Mines, however, found a cham- pion in the person of Mr. W. J. Shaw, who in- dulged in inuensloes against the conduct of his • brother Guardians; who. he said, were always find- ing fault with Mr... Mines. Mr. Longton also grew indignant at the thought that even at Christmas time, the children must have no additional festiv- ity. Christmas tithe is generally a time when a .... great deal of the usual restraints of society are laid aside, but late hours, even at Christmas time, aro • not. good for children.

The ' Guardians are lo.iiug no time in taking s.reps to fill the vacancy which will occur early - in February, owing to the retirement of Dr. Spinka for they had already advertised for a successor. A • number of the Guardians were inclined to be very liberal in fixing the salary for the new medical officer, for they wished to give him the same as Dr. Soinks is receiving. It was however, ultimately. decided to give him £2O per annum less. Past experience in similar positions shows that had the whole £2OO per annum been granted, it would very soon have risen above that sum, for public officials as a rule get a" rise before they have been in office very long.

A remarkably complete series of photographic views which have been taken during the construc- tion of the Ship Canal is set forth by Mr. T. Birtles, of Sankey-street, in. a pamphlet which he hits published. The views number something like one hundred and fifty, and practically illustrate every phase of the construction of the great waterway from. Eastham to Salford. The series is a singu- larly valuable record ,of engineering difficul- ties of the first magnitude which have been overcome, and the vivid portrayals which we have. here, of the various mechanical methods adopted iu making the canal, will be of the deepest interest in days to come.
MERLIN.

div.head: BOLD-ST. WESLEYAN SUN DAY SCHOOL.
div.p: BOLD-ST. WESLEYAN SUN DAY SCHOOL.
ANNUAL TEA MEETING.

The annual tea meeting ill connection with the Bold-st. Wesleyan Sunday School, was held in the schoolroom on Monday afternpon. A. good number sat down to tea and the tables were 'presided over by Mrs. Kirtlan, Mrs. Mason, Mrs. Brindle, Mrs. Gleave, Mrs. Collins, NimW.Dunn, and Mrs. Chorley. After the tea, the annual meeting was held at which the Rev. J. Kirtlan presided and was supported on the platform by the Revs. Owen Watkins and G. D. Mason.

The CITAIRMSN, in his opening speech, said that in the Bold-st. Sunday School, there was the greatest possible) unity between the superintendent, teachers and office bearers, and between the various teachers in the school.- This was one of the most hopeful signs in the Sunday school. It bad not always been so, and it might net always be so, but he hoped that the year they had en- tered upon would be one in which this blessed unity would not be broken. He was glad to say that there was a great deal of affection between the teachers and super- intendent. (Applause.) He was pleased to see that there wore three junior society classes in connection with the school, and he would like to see them greatly enlarged, especially the boys' class. He hoped the school would have 'a prosperous time during the present year. Mr. LINGARD (the Secretary) then nad the annual report of the school. He said that the school had been progressing satisfactorily. There were 49 teachers, 42 e& whom were members of society. The number of scholars. on the books was 500 which was an increase upon the- previous year. The average morning attendance was 110, and afternoon 260. Over 100 scholars were also- members of the church. This was a hopeful sign, and the young men took a great interest in the school. The- missionary society had received in offerings during the- past year £43 us. 60., which was an increase of RC us. 6-11 d. upon the previous year. Great praise was due to Mr. Jubb and the other collectors for this result. Th* Band of Hope membership was 250, but the average at- tendance weekly was rather small. There was a library under the efficient management of Mr. Dunn and Mr. Bodle, and they had 410 instructive .books, which the scholars greatly prized. Mr. Mellor, and Mr. Wilson, the school secretaries, Mr. Cross, the registrar, and Mr. Weaver, the treasurer, also deserved great credit. The vrarmest thanks were due ti the circuit ministers for the interest they manifested in the school, and also for their frequent attendance at the sch,.ol. The Bev. Owen WATKINS said that the ministers were
present at the meeting because they considered the

unday school to be not merely an auxiliary, but as a vital part of the church, and that the church.to be pr ply constituted must be an efficient Sunday school. fie rejoicedsto believe that at B)1d-st. there was an effi- _ _ _ . _ .

dent -Sunday school. • But he thought that out of 500 scholars they ought to have a greater pro- portion present on Sunday afrernQons. Mr. Watkins next went.on to give an interesting and humorous ac- count of how Welsh Sunday schools were conducted,and in conclusion wished the Bold-st. school a prosperous year.. An excellent programme was gone through during the evening. Mr. W. H. Wallington was heartily applauded for his rendering of the song "Day by day," and also 6' The village smithy" later in the evening. The choir under the conductorship of Mr. Petei Harrison. sang the anthem "The radiant morn hath passed away," in an excellent manner. Mr. Levi Richardson also gave "The Bay of Biscay," for which he was encored, and sang "Bonny Mary of Argyle." Miss Newcombe was a great favourite with the audience, and was encored on each occasion that she sang, her rendering of "The last Rosa of Summer," being very fine. Among the in- strumentalists. Mr. Hipkiss gave great satisfaction with clarionerte solo, and also in a clarionette and oboe duet with Mr. Ward, who also gave an oboe sole. Two violin solos were given by Miss Winnie Pigot, for which she was encored.. The accompaniment was ably per— formed by Miss J. E. Pigot. In addition to the vocal I and instrinnental part of the entertainment, the recita- tion of "How Jane Conquest gave the alarm." was very graphically eiven by Miss Bermett,and on being encored she recited " Which shalt it be ?"

At an interval in the • concert, prizes were given to scholars who had Fuccess full y missed an examination in the catechism. There were 35 -successful competitors, Miss Etiith J. Davies heading the list. Th 9 prizes were clistribteed ho the Rey: J. Kirtlan, and the prizi winners were, cheered by the audience as they went to the plat- form for the prizos. The entertainment vral brought to a close by the pronouncing of the Benediction.

On Tuesday evraiinrz. the annual tea meeting wag held in the sehoolroni... After the tea, a "living waliwock " exhibition was held at which members of the school were attired in all kinds of fantastical dresses. The en- tertainment concludol with a procession of the " Ex- hibitions "round the room.

div.head: ENGLISH AND RUSSIAN SOLDIERS.
div.p: ENGLISH AND RUSSIAN SOLDIERS.

News of a serious character has reached Lcndon from the Mediterranean squadron which has recently visited Greece. When our ships arrive:', in the Pirmus they found the Russian vessels there, and it is said that the antipathy felt towards the British by the Rus- sian seamen was so great that it was necessary for the commanders to arrange necer t) allow Russian and British seamen to ;.Y,r) ashore at the same time. If they had met ashore there is little dout4t that a ol lisi on wonth have occurred. As it was, when the Ern:dish boats passed the Russian ships they were vehemently hoJted and hissed by the seamen. This is looked up= as One , of the results of the Toulon 4eumstration.
