div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES

A DEFENDANT "is THE RIVER." At the Warrington Borough Court on Monday, Joseph Smith, 52 Evelyn-street,was charged with using obscene and profane language in Lodge-lane, on Christmas Day. The defendant did not appear when his name was called, but his sister stepped forward. " Why does not your brother appear ?" asked Mr. White (the magis- trates' clerk.) "He can't," answered Miss Smitb," be- cause he is in the river." This answer caused great sur- prise to everyone in the court, and Mr. White with a puzzlad look exclaimed. "In the river? What do yow mean? Is he drowned ?" "0 no! "was the reply," he is on a boat and he could not get back in time for the court.' Needless to say this reply convulsed the court, and it was some little time before the magistrates could recover their gravity and go on with the case. P.C. Meacock who proved the case, said that on the previous week, Six boos had been summoned and fined for committing the same offence at the same time that the present de- fendant was charged with. They used the most filthy expreesions. The magistrates inflicted a fine of ss. NEW YEAR'S EVE ROYSTEREDS. William Jones, 4 Stamford-st., Peter and William Row- son, 27 6tamford-st., and Alfred France, 9 Lythgoes- lane, were each charged at the Warrington Borough Court on Monday with disorderly conduct in Buckley-st. on January Ist.—P.C. Hollinesworth's evidence showed that at about 12 30 on the morning of January Ist he was on duty at Town's End, when he received informa- tion of a disturbance in Buckley-st. When he got there, he saw the four defendants making a noise in the street. Be law tat the windows of the house of Mr. Ma onion were all broken. When the defendants saw witness they ran, but Jones was captured with three or four pieces of brick in his possession. Be refused to give his name and address. The other defendants then came up and hustled the officer about and succeeded in rescuing Jones. The officer then went into Mannion's house, and found a great number of pieces of bricks lying inside the house. Constable Hollingsworth subsequently went into Stamford-st., and heard the defendants boasting of what they had done. The constable this time succeeded in getting their names mid addresses, but not without considerable danger, for Jones threatened to hit him with a poker...-Constable Gibbs gave corroborative evidence. —Margaret ltaannion said that there had been a dispute on the previous Saturday night, and late on Sunday night, the four defendants came into Buckley-st. inquir- ing for Mannicn's house. They at length found it, but the people inside had had warning and bolted the door. The defendants first kicked at the door, and when no one came out, they commenced throwing bricks and stones at the windows, and succeeded in smashing them all.— Ann Mannion and Kate Jones each gave corroborative evidence and the magistrates ordered each defendant to be bound over to keep the peace for six months, them- Selves in £lO, and one surety in £5. They were also ordered to pay the costs or in default were ordered to go to gaol for 14 days.
DISGRACEFUL ASSAULT UPON A W OMAN. - H WAVY SENTENCE.

James Kelly was charged on remand at the Warring- ton Police Court on Monday, with being drunk and dis- orderly in Turner-at. on Dec. 30; also with assaulting P.C. Evans at the same time and place, and further with assaulting Alice Houghton the same evening.—Police Con,tahle Evans said that at about 6 50 on the night of Dec. 30, he was at Town's End when he saw the prisoner in Turma-st. offerine to fight anyone who came near him. Witness went to him and told him to be quiet,but he became more violent, and hearing a complaint of the prisoner's conduct, he went into the house of Mrs. Tickle, and found a young woman named Alice Houghton in an unconscious state, with a pool of blood (ale-iut a pint. upon the floor caused by injuries inflicted by the prisoner) Witness thea took the prisoner into custody. On the way to the police station, he received several kicks on the ankle, and the assistance of another constable had to be obtained before the prisoner could he taken to the police statlon.—Alice Houghton said that she assisted Mrs. ' Tickle in cleaning the house, and on the day in question, the prisoner, who lodged with Mrs. Tickle, came into the house drunk. He pulled off his coat, and struck her in the face, which caused her to fall on the ground. He said that he had already done nine months for one woman, and he would do two years for her (complainant). He then jumped upon her, but she remembered nothing more for she became unconscious.—Jane Tickle gave corro- borative evidence, and said that Alice Houghton had been attended by a doctor ever since the time of the assault. —The magistrates sentenced prisoner to three months' hard labour for assaulting the police, and also three months' hard labour for assaulting Alice Hotlghton. ANOTHER SHOP DOOR THEFT. At the Warrington Borough Court on Saturday,Oswald Drinkwater, joiner, a native of Northwich, was charged with stealing from the shop door of James Murphie, 6, Buttermarka-st., about 520 p.m. on Friday, the sth inst., eix pairs of stockings, value 6s. Prisoner pleaded guilty. The evidence of the Chief Constable showed that the prisoner was seen to take the stockings from the shop door of the complainant and then go away. The manager of the shop was apprised of the theft, and the police were communicated with. D. S. Monaghan fenee that a man answering the description given, had sold three pairs of stockings at Mrs. C Leshes, Pinners 33row, for one shilling. D. S. Monaghan got possession -of the stockings, -• i 1 amongst other places visited he letied that two other pairs had been sold to Mrs. EEza- heth Forster. Mersey-St., far 9d., but when the prisoner offered to sell the sixth pair at Mrs. Gibbons he was detained, and the police sent for.—Mrs. Leslie deposed to buying three pairs of stockings from the prisoner for one hilling, and said she could buy them wholesale for ft.,. 61. per dozen. The manager for Mr. Murphie said there were no suet stockings in the trade at 4-o.per pair. The stockings stolen were tied near the door on a nail. Such exposure was a great temptation to buy them as well as te steal them. Mr, Hunt said they had had a considerable number of felonies lately, which ha d been due to the exposure of goods outside the shop, and the magistrates in other towns disallc wed costs to wit- in such cases. The prisoner who had only com- pleted a term of imprisonment the . previons day, was sent to gaol again tor two months with hard labour, Mr Bor,s7s (chairman) said the magistrates were not at all satiFfied with the account given by Mrs. Leslie as to the huying of stock rigs at the price stated. The pur- chaser ran very near being a partaker in the crime, as a stranger was unable to sell them at the price stated if he came by them honestly.

DISGRACEFUL STATE OF A DWELLING-HOUSE. At the Warrington Borough Court yesterd4y, Richard and Elizabeth Tranter, 38 Jdckey-st., were charged that they caused unnecessary stiff 'ring, to their five children bet':xeen December 5.1893 and January 5, 1894.—In- spector Uphill. said that on January sql at about 11.30 a.m., he visited the hou,e of defendants, and fcrAnd the house in a wretched condition, and a very smal; IV-t, although it was snowing heavily. The child Mary Ann, aged ten years was clothed with a jacket sad a little pidce of chemise and an old pair of clogs. She had stockings on. Her body was very dirty, and h-r hair was matted together with filrh and lice. The otivr children George, aged six years, James, aged four year. Elizabeth, aged three years, and Richard, aged four months were in a similar condition, being insrfficiently clad. The lai:ter was in a perambulator in which were a few filthy rags. The lower part cf the house was in a filthy conaition. The only food to be found in the

house,was half a loaf of bread. On going into the bedroom witness found the mattress rotting away, and filth was running about the floor of the room. Witness saw the male defendant who said that he worked at Dallam forge, and received 30s. a week, which he gave to his wife,and he had told her frequently to clean the children.—P.O. Foster and Dr. Bowden corroborated the inspector.—The female defendant on being sworn denied that she did not , give the children sufficient food. It was washing day when the inspector came.—Thc male defendant said that he could not help the condition of the children. lie had done his best to get his wife to look after them. Two witnesses, Mrs. Tatlock and Mrs. Graham, gave evi- dence that the children were sufficiently fed.—The magistrates ordered defendant to pay the costs and ad- journed the case for a month.

div.head: ALLEGED WILFUL DAMAGE.
div.p: ALLEGED WILFUL DAMAGE.

John Ashton, 24 Orchard-st., and Robert Eyes, 73, Howley-lane, were charged at the Warrington Borough Court, yesterday, that OR June 2nd, they did wilful damage to certain posts, the property of Joseph Welsby 64, Leonard-st. Mr. P. Davies represented the com- plainant, and Mr. Arthur Browne the defendants. Mr. Davies said that his client was a brickmaker in Howley. The defendants are wiredrawers,and on Jan. 2nd Welsby met Ashton and four other men, who were out of work at the time. They asked him if he would give them an allowance job. He told them that he could find them a job at making holes for stumps at the rate of 2d. a hole. They agreed to do the work and at once went to the place. When the men had been working twenty minutes they came to Welsby and asked him for an allowance. Welsby said that he would pay them either in mcney or in bread and cheese. They all went to the" Marquis of Granby" where they had is. of bread and cheese, and five pints of beer. They then went back to work, and soon afterwards said they wanted some more allowance. Welsby told them to go to the "Ring o' Bells." They went there and had five pints of beer. They came to Welsby again and insisted upon having more, upon Which he gave them six more pints. Welsby then went home, and Ashton and Eyes came to the field and pulled 22 stumps down agaiu, and what they could not pull up they smashed. They said that tilt, defendant was not going to have the laugh out of them.—Joseph Welsby gave evidence in support of his solicitor's state- ment, and said that the sum he claimed was 7s.—James Birchall, a labourer, in the employ of complainant said that he saw the defendants pull some of the stumps up. There was one of them broken, but he did not see the defendants break it. The defendants said that they were pulling them up because Mr. Welsby had not paid them for their work.—After further evi- dence from a witness named Hankey, Mr. Browne con- tended that no damage had been done by defendants. He denied that the beer was for the work done, but that Welsby had simply treated the men. He had not paid them according to his contract of twopence a hole, and the men with a mistaken idea of their rights had simply pulled up the stumps again without doing any damage. —The magistrates considered ttiat the complainant had acted in a very foolish manner in treating the men as he did, and dismissed the case.

div.head: MINOR CASES. • _ WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
div.p: MINOR CASES. • _ WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Bef ore Mr. F. Monks (chairman), Alderman Francomb, Messrs. J. W. Hayward, and S. Wright. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—The following were dealt with for this offence :—William Burton, 5, Albert-st. ; Rodelia Knockton, Erwood-st. • Annie Ryan, no address, and William Plinston, 61, Back Aikin-st., was discharged with a caution. _ _

ALLEGED ASSAULT.—James Taylor, 16, Howard-st., charged with assaulting his father, Samuel Paylor, on Dec. 26th. From the evidence of the father, it was very clear that the defendant had received sufficient punish- ment, and had been well flogged. The magistrates ac- cordingly dismissed the ease, remarking that the com- plainant was well able to take care of himself. STONE THROWING.—Thomas William Humphries, aged 13,2,Quay Fold, was fiaed is. for throwing stones to the danger of passengers in Liverpool-road on Jan. 2nd. OBSTRUCTING THE FOOTPATH.—AIfred Kenyon, aged 16 years, 5, Gaskell-street, was fined 24. 6d. for wheeling la truck on the footway in Church Place, on December 7th.

_ DISORDERLY Boys.—William Keighley-(16), 18, Hind. street, and James Morris (17), 26, Manchester-st., were each charged with disorderly • behaviour in Gaskell-st., on December `l..Bth. P.C. Evans stated that he saw a number of boys, the two defendants among them, run- ning up and down the street, knocking at the doors as they passed. He received several complaints from different persons, and he got the names and addresses of the defendants and reported them. The magistrates ordered the boys to be bound over for six months. CRUELTY TO A HotasE.—John Davenpart, Croft, was charged with working a horse while in an unfit state on Dec. 23rd.—P.C. Bell deposed to stopping the defendant driving a horse attached to a cart laden with hampers, at Market Gate. The horse was very lame.—lnspector Luff, R.S.P.C.A., said that the horse was fit for working on the land, but not on the roads. He considered that it was more an error of judgment than intentional cruelty on the part of the defendant in bringing the horse to town.—Defendant was fined in the costs. BREACH OF THE PEACE.—Michael Cunningham, James- street, and Michael Grant, 2, Robinson-street, were each charged with fighting in Dial-.9treet, on Jan, lst.—P.C. Chrimes said that there were three rien fighting, and the other man had been dealt with the previ,,us week.— Grant said that lie was not fighting, but was trying to separate Cunningham and the other man.—Cunninghain who pleaded guilty to fighting, also denied that Grant had been fighting.—Grant was accordingly dismissed, and Cunningham was bound over for six montlistand ordered to pay costs. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett (in the chair) and

div.head: Mr. E. J. Guest:
div.p: Mr. E. J. Guest:
DRUtili.—James Gillespie, travelling draper, last from Manchester, was fined 53. including cost, for being drunk in Buttermarkq-st. at five o'clock the previous afternoon.

THEFT FROM THE WORKHOUSE. —Catherine Smith was charged with stealing from the Union W'.,rkhouse,about 9.30 on Sunday morning, a red flannel singlet, the pro- perty of the Warrington Union. Prisoner pleaded guilty. Mr. Hunt (chief constatle) stated that the prisoner was employed in the laundry at the workhouse. Sunday last was her day out, and she visited the house of Bridget Collier, lios,!-yard, off Dial-st., and sold to her a flannel skirt and singlet she was wearing, for one shilling. The money was spent in drink. D.S. Monaghan heard of the matter,and visited the house in Rose-yard,and found a pawn ticket relating to the pledging of the singlet for 3s. 6d. at Mrs. Jackson's, and also found the shirt in the house. D.S. Monaghan went to the workhouse,ancl the prisoner was brought to the Police Sration. He (Mr. Hunt) believed the articles taken had belonged to persons who had died in the workhouse.—Mrs. Ward (matron) said the articles taken were not the Guardians' pro- pnty. They had belonged to people who had died in the workhouse, but friends didn't claim them, they, therefore, gave them away. She would have given the articles to the prisoner had she asked for them.—The magistrates committed the prisoner to gaol for fourteen days.
TAIIRSDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton.

ArroTHER DESERTER.—James King pleaded guilty to being a deserter from Her 1113jesty's Ist Yorkshire Light Infantry, at present stationed at Belfast. The prisoner was arrested at Orford Barracks by Sergeant William Healy, who requested to be recommended for the usual reward, which was granted. The prisoner was remanded to Strangeways Gaol to await an escort. FRIDAY. —Before Alderman Harrison (chairman) Mr. S. _ .

Wright, Dr. Garnall, and Councillor H. Roberts. DESERTER.—John Miller was remanded to Strangeways Gaol on the charge of being a deserter from H.M. 63rd Manchester Regiment stationed in Ashton-und9r-Lyne since October. P.C. Elollingsworth received the usual reward. MAINTENANCE ORDER.—Thomas jackson, Rose Inn, was summ med to show cause why he should not contri- bute to the maintenance of his child William Jackson at the Ship" Clio." Mr.P. Davies who appeared for defend- ant, applied for an adjournment of the case, because his client distinctly objected to his son being on the "Clio," although it Was stated at the time he was sent there that he was willing for his son to go. Mr. Jackson had drawn up a memorial to the Hems Secretary, and that was now under consideration.—The case was ad- journed for a fortnight. CRUELTY TO A BOREE.—Peter Dale!, Scotland-road, George Murgatroyd, and Patrick Magi nn, Arpley-street, were charged, the former with working a horse while in an unfit state, and the latter two with causinc, it to be worked on Jan. Ist. Inspector Luff, R.5.P.C.1., said that about four o'clock on New Year's Day, he was at Market Gate, when he noticed Daley driving a pair of horses attached to a 'bus with passengers to Latchford. One of the horses appeared to be suffering pain, and witness examined it. He found a wound about the size of a fire shilling piece under the collar, on which was a quantity of matter and blood. The horse belonged to Mr. Maginn, and Mr. Murgatroyd had charge during Mr. Maginn's absence.—P.C. lurner gave similar evi- cience.—Maginn said that the day was a very busy one, owing to the opening of the Ship Canal. It was owing to a mistake that the wrong collar had been put on that particular horse. Mr. MurgAtroyd was not in any way responsible for what was done with the horses.—The magistrates fined Magian las. and costs, and dismissed the charge against the other defendants.

On Tuesday morning, after the partial thaw, a large number of cattle were found frozen to death on Ilirriney marshes. A number of farmers and grazers are to be prosecuted by the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals for neglecting to feed their cattle dur- ing the bard weather. Mr. F. Marion Crawford says that" in the matter of physique there is a resemblance between Leo XIII., Pre- sident Lincoln, and Mr. Gladstone—lean, sinewy men all three,of a bony constitution and indomitable vitality, with large skulls, high cheek bones, and energetic jaws —all men of great physical strength, of profound capa- city for stidy,of melancholy dispcsition, and of unusual eloquence."
RUPTURE CURED.—S. J. SHERMAN, Hernia Specialist, 64, Chancery-lane, London. sends his book on rupture post free. Branch Chambers, 26, King-st., Manchester.—Advt.

RUGBY. ENGLAND T. WALES.

The victory, quite wonderful in its nature, of England at Birkenhead Park on Saturday will be no doubt a sur- prise, and very agreeably so, to those who, led away by the many triumphs of the Welsh clubs this season, had conjured up in their minds a severe disaster to the Eng- lish fifteen. The actual picture was widely different to the imaginative drawings of the Rugby Unionists who had seen no good in English football. It was a triumph for the Rugby Selecting Cemmittee, both for their choosing genuine scrimmagers, and shutting their eyes to" wingers " and shirkers of hard work, and further for the skill secured among the backs. There was some thing approaching a fright on Thursday when the news eked out that Lockwood had asked to be excused ; but anxiety was allayed by the international captain's recon- sidering his position, and consenting to take his place at three-quarter at much business inconvenience to himself. And as things went, it might have been ill for England had Lockwood's position been filled by the reserve, J. H. C. Fegan, who, while often brilliant, is not a consis- tently good player. The English team as a whole played a great game ; the forwards worked hard both in the scrimmage and in the open, but as usual the halves had no small share in the success. C. M. Wells, the Old Cambridge and the Harlequin half-back, was in his best ' form, and his quick pass was well appreciated by the three-quarters, where, apart from Lockwood, Murfitt (who had come into the team in lieu of Saville), Firth, and Hooper all did well. Taylor proved an admirable partner for Wells, and Byrne at full back did innumer- able good things. It was a little eurious that in the first instance of England and Wales meeting under the same Conditions in the disposition of the field, that Wales, the inventors of the font- three-quarter system, should be beaten at their own game, and at a time when they possessed such a floe array of talent outside the scrum- mage. Not unfrequently during the match the specta- tors saw some wonderful passing of quite mechanical regularity and precision, but it could not prevail against the fine defence of the Englishmen. But it was never- theless very beautiful to watch. Arthur Gould set his men an example in passing and kicking that was well followed by Conway-Rees, the Oxford captain, McCut- cheon, and Norman Biggs, although the last named has been more brilliant ist his day. However, England excelled in tackling, and the great combination of the visitors was, though often on the verge of suc- cess, almost invariably checked. And again with the scrummage, by no means wholly for them, the Welsh halves did not get the ball so often as their opponents on the other side. Bancroft had plenty of chances of de- monstrating his great ability as a full back ; but he has not often had to face such a stinging attack as that of Saturday. From the start the Engliehmen went to work as if they were determined to wipe out last year's loss at Cardiff, and how successful were their dexterity and resource is shown full well in the big score of five goals to a try, a score indeed that has only once been exceeded in the eleven games played between the countries • the instance was the eight goals and five tries scored by England in the first contest in 1880 at Blackheath on the famous Richardson's Field, long since given over to modern villa buildings. The present win was well merited in a brilliant contest. Wales played fourteen of the fifteen who took part in last year's victory at Cardiff, when the Welshmen, by better condition' alter being a long way behind at half time, outstayed their opponents, and just managed to win. England has certainly started well in her inter- national games, and the greater part of those figuring in Saturday's match will no doubt be found opposing Ireland in London on February 3. The English official's had their full share of anxiety through the bad weather, but Mr. Wallace, the lion. sec. of the Cheshire Union, had anticipated the frost by haying immense quantities of straw over the ground and he wrote late on Thursday that the only thing to prevent the game would be a heavyl fall of snow. Fortunately this ratter fear was not realised,while by the aid of fires the hard places in the ground were thawed. And when every- thing was ready for the game praise was not spared by the spectators for the provision made for everything. The atmosphere, though cool, was crisp, and the scene as the 10,000 people assembled on a bright wintry afternoon well illustrated the keenness of the British race in its sports: _ . _ _

Strict punctuality was observed, and it was barely half-past two when England started the game with the sun in their faces. What wind there was favoured the home side. The ball was well followed up and Ban- croft's kick being only feeble some sharp scrummaging (occurred in the Welsh quarters, indeed in the Welsh twenty-five. The English forwards made a great rush to the line and momentarily seemed certain to score. At this critical time a penalty kick enabled Wales to clear and some pretty work by the Welsh forwards in- fused an evenness into the play. The English halves stopped various rushes, and then Wales got the ball out to threequarters and soon Lockwood was seen in full cry for the Welsh goal. He was checked by Gould, and the Welsh captain had a subsequent hand in bring- ing down both Murat and Hooper. With the game open the Welsh backs were quickly prominent. Phillips passed the ball to Gould who, with Conway-Rees and McCutchenn in attendance, went away at a great pace and the English lines were in much danger. Byrne caused the visitors to fall back, but the skill of Conway-Rees, Gould, and Norman Biggs as drop kickers made the positi-n anything but secure for England. However, Taylor and Murfitt worked the ball more to the side of the around and a huge drop by Byrne was quickly afterwards almost at- tended with a goal. Wales had rather the better of the play after this, but cold hands and a hard ball were not cotplucive to every accuracy in passing. The English backs used their feet well, but the time slipped away and with more than two-thirds of the first half gone, the ball was in the English quarters. At this point one of the finest pieces of work in the match was seen and pro- duced a goal. It began by the ball coming out of a scrimmafte to Wells, who glided past his opponents and after a 50 yards' run sent the ball over to Hooper from whom it was teceivEd by Murat, who amid deafening applause grounded it behind the posts. Lockwood scored the goal. The sweets of scoring stimulated the English- men to greater efforts; the forwards went well in the scrummage and the play outside was full of brightness and preciSion. After a rush by the home forwards Ban- croft saved by kicking the ball against the boundary while Lockwood, Wells, and Morfitt each got nearly through. Then Hooper made a fair catch and from the free kick thus gained Taylor obtained a goal. Ends were then quickly changed and England possessed the signifi- cant lead of two goals (one from a try and the other from a "mark ") to nothing. The second half of the game was charactenzed with hard play, but ended in a vic- tory for England by five goals to one try.

div.head: SHOCKING BEAT Ii OF A FORMER
div.p: SHOCKING BEAT Ii OF A FORMER
RUNCORNIAN.
A FALL OF 300 FEET.

On Tuesday' evening, an inquest was opened on the body of William Broughton, aged 27 years,foreman fitter at the Richmond Waterworks. The deceased up to three years ago resided in Runcorn, and was in the employ of Messrs. E. Timmins and Sons. It appears that on Mon- day morning, whilst engaged at the Borough Waterwork Richmond, through tho breaking of a rope, he was pre- cipitated down a well 300 feet deep. About 11.30 he took his seat on a plank attached to which was a rope, ann gave the order to let him descend. No sooner had this been done than a crash was heard, and on looking down it was found that Broughtom had fallen off. On going down the well it was found that the poor man had crashed through the staging, hitting the girders, and then on to a heap of rough chalk, where he lay quite dead, and in a shockingly mangled condition, indeed, almost unrecognizable. On examination it was found that the rope supporting the plank was broken off near the wcod. The cieceased who belonged to an old Run- corn family had only been married three months. His remains will be interred at Richmond to-day.

div.head: WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Widnes Town Coun- cil was held in the Town Hall on Tuesday afternoon. The Mayor (Alderman F. H. Gossage) presided, and there were present Alderman J. W. Wareing, H. G. Timis, J. Williamson, J. Tilley, and G. Sadler ; Councillors C. E. Barlow, S. Quinn, W. Christie, J. Gough, H. O'Donnell, D. Wright, T. A. Bullough, G. I. Neil, T. Smith, W. W. Gossage, 11. B. Shores, T. Carney, H. Singleton, G. Davies, W. Hodgkinson, S. Owens, and T. Shuttleworth, Messrs. H. S. Oppen- helm (town clerk), T. Craik (assistant clerk), S. Hoyle (accountant), I. Carr (engineer), J. E. sin- Glair (surveyor), and W. Lowe (nuisance in- spector.)

div.head: COMPLIMENTS OF THE SEASON.
div.p: COMPLIMENTS OF THE SEASON.

Before the business of the Council commenced, the Mayor wished all the members a most successful new year. The experience of the first year of his mayoralty had been that of great pleasure, and he thanked the members of the Council for th.ir constant support of the Mayor's ruling, and also for the extreme courtesy he had always received from them. One untoward thing oc- curred last year. He referred to the dreadful coal strike which seemed to upset everything throughout the United Kingdom. He thought the thanks of the whole of the inhabitants of Widnes were due to those who so kindly worked upon the District Committee, and to all those who so generously subscribed to the funds, and to the gentlemen who acted on the committee for the distribu- tion of this fund. (Hear, hear.)
HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.

This Committee's minutes contained particulars of a claim by Mr. F. J. Poole, solicitor, on behalf of Mr. E. P. Evans for payment of 2.10 15s. bd., amount of damage alleged to have been si,stained to horse and trap in Mil- ton-road. The Town Clerk was instructcd to reply there- to, repudiating any liability on the part of the Corpora- tion ; also that the tender of Mr. William Farrant for the supply of provender for a period of three months at the prices quoted, be accepted.—The confirmation of the minutes was moved by Alderman Sadler, seconded by Councillor Christie.—Councillor Shores called attention to the state of Albert-mad, in which the sewer gas was very prejudicial to the health of the inhabitants.— Alderman Sailer promised that it should be attended to. Councillor Gough moved that the minutes be referred back to the Committee until they took into consideration the railway crossings at West Bank-street, and West Bank dock. On two previous occasions he had called the Committee's attention to the crossings, but nothing had been done although they were very dangerous. He supposed that they would lock the stable when the horse was gone.—Councillor O'Donnell seconded the amend- ment.—Alderman Williamson said that he would sup- port the amendment if it were altered so as to be an in- struction to the Committee to alter the crossings.— Councillor Gough agreed.—Alderman Sadler said that there was a question of whether the Committee had power to alter the crossings, but the matter should have the Committee's attention.—The Mayor appealed to Councillor Gough to withdraw his amendment on the promise of Alderman Sadler.—Councillor Gough con- sented to do so, and the minutes were passed unani- mously.

div.head: HEALTH COMMITTEE.
div.p: HEALTH COMMITTEE.

This Committee's minutes contained the following reports : Infectious Diseases Hospital—Number of pati- ents at last meeting, 13 ; admitted since, 2; discharged since, 11 ; died since, 2; patients still in, 7.—Accident Hospital—Number of patients at last meeting, 9; admit- ted since, 2 ; discharged, 4.; died, 0; patients still in, 7. —The 'Medical officer reported that the births during the month bad been 77, equal to 3008 per 1000; deaths dur- ing the month had te‘n 71, equal to 284 per 1000. The cases of infectious disease were considerably less. The high death rate was due to influenza.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Councillor Neil, seconded by Councillor Smith.

GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. This committee's minutes recommended that the tender of.the United Alkali Cos, Ltd., for the purchase of the surplus coke (estimated at 5,000 tons) from the gas works. during the ensuing year, be accepted at the price quoted. They also reported that the illuminating power of the gas of Widnes on the 10th and 21st December, was 18.24 and 19.25 candles respectively. Accounts amount- ing to £1,610 123. 8,1., on gas account, and £342 53. on water account, total £1,952 17s. 81, examined and passed for payment.—Alderman Tim mis in moving the confirmation of the minutes called attention to the pluck shown by the borough employers at the time that the accident occurred at the gas works, on the Bth Deaem- ben They went to work, led on by the engineer, and if a second fall of the chimney had taken place therd would have beep no way of escape. He thought it right to call the council's attention to this plucky and courageous action. A small present had been made to each man by the committee. The new gas holder at Ditton had been doing its work properly.—Councillor Bullough seconded the motion.—Carried.
GENERAL PURPOSES AND PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE.-
AI,DERMANIC ROBES.

This committee reported that the question of the train service having again been discussed, it was resolved— " That in the opinion of this committee the present facili- ties afforded by the L. and N.-W. Ry. Co., for the carri- age of passengers in connection with the lines of the Company. running into and through Widnes, both as regards train service—particularly through traffic—and station accommodation are not reasonable,and are totally inadequate to the requirements of the borough, and that in failing to comply with the very reasonable require- ments of the Corporation, the directors of the L and N. W. Ry. Co. have treated the public wants with a lack of consideration, which is much to be regretted, and that the Town Clerk be and is hereby instructed to forward a copy of this resolution to the Secretary of the Company, and to request that the directors may be good enough to give the matters therein mentioned their further and early attention." It was also resolved "that at all future meetings of the Town Council, and also on all public occasions when in attendance in their official capacities, and otherwise, as the Mayor may from time to time direct, the Mayor and Aldermen for the time being of this Borough shall res- pectively be attired in suitable official robes; those worn by the Aldermen to be uniform in material, design, and colour, and to be approved of by the Mayor."—Alderman Wareing moved the confirmation of the minutes. Refer- ring to the aldermanic robes, he said that the resolution was the outcome of the expressed wish of the Council although the aldermen were not unanimous in wishing to be robed.—Councillor Shores seconded the minutes.— Alderman Timmis moved as an amendment that the paragraph relating to aldermanic robes be left out. He did not want to wear a robe. (Laughter.) He rather ' objec' ed to wearing one. He did not quite see what good the robes were going to do any of them. If the robes were going to add dignity to their persons, wisdom to their discussions, fluency and brilliancy to their speeches, he thought that the other members of the Council would need the robes quite as much as they di4. (Laughter.) The amendment lie proposed was that either all or none of the Council wear the robes. If the aldermen were to wear robes, then the councillors should wear robes also. —Alderman Sadler seconded the amendment.—After an amusing discussion in which it was elicited that the aldermen would have to buy their own robes, the amendment was put, and lost, there only being nine in favour, including all the aldermen.—The minutes of the Committee were thenscarried unanimously.
FINANCE COMMITTEE.

Accounts to the amount of £4,33325. Bd. were recom- mended for payment.—The accounts were moved by Councillor Owens. seconded by Councillor Flodgkinson. —Alderman Williamson said that his witnesess at the fever hospital inquiry did not cost the town a penny.— The minutes were passed. LIBRARY AND TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION COMMITTEES. Councillor Wright moved and Councillor O'Donnell seconded the adoption of the minutes of these committees which recommended that the town clerk make applica- tion upon the form now submitted,for a series of science lectures under the Gilchrist fund ; that arrangements be made for issuing books at Farnworth at a cost not to exceed 10s. per week. A letter had been received from the department of science and art, London, referring to the application of this authority for a building grant from the department, and stating that the Lords of Committee of Council on litlucation had been pleased to authorize a grant of £l,OOO in respect of the rooms to he devoted to science and art respectively, and enclosing form of application for payment of the amount. It was also resolved that the mayor, the chairman, and the town Clerk he requested to make arrangements for the formal lavihg of the foundation stone of the proposed technical schools and free library.—The minutes were carried.—This concluded the business of the council.

div.head: POLITICS IN NEW ZEALAND.
div.p: POLITICS IN NEW ZEALAND.

A correspondent who has been resident for many years in Christchurch, NZ., writing to the " 'lmes ' with regald to the present state of affairs in New Zealand, says :—" New Zealand financially is now in a very good position, and will continue to progress if mischievous government does not retard it. Party .government here is a huge mistake, for the chief object of every ministry is to keep in office, and consequently bills are brought in and dropped in order to retain or gain support. nen, again, the payment of members (£240 for the session and a free railway pass) induces many of the Labour party and needy adventurers to seek election for the sake of emolument. and with the hope ot getting some pickings as well. Our elections, as you known, have just taken place,and resulted in the return of the Radical Government to power with an increased majority. This lithe first time wel'have had female suffrage, and it has certainly told, as I feared it would, against the conser- vative party. The Wesleyan and prohihition of liquor people are very numerous, and two or three very good members have lost their seats owing to these votes, in- cluding the leader of the Opposition. Nor do I see any prospect of matters mending against the next elec- tion."

At a meeting of the Sheffield City Council on Wednesday it was decided by 19 votes to 16 that all betting and gambling news should he blotted from the papers taken at the varimis public frto libraries in the city
RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUI HO. RITY.

Stokes, H. E. Ileyward,S. Woodward, J.N.Williams, C. W. Davenport, J. Brandreth, T. Lewis, J. Parr, E. Bratherton, J.Weir,T.Baxter, C.C. ; J.Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (deputy clerk), and J. div.head: DAIRIES AND COWSIIEDS.
div.p: DAIRIES AND COWSIIEDS.

The committee appointed to draft byelaws for the re- gulation of dairies and cowsheds under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Acts, presented a draft copy, which was adopted and ordered to be forwarded to the Local Government Board for approval, on the motion of Mr. Williams, seconded by Mr. Woodward.
FEVER AT HALTON AND KINGSLEY.

- Dr. Adams in his report stated that nine cases of scar- let fever had occurred in one house at Halton, and he had also visited seven fresh cases of scarlet fever in Kingsley. The schools if re-opened would rcquire the greatest care to secure that no children from infected houses attended.

div.head: URBAN POWERS FOR FRODSHAM.
div.p: URBAN POWERS FOR FRODSHAM.

The Local Government Board in forwarding copies of the order which they had issued investing the Rural sanitary Authority with certain urban powers as re- garded the contributory place of Frodsham township,. and declaring the expenses incurred by the Authority in the execution of these powers to be special expenses,. and stated that they would come into force on February sth.

div.head: PHTHISIS.
div.p: PHTHISIS.

Letters were received from the Congleton, Northwich, Wirral, Birkenhead, Altrmcham, Tarvin, and Chester Unions, stating the actiNns they had taken regarding the recommendations of the County Council to include phthisis in the notification of infectious diseases. In sume cases no action had been taken whils in others they declined to accept the suggestion. FRODSIIAII W kTER SCHEME,

The minutes of PrAsham Parochial Committee was submitted and showed that eight tenders had been re- ceived for the construction of the waterworks and reser- voir. The Committee resolved, on the motion of Mr. Heywood, seconded by Mr. T. Riley, that the tender of Messrs. Olenezer Timmins and Sons, of Runcorn, be ac- ' cepted. The amount of the tender was £3,loo.—Mr. Heywood moved and Mr. Williams seconded the motion.. The latter gentleman said in giving this tender to Messrs Timmins, the Committee were influenced to some con- siderable extent by the fact that they were a local firm. Although their tender was somewhat higher than the low- est—it was the lowest but one—the Committee deemed it better to have their own labour. Further than that Mr. Tiinmins had said as far as possible he would employ Frodsham labour on the wwrk. It would be gratifying to the people of Frodsham to know that such was the case. There were a great many men out of employment and it would be a great comfort to them to read this in the newspapers. (Elear, hear.)—The minutes were then adopted.

div.head: NO RLEY SCHOOLS.
div.p: NO RLEY SCHOOLS.

Dr. Adams reported having inspected Norley School and found that the sanitary arrangements were defec- tive and this was also the case with regard to the ven- tilation which should be remedied by both inlets and outlets of adequate dimensions. No water supply existed unless the rain cistern were regarded as such,but he was told water was never drunk. It was proposed to carry water from the Vicarage pump, other defects in the schools had been mentioned but they did not concern them as a sanitary authority.—The Rev. C. R. Nunn in. acknowledging receipt of the medical officer's report inquired what precise alteration would satisfy the authority. The ventilation . would be effected as advised. The enlargement suggested would be made,. and improved drainage executed. Anything more , would necessitate rebuilding entirely, and at present he thought his co-managers would not prefer to do this.—On the motion of Mr. Heywood seconded by Mr. Woodward, the clerk was instructed to inform Mr.. Nunn that the authority would be satisfied if the medical officer's recommendations were carried out to. the letter.—An inquiry from Mr. Nunn as to the amount of fever existing in Norley was referred to the Medical Officer.

div.head: FEVER IN KINGSLEY.
div.p: FEVER IN KINGSLEY.

Mr. Woodward said one of the day schools at Kingsley was re-opened on the previous day, ar d the logical con- sequence would be that the Sunday schools would be re-opening. Although a schoolmaster might be very watchful, they could not expect the same care in the case f managers of the Sunday schools. He considered it a most unthpughtful and inconsiderate action on the part of the managers of the school. There had been seven fresh outbreaks of fever within the last three weeks, and there had been one death. There was no hardship in the schools being closed for they had the grant for the ensu- ing examination in consequence of the compulsory clos- ing of the schools. It almost appeared as though the managers thought the Authority were acting towards them in a spirit of animosity whereas they had only one desire and that was to stamp out the disease. It was a .pity they did not loyally co-operate with the Authority. He moved that the Clerk write to the managers asking them to continue to close their schools, and if the reply was not satisfactory report the matter to the Education Department.—Mr. Hanby seconded.—Carried.

div.head: WESTON WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: WESTON WATER SUPPLY.

The Inspector reported that about 100' houses in Wes- ton were without a sufficient supply of water.. The whole of these houses were connected with the. mains of Runcorn waterworks, but the authority had no power to come upon the Waterworks Co.—The Clerk: No we can only call upon the owners to provide a proper supply.— Mr. Heywood suggested that the clerk should write to Runoorn Improvement Commissioners who now owne4 the waterworks.—The Clerk said he should not venture to do that ; they might be told to mind their own busi- ness. The authority had no power over Runcorn Com- missioners in regard to water. The people themselves had the remedy in their own hands. If they had not got a supply they could compel the Commissioners to give them a supply, because Weston was within the limits of the Water Act.—The Chaiman : If the owners of the houses apply to the Commissioners, and they will not give a supply, cannot we do something.--The Clerk we can only deal with the owners of the houses. In reply to Mr. Heywood the Inspector said they were working class houses.—Mr. Heywood .said he thought •the Authority ought to bring a little pressure.to bear upon the owners, and the owners must bring pressure upon the Commissioners. He proposed that the owners 14e served with @rders to provide a proper supply of water for their property, otherwise the houses would have to be closed.—The Chairman : That will entail some work if there are ninety owners.—Mr. Stokes : There are only about twelve.—The Inspector said at the upper end of Weston the people could just draw water when there was fifteen feet in the reservoir, but if the people in the lower parts of the township were draw- ing water, the people in the higher portions could not get water when there was 21 feet in the reseruoir. The mains were unsufficient. The motion was carried unani- mously.

SEWBRAGE EXTENSION AT WALTON. INFERIOR. The Inspectr reported that the Committ..e appointed to consider this question had decided that the present s.wers be extended to a distance of about 75 yards, and the Inspector was instructed to obtain tenders for the work. There was no other business of public interest.

div.head: ANARCHIST YAILLANT.
div.p: THE ANARCHIST YAILLANT.
CONDEMNED TO DEATH.

The trial of Vaillant, the perpetrator of the bomb out- rage in the French Chamber, took place on Wednesday at the Seine Assizes. In answer to questions by the pre- siding Judge, the prisoner said it was M. Argellies, de- Duty for Corbeil, who gave him the ticket by which he gained admission to the Chamber. It was at the depu- ties that the bomb was aimed, and he should have pre- ferred to strike every deputy present rather than a single person among those seated around him in the gallery. He acted as he did because he was carrying social war against parasites. The prisoner read a state- ment he had drawn up, in which he declared that his act was the outcome of the miseries which the people endured. He desired to bring about the regeneration of society. "In my duel against society I have only wounded my adversaries. . . Strike me in my turn, if you will," he added melodramatically ; " but what will be the verdict pronounced against you in the history of nations 7" At the close of the case for the prosecution the prisoner said he could produce forty wit- nesses to prove how good and humane he was, but as they were all Anarchists he had not thought it his duty to have them cited. The prisoner's council argued that he could not he condemned to death. The jury, how- ever, found Valliant " guilty of assassination with pre- meditation and without extenuating circumstances," and sentence of death was passed.

Lord Lovelace, who has just died at the advanced age of eighty-seven, was almost a vegetarian. For many years he had eaten no animal fohd except an occasional pigeon, and he ventured on this animal variation at very rare intervals.

The following names, well-known in literature,appea,r in the list of those who have recently joined the Roman Catholic Church :—Mr. Marion Crawford, Miss Braddon, Mr. F. Anstey, and Mr. T. Fisher Unwin. Jahn Dubel, who has been elected constable of the eighth ward, Brooklyn, U.S.A., is a coloured man who runs a bootblack's box, and was put up for fun, but he will draw five hundred pounds a year just the same. Since the invasion of Russia by Napoleon, 82 years , ago, it has been the custom for the priests in the St. ' Petersburg churches to "solemnly curse" the French on every Christmas Day. But Cronstadt and Toulon have "changed all that," and last Christmas the annual commination service was for the first time omitted. It would have been absurd to continue it after the scenes at Toulon and Paris, which are supposed to have obli- terated the memory of the conflicts in which liussians and French have so often ben engaged.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

div.head: POULTRY LECTURES AT FRODSEUAL
div.p: POULTRY LECTURES AT FRODSEUAL

Mr.. Richard P. Ward, organising secretary to the Cheshire County Council Technical Instruction Corn- mittee, wrote to the clerk stating that the resolution passed at a meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was laid before the Technical Instruction Committee. He was desired to state that full arrangements were made for a knowledge of the poultry lectures at Frod- sham being known. The notices were forwarded to Mr. Harrison for distribution a.nd that gentleman had furnished them with a list of the places in which Lie so distributed. A second set was also sent to the follow- ing gentlemen, who kindly undertook to see to them.: Mr. Dunsford, Mr. Rigby jan., mad Mr. Beck. Frodshant was the only place where a good attendance had not been secured and the reason no doubt was the wantof a small local Committee to take an active interest in the matter. In every case where such existed good attend- ances were obtained. In making these lectures known, such means were taken either by hand bills or posters, or both as the local people assured him.(Mr.Ward) would be most suitable.—Mr. Heywood contended that the lectures failed for want of proper advertising. As to forming a local committee he did not think people in a place would take up the matter and form a ,committee without they had some instruction from head quarters. They had been snubbed before with officials from the County Council and otherwise. ---- •
FINANCE.

Mr. Brandreth presented the report of the Finance Committeo, who recommended payment of accounts amounting to £B7B O. 91. The balance in the treasurer's hands was £3,372 8.,;. 8,1. The County Council precept was due, but they had not sufficient money to pay it It was decided to summons the overseers of Alvanley and Kingswood, for non-payment of precept.
THE COUNTY RATE BASIS.

Mr. Reginald Putts, Clerk. to the Cheshire Council, wrote stating that in consequence of certain resolutions having been passed by the Guardians of the Chester, Nantwich, Northwich, and Runcorn Poor Law Unions on the subject of a new county rate basis being at once prepared, the committee had requested him to intimate that they had given the necessary instructions for the preparation af a new basis. He was to explain that it was absolutely essential to the principle adopted, in ar- riving at a new county rate basls,that it shall be fair and equitable to the county as a whole ; and having regard to the great diversity of practice followed by several union assessment committees in arriving at the gross estimated rental of the rateable hereditaments in their respective unions, and to the difference in the deduction from the several classes of property, to arrive at the net rateable value thereof, and also to the fact that some of the unions had not been valued by professional and in- dependent valuers fur a number of years, the committee had decided not to adopt either the gross or net poor rate assessments by themselves as the standard upon which to levy the county rates.as suggested by. the Guar- dians of the Northwich, Chester, and Runcorn unions. For many years past in the county, the property tax (schedule A) Assessment had been as far as practicable,. adopted in preparing the County Rate Basis and the Committee had determined, with the concurrence of the council to adopt this course again. The clerks to the several commissioners of taxes in the county, furnish to the committee, returns showing the gross value of the different classes of property in each township, without regard to the character of the property which such total value represents, but the Com- mittee made the following deductions from each of the several classes of property making up such total value and these deductions are identical for each and every township in the county. The deductions from each of the several classes of property so made are s (1) Land occupied by itself without houses or buildings, per cent.; (2) farm houses dwellings, and buildings and land occupied therewith, per cent..;: (3) dwelling- houses, whether occupied with or without gardens at- tached, shops and warehouses of the gross annual value of £lO and upwards, 10 per cent.; (4) cottages occupied with or without gardens at,ached, shops, warehouses ' and other building 3 under the gross annual rental of £lO, 15 per cent.; (5) tithe rent-charge for the town- ship, 10 per cent. ; (6), mills, mines, factories, gas and water works, &c., DI per cent. In a great many cases townships contiin certain rateable heredita- merits which are not included in the profit tax assess- ments of the township. In such cases the net poor rate assessment of such property from the latest supple- mental valuation lists are taken. The• Committee was anxious that each Union Assessment Committee should be made conversant with the .principle they were adopting in preparing the new basis or standard, which principle they felt satisfied was the only equitable • one to adopt,having regard to the circumstances before ex- plained.—The communication was listened to without comment.

div.head: PROSPECTS OF ANOTHER COAL WAR
div.p: PROSPECTS OF ANOTHER COAL WAR

THE RAILWAY COMPANIES AND COAL.. CONTRAC CS. A London correspondent 'Writes :—The struggle be- tween the coalowners and the railway companies whose contracts require immediate renewal threatens to be a fierce one, and may possibly produce another coal war. The managers of those companies are, I am informed, most bitter in their resentment against the attempt to extort higher prices from them in the face of depressed railway business and trade generally. They will resort to any method of evading the demands of the eoalowner, and in some cases will only buy for consumption from hatid to mouth. The number of trains and men employed reduced by the late stoppage have in several important instances not yet been restored. The London and North- Western Company happen to be in the fortunate position of not being obliged to make fresh contracts till the middle of the year, when prices are almost certain to be normal.

div.head: WEALTH AND PENURIOUSNESS.
div.p: WEALTH AND PENURIOUSNESS.
AN EXTRAORDINARY STORY.

A man, for many years resident at Keighley, who had lived so penuriously that he was generally regarded as being in poor eircumstAnces, was, says the" Westmins- ter Gazette" at his death, towards the close of last year, intestate, found to have left. £7,000. The fortune has now come into possession of the only near relative, a middle-aged sister, who has been accustomed all her life long to perform domestic duties for other people. But her former life has such a charm for her, or she has so great a desire to earn her daily bread, that she lives amid the humblest surroundings, and goes out washing or charing at least one half day per week, at the rate of 3d. per hour.

div.head: LYNCHING EPISODE.
div.p: A LYNCHING EPISODE.
TRACKED BY BLOODHOUNDS.

HENDERSON,KENTIICKY, 4VEDNESDAY. —On Tuesday last Joe Willett, a burly negro of brutal appearance, crimin- ally assaulted Mrs. Morgan,a whi!-e woman, a widow of about sixty years of age, who lives in an isolated cot- tage. Alarmed by the woman's cries, Willett fled to the woods. A posse of citizens was at once organised, led by Edward Johnson, a nephew of the woman assaulted. A couple of bloodhound, were outlined at the county gaol, and with the assistance of the brutes Willett was tracked to a swamp covered with thick brushwood not far from the Ohio river. When at bay, the ntgro, who was armed with an old fowling piece., turned on, his pursuers, and fired, killing one of the hounds and inflict- ing injuries likely to prove fatal on two men of the party. He was finally captured after being shot through both arms, when he was seized and hurried to a clear- ing in the wood,where he wab tied to a tree. According to the last accounts, the mob smeared him from, bead to foot with kerosine oil, and were heaping dry twigs about him preparatory to burning him at the stake.

div.head: MR. A. B. FORWOOD AT PRESCOT.
div.p: MR. A. B. FORWOOD AT PRESCOT.

On Tuesday evening, in the Assembly rooms, Present, a largely attended meeting of Conservatives and Union ists whs held, under the presidency of Mr. Jahn D. Banks. Among others on the platform were the Hon. Lord Stanley, M.P., the Right Hon. A. B. Forwood, M.P., Messrs. W. A. Cookson (Seaforth), F. J Leslie, F. Rad- eliffu, A. Mackenzie Smith (Roby), C. Culshaw, and G.

Cochrane, Dr. Hail, &C. Mr. A. B. Forwood, M.P.,' Secretary to the Admiralty US the last Administiation, in a speech dealt again with the condition of the navy and the recent discussion in - the House of Commons with regard thereto, and urged that in order to cope with the navies of other nations a • More extended shipbuilding programme should be un- dertaken by the Government. The Most interesting Portion of his speech, however, was that in which he, as a Member of the Admiralty, responsible for the construc- tion of H.M.S. Resolution, defended the seaworthiness of the vess,-: :ezainst the serious allegations recently made regarding. aer behaviour in a gale. Mr. Forwood stated that the v,ssel's designs had been submitted to and ap- proved i:y committee of the most experienced admirals in the and that the utmost care had been taken to Make the ,hip thorougbly seaworthy and efficient. But the vess, I had left port in the depth of winter, and be- fore thee on board had had an opportunity of becoming. thoroughly at home in her; and she had encounterea a severe storm before she was thoroughly secured against it. What happened, he said, was not the fault of the Ship, but was due to preventable causes on the part of those in charge. A green crew and officers unaccus- - torned to large vessels might naturally have become somewhat alarmed by the rolling of the ship, but there was no danger whatever of the vessel caps;zing. The case of the Eesolution confirmed an opinion which he had long held, that naval officers of modern days had not the oPportunity of seagoing experience which they had a hundred years ago • and this condition ef things, he thought, ought to be remedied.

div.head: BOYS WHO RUN AWAY TO SE&
div.p: BOYS WHO RUN AWAY TO SE&

"Do we see many runaway boys ?" said a recruiting agent for the Royal Navy who is stationed in an impor- tant manufacturing centre. "I should think we do. But before a lad is accepted for the Navy we must have this (a certificate of birth), and this form (a document in which parents give their consent to their son becom- ing a bluejacket) must be filled up. Sometimes, if a lad has a bad home, we manage the consent ourselves, and sometimes a lad deceives us. How? I'll tell you of a case. A boy came to a certain recruiting depot accompanied by a gentleman isho said he was the Youngster's guardian. Now that he has been in the Navy a few months, he doesn't like the life he is obliged to lead, and he says that his parents are alive and do not know where he is. I expect we shall have to let inn go. Boys who run away with the intention of go- ing to sea, however, generally make . for a port in the expectation that some captain in the mercantile marine Will welcome them with open arms. The Landing Stage at Liverpoolis i wonderfulfocus for lads who leave home ' iXL this frame of mind. You may see them there very eltm—indeed,the officials have become so familiar with this particular class of youth that they can detect them 'With unerring certainty."—"
