AN-D R-ATIONA LIKE. Sir,—Among your many readers,' have been very much ' amused he the above gentleman's exposition of so-called rationalism. But what surprises me most is that he is not at all consistent. Why potter around the Tory- rationalism of Lecky, Huxley and Co., when the logical end—the only consistent end of so-called Rationalism, ith a big R—is putting forward its claims—l mean 'achy ! Any educated Anarchist, will show fiim the point in la 7: reasoning where he becomes both illogical and ab- surd. For a man to sneer in the beginning of his letter at" imaginary Salvation" and" fanciful falls," mean- ing by this last, the primeval fall of man, and then at the end of the effusion to glorify reason as" God's gift," and while condemning dogmatism to dogmatise more than the Pope—all this is as illogical, to quote Mr. Peer's tet.e-noir Dr. Mivart, " as illogical as agnostic- igtn. ." For the rest, any student of history, will tell Mr. Peers in spite of his vaunted reason that the world was bet- ter off and the masses of men far and away happier (which seems to be all the world cares tor now-a-days) in the so-called dark ages, than they are at present, that their ideal was higher,and their outlook rosier, than in this soi-disant " enlightened" (sic) 19th century. Not only, I repeat, will historical students tell him this,but almost any thinker of eminence both Catholic, Protestant and Anarchist. Why talk of the bloodstained pages of ecclesias- tical history, when Matabele wars, starving thousands, bomb-throving, murders and suicides, stare him in the face. May I ask Mr. Peers to look out on the world around him, and to use an Anarchist dictum" learn to aobserve."—Yours faithfully,
JOHN S. HOWELL. 9, Montznmery-road, Chiewick, Lo ndon, NV. 6th January, 1894. .
MR. IVIIITIIAM ON LIFE'S DISPARITIES.

Sir.—The sepia-tinted picture my friend Mr. H. Whit- ham draws of American labour life is very depressing reading. Hunger and starvation on one hand,and vulgar display on the other. A sad picture truly; but, whilst being in full sympathy with all this suffering, I should like to have some few things in " bomb throwing" cleared up. First, as to the " $29,000,000 worth of diamonds." Is it .not rather a violent assumption t all these were diamonds ; and,negleeting the patent vul- garity of this be-jewelled snobbery, is it not an equally violent assumption to say that all these glittering baubles were" spoils "of the' spAiator " ? Were none of these bought honestly by honestly earned money ? Verily eyes filled with tears are not the best for seeing clearly, else it would be unnecessary to point out that this wholesale condemnation is neither just nor generous. la this antithesis of be-jewelled opulence and ragged ,squalor, the whole question of the right of one man to :hold possession of more than it suffices for bare subsist- ance is involved. Has any man the right 'to be rich while ethers are starving ? Again has the poor man the right to demand relief from the rich ? Your contributor seems to think he has. Let us look this thing squarely in the face, shirking none of its issues. He would undoubtedly be a very poor specimen of humanity who would knowingly leave a fallow man to starve if he could relieve him, and he deserved to be relieved. Without dipping further into this invidious question, let us turn to the 'boita-fide out of work workingman. Why is he out of work and why does he starve when so placed ? To see the answer to this more clearly, let us ask how he behaves when pros- pering ? Too frequently he eats and drinks—especially the latter—and takes no thought for the morrow. He too often invests his spare cash in most unprofitable ventures—the publics n,who too often drowns all the man within him, or the parson who would fain have him neglect the facts of this world in order the better to swallow the figments of another. But the two great causes of this poverty and distress are over production in work by machinery, and over production of the family at home. In this last, most of the poor man's difficulties find their source. We have been talking of "rights "—the poor man's rights. But, has any man the right to bring into the world beings whom lie Las no sure prospect of adequately maintaining? Only one answer can be given to this question—no! But the children—the over-production of poor families—to-day will be the unemployed of the future. Who, then will he responsible for the maintenance of these who have" a natural right to a livelihood ?" Who ? At present it is they who exercise the virtues of thrift and self-restraint, who are called upon to keep those who have neglected and despised these virtues. Society ought to safeguard its interests by compelling every man to lay by a weekly sum as a store for such contingencies. The poor regard the workhouse with aversion as a disgrace. Rightly considered this ought not to be so. No man who has been paying poor rates, directly or indirectly, and who subsequently by unavoidable circumstances is com- pelled to seek shelter there, need be ashamed of so do- ing. To him it is merely as a provident society, to which he has subscribed, and by which he is now in benefit. It is the loafers and malingerers who have put the institution into such had odour. If these,and super- annuated deetors,were cleared out, there would be more left for the deserving poor. •As toethe question of bomb throwing. While I think this, or any other means almost, good enough to be used against such an execrable tyranny as that of Russia— whose emperor is ever makine war upon the best of his subjtcts—l cannot too forcibly execrate its use in con- stitutional countries where the laws, had as they may he, are subject to the will of the people. Here such means are entirely unjustifiable. Mr.Whitham is troubled about the connection of business and "Christian ethics." What are " Christian ethics ?" The best bit of ethics I know is "Do as you would be done by," but this is not a Christian maxim, except by adoption, but a heathen •Chinee ! Fancy " Resist not evil" as a business prin- ciple! Business on Christian ethical principles will not pay. Buying in the cheap and selling in the delr market will be a vital business principle when Chris- tianity is forgotten, except as a phase of ecclesiastical history from whose ruins a better system has grown.— Truly yours,

lion and a lamb together, form a ring and shout" fair- play." It is a marvellous thing that men of reputed intelli- gence can be found to defend on the ground of morality a condition of things such as that I have described. For truth's sake let us give it its proper name. In previous letters I have shown that the miners as a whole have , not been guilty of violence or intimidation, and there- fore fail to perceive the relevancy of Mr. Peer's argument against attempting to attain a certain end irrespective of the means employed_ A man who can wink at the immorality of the conditions described above, while designating a remonstrance uttered against "blacklegs," as crime must be in a very parlous condition indeed. He makes much fuss about little peccadillos while apparent- ly approving offences of real magnitude. I would apply the golden rule in a different way. I would not only urge men to do unto others, Sze., I would render it easier for them to carry the rule into practice. I would go further. I would make those who were unwilling do unto others as they would like to be done by. There should be no exemptions in favour of these men.lt should not be a question of choice with them. Neither should it be in their power to make it difficult for other men to do right. And I would do these things by means of Socialism of which we shall hear much more in the next few years.—Yours, &c.,
COMMON JUSTICE.
WARRINGTON YOUNG MEN'S CHRIS- TIAN ASSOCIATION.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Young Men's Christian Association was held in the Lec- ture Hall, Friar's-green, on Tuesday evening, the chair being occupied by Dr. Starkey Smith, in the absence of Mr. Wm. Owen.

Mr. W. H. BAYLEY (secretary), submitted his annual report, in which it stated that the association was at present in a better condition than at at any other time in its history, and was qualified to do the work it had in hand with better results than in former years. kflear, hear.) A very important step was the formation of a ladies' auxiliary. With Mrs. John Fairclough as secre- tary, this auxiliary would be of great help in many ways. A special arrangement had been made .with the Committee of the Gymnasium, and they would like to see the members join the classes. In addition, swimming and cricket clubs were likely to be formed. The lectures and entertainments durieg the past three months had been well attended, and were very success- ful. A conversational bible class was held every Friday evening. The P.S.A. movement, which was starte I in January last, had also been successful, and seemed to have done much good,the membership having steadily increased since the commencement of the movement. The 'present was the jubilee year of Y.M.C.A's and they hoped t) take part in its celebration. It had been arranged to hold a jubilee conference in London, when it was expected that 1,500 delegates would attend. (Ap- plause.) Mr. STRINGER (treasurer), in his report, stated, that they had a balance in their favour of £7 63. Bd., but there were some outstanding accounts which amounted to £6 133., leaving them a balance of 133. Bd. The fur- nishing account lett a balance in their favour of us. 61. (Applause.) Mr. KENT delivered a short acc.unt of the work doße by the P.S.A. movement. The scheme was commenced on the second Sunday of last yea,r,and they held their anniversary on the previous Sunday. (Applause.) They could, he thought, congratulate themselves on having done some useful work during the year. (Applause.) There were 14 members the first Sunday,and they finish- ed the year with 47. (Hear, hear.) The average atten- dance for the last quarter was 49, which he considered eminently satisfactory. Their meetings had been bright , and cheerful, and they had started the New Year hope- fully. ( Appla use.) The Bible Class, Shorthand Class, rennis Club and other reports were submitted, and were all of a satisfac- tory character.—The Chairman commented on the -ex- cellent nature of the reports, and after the election of officers and committee for the ensuing year the meeting terminated.

div.head: JOHN PEERS.
div.p: JOHN PEERS.

SOCIALISM ,AND MORALITY. Sir,—After a season of charades, acrostics and conun- drums one would hale thought that the intellectual training thus gained would have enabled Mr. John Peers ti) underitand what a "had old ethical principle" is. He confesses that he does not. This is really very strange for a man with some pretensions to scientific knowledge. Nevertheless he talks about "ethical prin- ciples" and "moral laws" as if he knew all about them. Ethics, of course is a science, a science of speculations, of doctrines, of inferences, of theories, and there are about as many systems of ethics, I should think, as there are " ethical principles." Which particular system of ethics Mr. Peers subscribes to I know not. It may be that he has formulated a system of his own by the eclec- tic method, picking a little bit out of this system and a little out of that until at last he has got quite a patch- work of moral philosophy; a coat of many colours so to speak. When Mr. Peers has shown that every scientific, theory that has ever been advanced has been proved ' true there will then be some force in his comparison of nay phrase "had old ethical principle," with those others he mentions—"a good had man" or "black white man." But it is hopeless for him to attempt the task. Why,the way in which moral philosophers have disagreed on the question of ethical principles is notorious. Take Butler's doctrine of conscience, for instance. Butler formulated the doctrine that conscience is the supreme authority as to what is right or wrong. Of course men's conscierces differ. In some countries polygamy is prac- tised. It is considered quite the proper thing. Our sense of propriety and morality would be outraged if we had living next (7. r to us a man with half-a-dozen wives. Another exponent of ethics steps in and says that the doctrine of conscience holds an insecure posi- tion, because it is unrelated to reason. You see one sass the principle is good and the other says it is not. Ethical inquiry seeks to determine the principles by which conduct is to be regulated ; it deals with what ought to be and not with what is. Your intelligent readers know this as well as I do. Mr. Peers assumes that we know all that there is to know in regard to our duty one to another, and to society. If he declared that we know a great deal more than we practice he would be nearer the mark. It is experience that entitles us to say that our perception of a moral ideal becomes more clear as it is realized not only in the individual but in society. Yeti will find this ex- pressed in some treatises on ethics and this leads us to the point under discussion. The " man in blue" spoken of by Mr. Peers is not always tha solid embodiment of sound ethics, or he would not allow the owner of lard to take from it a value which had been created by the community ; and would not allow a coalowner to do as he liked with minerals that he had never seen. But no doubt there are rules upon which Mr. Peers and I might find ground for agreement. Let us take the golden rule," Do unto others ass's would men should do to you." Haying made Up our minds as to this, the next step would be how to put it into practice. Well this is the way Mr. Peers would do it. He would allow a coal- owner, or any other wealthy employer of labour for the matter of that, to set two starving men in competition with each other for certain work, in consequence of whose poverty the wealthy man would grow richer ; or he would permit the wealthy man to lock out the worker until he was obliged to come to his terms from sheer starvation. When the poor man grew restive he would pick up a bundle of " ethical principles" or " moral laws," and fling them at him. All the time he would be shouting "liberty " and "freedom of contract," although he must see that there could be no liberty and no free- dom in the conditions at all. You may as well put a

div.head: ALARMING ACCIDENTS AT HANDOCK. --- COLLISION ON THE NEW ST. HELENS RAILWAY.
div.p: ALARMING ACCIDENTS AT HANDOCK. --- COLLISION ON THE NEW ST. HELENS RAILWAY.

A couple of serious accidents, resulting in great damage to rolling stock, occurred on the new line of the Liverpool, St. Helens, and South Lancashire Railway Cotnpany now in course of construction at Haydock, near St. Helens, on Friday, afternoon last week. The work of constructing the line is being carried out by Messrs. S. W. Pilling and Co., con- tractors, whose men have almost completed the section between St. Helens and Lowton Junction, a distance of about nine miles. The accidents both occurred at the subway or tunnel, about 100 yards in length, under the extensive railway sidings of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., near the Queen Pit, Hayclock. For some days the contractors' men had been working the traffic on the single line system, and shortly after noon on Friday two locometives, each drawing a train of waggons, ran into each other in the tunnel re- ferred to. The line at this point forms a sharp curve, and neither driver was able to see the ether train until just before the collision. The results were disastrous. Several waggons of both trains were literally smashed to splinters, while others were damaged and thrown from the line. Both engines also sustained damage. The drivers and stokers, one or two of whom jumped from their engines,on seeing the clanger,were uninjured, thir escape being marvellous. Information of the accident was at once conveyed to the officers of the firm, and a large staff of men set to work clearing away the debris and replacing the unbroken waggons upon the mctals. These operations occupied some hours, and directly after their completion another serious accident happened to a train of waggons geing in the direction of Golborne from Flaydock. The train was moving at a fairly good sneer.] and got safely through the tunnel tin- der Messrs. Evans' sidings. Just beyond that point the line—a temporary one used by the contractors—makes a somewhat steep accent to the top of the cutting, and while on the incline the engine left the rails. Fortun- ately the engine kept an upright position, and the driver and stoker escaped uninjured. Nearly all the train waggons left the rails, and some were badly smashed beyond repair. A number of men employed by Messrs. Pilling and Co. were riding on the waggons to Ashton and Golborne, where they reside, and these sus- tained bruises and a severe shock. A youth named Sktlhorn, residing at Golborne, was the most seriously injured. It is stated that he was riding on the engine, and after the mishap it was found that one of his thighs was fractured. He was removed to the Hayciock Cot- tage Hospital, where he was attended by Dr. Hayward, who found it necessary to amputate the broken limb on Saturday morning. The dis., bled engine and train were left in the cutting until Saturday, when the line was again cleared for traffic.

div.head: BUXTON'S NEAPOLITAN CHOIR
div.p: BUXTON'S NEAPOLITAN CHOIR
AT EARLESTOWN.

Mr. Harry Buxton's Neapolitan Choir commenced on Monday night, a week's visit at the To..vii This is the third occasion an which Mr. Buxton has appeared at Earlestown, and the reputation he estaigli.bed there has on the present occasion stood him in ,good stead. The choir has been considerably strengthened and improved, and with the addition of other novelties, Mr. Buxton is able to present an enter- tainment, so varied as to suit the most fastidious tastes. The hall on each occasion has been nicely filled with a most appreciative audience, and the various items have been received with unstinted applause, encores being also frequent. In additicin to the vocal and instrumental contributions, dioramic tours are given, conducted by Madame Buxton, whose descriptions of the places visited are lucid and instructive. To vary the monotony of the tours, several vocal items are given, which tend to make the journeys pass most pleasantly. On M4nday evening " Holiday rambles in Ireland," was depicted, and on Wednesday " Switzerland and Italy," whilst on Tues- day, 'the pictures were of a miscellaneous character. The Buxton family take a leading part in the entertain- ment, the singing of Miss Flora Buxton, being exception- ally good. Miss Maud and Mr. Fred, are very capable artists in their various parts, (Nladarrie Buxton was much appreciated, as a reciter, her "Women of Mumbles Head," with illustrations, being capitally (-riven. The song " Hear dem bells," by Miss M. Buxton, was received with applause, the distant bell effect greatly adding to the charm of the song. Miss Ashton and Miss Fa Craig are also two . capable. artists, both possessing voices of rich compass the pleasing part perhaps being their distinct articulation. Miss Kitty tV ondford was often encored for her hum- orous singing, her songs being given with the needful effect, and without the slightest trace of vulgarity. A valuable adjunct to the entertainment is the ventrilo- quial exhibition of Pro. Alex. Fox, who with figures and animals, keeps the audience continually in a state of wonder and merriment. Mr. W. Kingsley,hand bell ringer, who his appeared before the Queen at.os- borne, brings" down the house," with his clever mani- pulation of the bells, his performa nee on every occasion being deservedly encored. Taken altogether, the enter- tainment is at once pleasing and refined, and as they oc- cupy the hall for two nights longer, those who have not vet paid a visit should avail themselves of the oppor- tunity still remaining. On Thursday evening the hal was flue l with an audience which appreciated to the full the various items submitted. On this occasion the enter- tainment was of a miscellaneous character, the dioramie tours being abandoned fur this night. Miss Flora Buxton Miss Ashton and Miss Craig and Miss Woodford were again to the fore, each winning honours in their respec- tive parts. Madame Buxton recited with much pathos the beautiful story of " Jane Conquest" ; the various incidents being illustrated by the lantern. The part song " Excelsinr " was also illustrated, and was well received by the audience. The other artistes also cleverly performed their alloted tasks, and gave evident satisfaction to the large audience ass tubed

div.head: RUGBY FOOTBALL.
div.p: RUGBY FOOTBALL.

With respect to the sub-line "Rugby football" I was tempted to observe, in a tone not unmixed with sadness " there is none." So far as its local application goes, this statement would not have erred on the side of un- truthfulness ; hut generally speaking one is bound to admit that there was football—at Birkenhead Park, on Saturday, when England tried conclusions—and tried in another sense, tQo—with the champions of the leek and hilly Wales. At Warrington on Saturday, not even a junior team delighted the admirers of the game with an exposition ; it was very discouraging ; indeed, it was a " frost." This is not a premeditated pun, although ; since the frost was at the bottom of the whole matter, it may look suspiciously like premeditation. The field at Wilderspool was so emphatically " bony" that after testing it in the morning the officials seem to have ar- rived at the opinion that play that afternoon might have an injurious effect upon the bone—not that of the field —simply that of the players.

A great number of Warringtonians took a trip over to Birkenhead Park to witness the famous match,and there is no doubt they were pleased with England's victory. Some idea of the crowd of spectators who were present can be obtained when it is stated that the "gate" realised almost MO.

Bpaliing of the match the " Athletic News" says "In a couple of teams containing so many sprinters it was rather remarkable that one of the tries should have been scored by a player whom imagination in her most reckless mood would never describe as a Deertoot. Yet such was Bradshaw's ability and strength that when he fairly got into his stride he would not be turned away from his purpose, and it was laughable to see how some of his opponents cleared out when he was making his terrible run.

" We never got one proper glimpse of that beautiful passing game which the Welshmen patented a few years ago, and Englishmen had to pay royalty on last seaion. Now the patent has expired, and we use the system—at any rate on Saturday—with far more advantage than our friends do. Perhaps we have found out the weak spots by experience, for certainly some of the English backs seemed to know how to prevent the Welsh machi- nery from getting to work, and after that the rest was easy."

div.head: GYMNASIUM.
div.p: THE GYMNASIUM.

The other week I mentioned that the Warrington eight wnuld probably be drawn with the Dobobran eight in the 200 guineas Shield Competition. It transpires that they have been drawn with Stockport. The two teams will meet on the 21111-4 but it has not yet been settled which town is to be chosen as the " scene" of the battle. It is probable that Wazrington will be honoured in this direc- tion, for from what I can gather, the Stockport "eight" are of a very modest and retiring nature, and they pre- fer to play away from the gaze of "relatives and friends." About appropriating victories, however, they are not quite so shy, so Warrington ought to keep them- selves on the "top-notch" strain.

By the way, the display which is to take place at the Gym. to-night (Saturday) is going. to be one of the most interesting demonstrations that has occurred in the building, if all that l'hear is correct. About its origin- ality there is no doubt-. This is a performance to be given on the kori:ontal.!—not parallei—bars,by Mr. Kins- ley. I have had a glimpse of the exercises the clever conductor is going to perform, and I am quite safe in predicting that theie will be some enclarnations of "marvellous !" before he gets through with the work. Then respecting the tug of war which is to take place between the Gym. team andthe Tinotball team, I would advise those who indulge in that undesirable practice of betting, to follow Punch's advice, and "Don't." Any- how, in case they do not respect this well-intentioned counsel let them chose the lesser evil,. and "pot it on" the Gym. team. These sinewy young men have been rather surprising the "men ()Heather," during the week.

It is well therefore to take advantage of any that offers itself.. The skaters, had a glo- rious time of it during the latter part of last week and until Monday in this .‘,.,,eek. Ei.2er7r, available pit was covered with a batch of skaters.. Even the canals were not left free. The London and ilbrth Western. railway, however, declined to allow the Sankey canal to freeze hard enough for skating, for they kept the ice boat busy and promptly cracked up the ice as soon as it 2ormed.

There is now no traffic on the Old (luny Canal at. Walton Arches, so that here the skater could L-ajoy him- self to hits heart's content. On Monday, the-ice was in splendid condition and in the afternoon a large number of men, women, Szc., including a•onw„.testeil, its bearing power. The ice was very thick in the'tnidille but trea- cherous at the side, and as a result, three indi4-icluals felt the water underneath, though fortunately with no ser- ious consequences. One of those who "-went through " was the cow. To skaters the ice was eracell3nt especially about a mile or two past Walton Arches, where tbere was no snow whatever upon ii ;it looked Ehzs a sheet of glass.

At the Longford Meadows on Saturday and Sunda.y,a great number of skaters were seen indulging:in the only other exercise besides dancing, which. possesses " the poetry of motion." Singular to say, the maj-Ority of them were attired in the very latest skating costumes,and the result was decidedly pleasing. THE NEW ROAD TO ITALTON.

During the last few weeks considerable progres,has been made in the making of the in9w road acres the river,which is to connect River-road, and to be the high- way from Warrington to Walton,and surroundint, town- ships. A jetty ha i been constructed across the river* where the road is to cross it, and during the week a mass ! of rock and earth has been tipped into th river. Train.. load after train load has been discharged into the stream until now the beak has become high enough to stop the flow of water, azid thus forms a terminus to the wiad- ing stretch of river at Wilderspool. The dredging of the river diversion at this point is now almost completed.

div.head: DEMOASTRATION OF UNEMPLOYED.
div.p: DEMOASTRATION OF UNEMPLOYED.

A deputation representing about 700 of the unem- ployed waited on the manager of the Ship Canal at Manchester on 'Thursday to protest against the employ- ment of dock labourers from a distance to the exclusion of the Salforti unemplo3ect They were informed that the company had been compelled to employ skilled labour, and as many local men as possible had been taken on. The men afterwards held a meeting, at which the reply was denounced as unsatisfactory. A procession of about I,oofd afterwards marched tt. the Salford Town Hall, where a deputation waited upon the Mayer, who promised that he would use his influence with his co-directors on the Ship Canal Board to employ as much local labour as possible. Perfect order was maintained at all the meetings, and the men finally dis- persed quietly.. On Thursday morning there were eight or nine vessels loading in the docks.

30,699 (4th January, 1894.) Investing Rural Sanitary Authority with Urban Powers:: Determining" Special Expanses." RUNCORN UNION. Contributory Place of Frodsham Township. Folicq-'1,10.10;a. - • • rrO THE GUARDIANS OF THE POOR of the 1 RUNCORN UNION, in the county of Chester, being the sanitary Authority for the Rural Sanitary District of that Union And to all others whom it may concern. WHEREAS by certain Orders dated the 22nd day of October, 1881, and the 10th day of October, 1893, issued in pursuance of the Public Health Act, 1875. We the Local Government Board, invested the Guardians of the Poor of the said Runcorn Union, as such Sanitary Authority as afore- said, w:th certaTn of the powers, rights, duties, capacities, liabilities, and obligations of an Urban Sanitary Authority as regards certain portions of their district, includ- ing the Contributory Place of Frodsham Town hip ; And Whereas, We have received and duly considered an application on .er Section 276 of the said Public Health Act, 1875, from the said Sanitary Authority to put in force within the said Contri. utory Place of Frodsham Township certain provisittas of such Act as hereinafter mentioned : NOW THEREFORE, in pursuance of the powers given to US by the Statutes in that behalf, We hereby declare and , Order as follows : ARTICLE I.—Until we by Order otherwise direct the provi- sions of the first paragraph of Section 161 and the provisions of Section 163 of the said Public Health Act. 1875, shall be in force within the sid Contributory Place of Frodsham Town- ship. and the said Sanitary Authority shall be invested with all the powers, rights duties, capacities, liabilities, and obli gations of an Urban Sanitary Authmity,under such provisions witl,in the said Contributory Place. ARTICLE ll.—The expenses incurred or payable by the said Sanitary Authority in the execution of the powers con- ferred upon them by Article I. of this order. except so far as such expenses may relate to the Establishment and Officers of the said Sanitary Authority, shall be deemed to be "Special Expenses" within the meaning of the said Public Health Act. 1875, and shall be charged as such upon the said Contributory Place of Frodsham Towhship. ARTICLE lll.—This Order shall come into operation on the Fifth day of February, One Thousand Eight Hundred and Ninety-four, and the said Sanitary Authority shall cause it to be published once in some newspaper circulated within their District before that date. Given under the Seil of Office of the Local Government Board this Fourth day of January, hi the year One Thousand Eight Hundred and Ninety-four. HENRY H. FOWLER, President, S. R. PROVIS, Assistant Secretary.
